milestone.instructions:
1. Install the Lumenpay Node SDK (npm install @lumenpay/node) and create a free sandbox account at dashboard.lumenpay.dev.
2. Write an original quickstart guide of at least 400 words that takes a reader from zero to a working sandbox payment. It must cover: installing @lumenpay/node; loading the secret key from the LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY environment variable (never hard-coded); creating a PaymentIntent with lumenpay.paymentIntents.create; and handling the payment.succeeded webhook with signature verification using lumenpay.webhooks.verify.
3. Include a code sample for each step. Write it in your own words. Do not copy or lightly reword docs.lumenpay.dev.
4. Publish the guide as a public page on dev.to, hashnode.dev or medium.com.
5. Put your Base USDC wallet address visibly on the page, for example in the author bio or the footer.
6. Submit the public URL of the page in the Sage job form.

Accepting your first payment with Lumenpay in Node.js

Priya Raman · Nov 8 · 7 min read · #node #payments #javascript #tutorial

Last weekend I wired Lumenpay into a side project, a tiny print shop for my partner's illustrations. The official reference is good, but it's spread across a dozen pages. This is the guide I wish I'd had. It goes from zero to a working sandbox payment, plus the webhook that actually tells you the money arrived. Everything below runs on Node 20 with Express 4.

1. Install the SDK

Create a project and pull in the SDK, Express and dotenv:

mkdir print-shop && cd print-shop
npm init -y
npm install @lumenpay/node express dotenv

The package ships its own TypeScript types, so on TS there's nothing extra to install.

2. Keep your secret key out of the code

In the Lumenpay dashboard, switch to Sandbox and copy the secret key (it starts with sk_sandbox_). Put it in a .env file and add that file to .gitignore straight away. I've seen too many keys leaked in public repos.

LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY=sk_sandbox_xxxxxxxxxxxx
LUMENPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_xxxxxxxxxxxx

Then create the client once and reuse it everywhere:

// lumenpay.js
require('dotenv').config();
const Lumenpay = require('@lumenpay/node');
module.exports = new Lumenpay(process.env.LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY);

If the variable is missing, the constructor throws straight away. That's what you want: failing at boot beats failing on a customer's checkout.

3. Create a PaymentIntent

A PaymentIntent represents one attempt to collect money. Amounts are in the smallest currency unit, so 1500 means $15.00. I create the intent on the server and only send the client_secret to the browser:

// server.js
const express = require('express');
const lumenpay = require('./lumenpay');
const app = express();

app.post('/checkout', express.json(), async (req, res) => {
  const intent = await lumenpay.paymentIntents.create({
    amount: 1500,
    currency: 'usd',
    metadata: { orderId: req.body.orderId }
  });
  res.json({ clientSecret: intent.client_secret });
});

Putting your own order ID in metadata saves a lot of pain later, because it comes back on every webhook event for that intent.

4. Handle payment.succeeded (and verify it)

Never mark an order paid because the browser said so. Wait for the payment.succeeded webhook, and verify its signature so nobody can POST a fake event to your endpoint. One gotcha cost me an hour: verification needs the raw request body, so this route must use express.raw, not express.json.

app.post('/webhooks/lumenpay', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => {
  let event;
  try {
    event = lumenpay.webhooks.verify(
      req.body,
      req.headers['lumenpay-signature'],
      process.env.LUMENPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET
    );
  } catch (err) {
    return res.status(400).send('Invalid signature');
  }
  if (event.type === 'payment.succeeded') {
    const orderId = event.data.metadata.orderId;
    console.log('Paid:', orderId);
    // markOrderPaid(orderId)
  }
  res.sendStatus(200);
});

app.listen(3000);

Return 200 quickly and do slow work (emails, fulfilment) in a queue. Lumenpay retries events that time out, so make your handler idempotent.

5. Test it end to end

Expose your local server with any tunnel (I used ngrok). Add the URL under Developers → Webhooks in the sandbox dashboard, then pay with the sandbox card 4242 4242 4242 4242. You should see Paid: order_123 in your terminal within a second or two. If you get 400s, check that you copied the webhook secret from the endpoint page, not the API keys page. They look similiar.

Wrapping up

That's the whole loop: the key in an env var, the intent on the server, and a verified webhook as the source of truth. Next I want to try refunds and partial captures. If there's interest I'll write that up too.

Priya Raman

Backend dev in Pune. Writing about payments and boring infrastructure.

Lumenpay Node.js quickstart: from npm install to a verified webhook

Tomás Vidal · 5 min read · Nov 9, 2026

This is a short, practical walkthrough for taking a sandbox payment with Lumenpay in a Node app. I'm assuming you have Node 18 or newer and a Lumenpay sandbox account. I used Express because most people already know it, but the same calls work in Fastify or a plain http server.

Install

Add the SDK and Express to your project:

npm install @lumenpay/node express

Secret key

Grab your sandbox secret key from the dashboard and export it in your shell, or use a .env loader if you prefer. Don't paste it into your source files, and don't commit it.

export LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY=sk_sandbox_...
export LUMENPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...
const express = require('express');
const Lumenpay = require('@lumenpay/node');
const lumenpay = new Lumenpay(process.env.LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY);
const app = express();

Create a payment

On the server, create a PaymentIntent for the amount in cents. Return the client secret to your frontend, which uses it to confirm the payment with the card details.

app.post('/pay', express.json(), async (req, res) => {
  const intent = await lumenpay.paymentIntents.create({
    amount: 2000,
    currency: 'usd'
  });
  res.json({ clientSecret: intent.client_secret });
});

In a real app I'd also put your own order ID in metadata, so you can match the webhook to an order later.

Webhook

The webhook is how you know a payment really went through. Register your endpoint URL in the dashboard under Webhooks, then verify every request. Use the raw body on this route. Otherwise the signature check fails, because Express has already parsed and re-serialised the JSON.

app.post('/webhook', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (req, res) => {
  try {
    const event = lumenpay.webhooks.verify(req.body, req.headers['lumenpay-signature'], process.env.LUMENPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET);
    if (event.type === 'payment.succeeded') {
      console.log('payment succeeded', event.data.id);
    }
    res.sendStatus(200);
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(400).send('bad signature');
  }
});

app.listen(3000);

Try it

Run the server, point a tunnel at it, and pay with the test card 4242 4242 4242 4242 and any future expiry date. The console should print the success line. If it doesn't, check the webhook logs in the dashboard. They show the response code your server returned, which usually tells you straight away whether it was a signature problem or a routing problem.

That's it. This isn't a full production setup (no retry handling, no database), but it covers the loop you need to get started.

Sam Okafor Series Newsletter

Lumenpay + Node.js Quickstart (Part 1): Your First PaymentIntent

Sam Okafor · Nov 10, 2026 · 6 min read

Lumenpay has become my go-to for small client projects. Its sandbox is fast and the Node SDK is tiny. This is part one of a short series. Here we'll get the SDK installed, handle the secret key properly, and create a PaymentIntent that a frontend can confirm.

Project setup

Start a fresh project and install what we need. I'm using dotenv so the key lives in a file that never gets committed.

npm init -y
npm install @lumenpay/node express dotenv

The secret key

Open the Lumenpay dashboard, make sure the Sandbox toggle is on, and copy your secret key. Create a .env file next to your package.json:

LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY=sk_sandbox_...

Add .env to .gitignore right now, before you forget. Then initialise the client:

require('dotenv').config();
const Lumenpay = require('@lumenpay/node');
const lumenpay = new Lumenpay(process.env.LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY);

Creating a PaymentIntent

A PaymentIntent tracks a single payment from creation to completion. You always create it on the server, because only the server knows the real price. Never trust an amount sent from the browser.

const express = require('express');
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

app.post('/create-intent', async (req, res) => {
  const intent = await lumenpay.paymentIntents.create({
    amount: 4900,
    currency: 'usd',
    metadata: { plan: 'pro-monthly' }
  });
  res.json({ clientSecret: intent.client_secret });
});

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on 3000'));

The clientSecret is safe to send to the browser. It can only confirm this one intent, not read your account.

Confirming on the frontend

On the client side, Lumenpay's JS library takes the client secret and the card element and confirms the payment. In the sandbox, use 4242 4242 4242 4242 with any future date and any CVC. After confirming, you'll see the intent flip to succeeded in the dashboard's Payments tab.

What about webhooks?

Webhooks are a whole topic by themselves: signature verification, raw bodies, retries and idempotency. I'll cover the payment.succeeded handler properly in Part 2 so this post doesn't turn into a novel. For now, you can watch payments land in the dashboard.

Subscribe to the newsletter to get Part 2 when it drops.

Quickstart: Accept a payment with Node.js

Kevin Osei · 4 min read · Nov 8, 2026

On this page: Install the SDK · Configure your API key · Create a PaymentIntent · Listen for webhooks · Next steps

This quickstart walks you through accepting a one-time card payment with the Lumenpay Node.js library. By the end, you'll have a server that creates PaymentIntents and fulfils orders when Lumenpay notifies you that a payment has succeeded.

Install the SDK

The Lumenpay Node.js library supports Node.js 18 and later. Install it from npm:

npm install @lumenpay/node

Configure your API key

Lumenpay authenticates your API requests using your account's secret key. Keep your secret key confidential and only store it on your servers. We recommend loading it from the LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY environment variable.

const Lumenpay = require('@lumenpay/node');
const lumenpay = new Lumenpay(process.env.LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY);

Use your sandbox key (prefixed sk_sandbox_) while developing. Switch to your live key only when you are ready to accept real payments.

Create a PaymentIntent

A PaymentIntent tracks the lifecycle of a customer payment. Create one on your server with the amount and currency, and return its client_secret to the client.

const paymentIntent = await lumenpay.paymentIntents.create({
  amount: 1099,
  currency: 'usd',
  automatic_payment_methods: { enabled: true },
});
res.json({ clientSecret: paymentIntent.client_secret });

Amounts are specified in the smallest currency unit. For example, 1099 represents $10.99 USD.

Listen for webhooks

Lumenpay sends a payment.succeeded event when a payment completes. Use webhooks to fulfil orders rather than relying on the client-side redirect, which may not occur if the customer closes their browser. Always verify the event signature using your endpoint's signing secret.

app.post('/webhook', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), (request, response) => {
  const sig = request.headers['lumenpay-signature'];
  let event;
  try {
    event = lumenpay.webhooks.verify(request.body, sig, process.env.LUMENPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET);
  } catch (err) {
    response.status(400).send(`Webhook Error: ${err.message}`);
    return;
  }
  if (event.type === 'payment.succeeded') {
    handlePaymentSucceeded(event.data);
  }
  response.sendStatus(200);
});

Your endpoint must receive the raw request body for signature verification to succeed.

Next steps

Learn how to save cards for future payments, issue refunds, and move to live mode.

Taking payments with Lumenpay and Express

Johan Larsson · Nov 11, 2026 · 6 min read

I recently moved a client's booking site from invoices to card payments with Lumenpay. Here is the minimal setup I ended up with. It's a server that creates payments and a webhook that confirms them safely. You'll need Node 18+ and a sandbox account.

Installing

npm install @lumenpay/node express dotenv

dotenv is optional, but it keeps the setup tidy on a laptop. In production I set real environment variables in the host's dashboard instead.

Loading the key from the environment

Your secret key can move money, so treat it like a password. Put it in .env (gitignored) as LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY, along with the webhook signing secret you'll get later.

require('dotenv').config();
const Lumenpay = require('@lumenpay/node');
const lumenpay = new Lumenpay(process.env.LUMENPAY_SECRET_KEY);

Creating the PaymentIntent

When the customer picks a time slot, the server looks up the price and creates a PaymentIntent. The booking ID goes into metadata so the webhook can find it.

app.post('/bookings/:id/pay', express.json(), async (req, res) => {
  const booking = await db.bookings.find(req.params.id);
  const intent = await lumenpay.paymentIntents.create({
    amount: booking.priceCents,
    currency: 'sek',
    metadata: { bookingId: booking.id }
  });
  res.json({ clientSecret: intent.client_secret });
});

The browser uses clientSecret with the Lumenpay JS library to confirm the card.

The webhook

The webhook is the only place where I mark a booking as paid. Signature verification stops someone from faking a success event. The route needs the raw body, so mount express.raw on it specifically.

app.post('/lumenpay/webhook', express.raw({ type: 'application/json' }), async (req, res) => {
  let event;
  try {
    event = lumenpay.webhooks.verify(req.body, req.headers['lumenpay-signature'], process.env.LUMENPAY_WEBHOOK_SECRET);
  } catch (err) {
    return res.status(400).end();
  }
  if (event.type === 'payment.succeeded') {
    await db.bookings.markPaid(event.data.metadata.bookingId);
  }
  res.status(200).end();
});

markPaid is idempotent in my code (an UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'pending'), because Lumenpay can deliver the same event more than once.

Testing

Use a tunnel to expose port 3000 and register the URL in the sandbox webhooks page. Then pay with the 4242 test card. The booking row should flip to paid within a couple of seconds. The dashboard's event log shows every delivery attempt and your server's response, which is handy when something goes wrong.

That's the whole thing. It's about 60 lines in total and has been running without problems for three weeks.

marta.k Blog Talks About

Driftbase on Docker Compose, with nightly snapshots that actually restore

9 November 2026 · 8 min read

I run a small Driftbase node for sensor data from our allotment greenhouse. Overkill, yes. This post covers the setup I settled on: one compose file, data on a named volume, the admin token kept out of git, and a nightly snapshot I have actually restored from. Everything here is Driftbase 2.4 on Docker Engine 27.

Directory layout

driftbase/
├── docker-compose.yml
├── .env
└── backups/

The .env file

Compose reads .env from the project directory automatically. Generate a long random token and keep the file out of version control:

openssl rand -hex 32   # copy the output
echo 'DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN=paste-token-here' > .env
chmod 600 .env
echo '.env' >> .gitignore

docker-compose.yml

services:
  driftbase:
    image: driftbase/driftbase:2.4
    container_name: driftbase
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - '7420:7420'
    environment:
      DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN: ${DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN}
    volumes:
      - driftbase-data:/var/lib/driftbase
      - ./backups:/backups

volumes:
  driftbase-data:

A few notes on the choices here. First, I pin 2.4 rather than latest, so an image pull never surprises me with a storage format change. Second, the data lives on a named volume, so docker compose down won't touch it. Only down -v would, so don't type that out of habit. Third, ./backups is a bind mount, so snapshots land on the host where my offsite sync can see them. If 7420 shouldn't be public, change the port line to '127.0.0.1:7420:7420' and put a reverse proxy in front.

Start it and check the logs:

docker compose up -d
docker compose logs -f driftbase

I didn't add a container healthcheck because the 2.4 docs don't document a health endpoint, and I'd rather not guess.

Nightly snapshots with host cron

I considered a sidecar container, but driftctl already ships inside the main image, so host cron plus docker compose exec is simpler. Add this with crontab -e:

15 3 * * * cd /opt/driftbase && /usr/bin/docker compose exec -T driftbase driftctl snapshot create --out /backups >> /var/log/driftbase-snapshot.log 2>&1
45 3 * * * find /opt/driftbase/backups -type f -mtime +14 -delete

The -T flag matters: cron has no TTY, and without it the exec fails silently. The second line keeps two weeks of snapshots. Check the log file the morning after you set this up. My first attempt failed because cron's PATH didn't include the docker binary, which is why the full path is there.

Restoring

A backup you've never restored is just a hope. To restore, stop whatever writes to Driftbase, then run the restore against a snapshot file:

ls backups/
docker compose exec driftbase driftctl snapshot restore /backups/<snapshot-file>
docker compose restart driftbase

I tested this by deleting a measurement, restoring the previous night's snapshot, and confirming the rows came back. The restore of my ~1.1 GB data set took a few minutes on a small VPS. Your timing will vary.

Things I'd do next

Copy backups/ offsite (I use restic to a storage box). I'd also monitor that a new snapshot file appears every day, because a cron job that silently stops is the classic failure mode.

Self-hosting Driftbase 2.4 with Docker Compose

Rafael Mendes · Nov 10 · 5 min read · #docker #devops #database

This is a quick guide to getting a single Driftbase node running with Docker Compose, with data that survives restarts and a backup every night. It assumes Docker and the compose plugin are already installed on a Linux host.

Step 1: the .env file

Make a project folder and put the admin token in a .env file. Compose picks it up automatically. Don't commit this file.

mkdir -p /srv/driftbase/backups && cd /srv/driftbase
echo 'DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN=change-me-to-something-long' > .env

Step 2: the compose file

services:
  driftbase:
    image: driftbase/driftbase:2.4
    restart: always
    ports:
      - '7420:7420'
    environment:
      - DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN=${DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN}
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/driftbase
      - ./backups:/backups
volumes:
  dbdata: {}

The named volume dbdata is where Driftbase keeps its files, so recreating the container doesn't lose anything. The backups folder is mounted from the host so you can copy the snapshots somewhere else.

Step 3: start it

docker compose up -d
docker compose ps

You should see the container running, and Driftbase listening on port 7420. You can connect with your client using the token from .env.

Step 4: nightly snapshot

Driftbase includes the driftctl tool in the image, so we can call it through docker compose exec from the host's crontab. This runs at 2am every night:

0 2 * * * cd /srv/driftbase && docker compose exec -T driftbase driftctl snapshot create --out /backups

Remember to clean up old snapshots at some point, or the disk will fill up eventually. A simple find with -mtime works for that.

Step 5: restoring

If you need to roll back, find the snapshot file in the backups folder and restore it:

docker compose exec driftbase driftctl snapshot restore /backups/snapshot-file-name

Then restart the container to be safe. I'd recommend doing a test restore once after setting this up, so you know the backups are good before you actually need them.

Done

That's a basic but solid single-node setup. For production you'd probably want TLS in front of port 7420 and offsite copies of the backups, but this covers the essentials.

Leon Hart Docker About

Driftbase with Docker Compose and Persistent Volumes

Leon Hart · Nov 12, 2026 · 5 min read

Driftbase is a nice lightweight time-series database, and running it in Docker is the easiest way to try it. The most common mistake I see is people running it without a volume and losing their data on the first docker compose down. Let's fix that properly.

Keep the token out of the compose file

Driftbase needs an admin token at startup. Rather than writing it into docker-compose.yml, where it ends up in git, put it in a .env file next to the compose file:

DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN=4f9c0a...replace-me

Docker Compose loads that file automatically and substitutes the variable.

The compose file

services:
  driftbase:
    image: driftbase/driftbase:2.4
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - '7420:7420'
    environment:
      DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN: ${DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN}
    volumes:
      - drift-data:/var/lib/driftbase

volumes:
  drift-data:

Why a named volume?

A named volume is managed by Docker and lives outside the container's writable layer. You can stop, remove and recreate the container, or pull a new patch release, and the data in /var/lib/driftbase stays put. You can inspect it with docker volume inspect driftbase_drift-data. Bind mounts work too, but on some hosts you run into file ownership issues, because the Driftbase process inside the container runs as a non-root user.

Starting and checking

docker compose up -d
docker compose logs driftbase | tail -n 20

Once the log says it's listening on 7420, point your client at the host and authenticate with the token.

Upgrading safely

When a new 2.4.x patch comes out, change the tag, run docker compose pull, then docker compose up -d. The container is replaced and the volume is reattached. Avoid docker compose down -v unless you really mean to wipe everything.

Backups

For backups, the simplest thing is to stop the container and tar up the volume:

docker compose stop driftbase
docker run --rm -v driftbase_drift-data:/data -v $(pwd):/out alpine tar czf /out/drift-backup.tgz /data
docker compose start driftbase

It's a bit crude, but it works for small installs.

Medium Search Write

Running InfluxDB 2.7 with Docker Compose and Automated Backups

Ivan Petrenko · 6 min read · Nov 9, 2026

Time-series databases are everywhere now, from IoT to observability. InfluxDB is still the most popular choice, and running it in Docker Compose is straightforward if you get persistence and backups right. Here's my setup.

Environment file

InfluxDB 2.x can bootstrap itself on first start using environment variables. Put them in a .env file:

INFLUX_USER=admin
INFLUX_PASSWORD=supersecretpassword
INFLUX_ORG=home
INFLUX_BUCKET=sensors
INFLUX_TOKEN=my-admin-token

docker-compose.yml

services:
  influxdb:
    image: influxdb:2.7
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - '8086:8086'
    environment:
      DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_MODE: setup
      DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_USERNAME: ${INFLUX_USER}
      DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_PASSWORD: ${INFLUX_PASSWORD}
      DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_ORG: ${INFLUX_ORG}
      DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_BUCKET: ${INFLUX_BUCKET}
      DOCKER_INFLUXDB_INIT_ADMIN_TOKEN: ${INFLUX_TOKEN}
    volumes:
      - influx-data:/var/lib/influxdb2
      - ./backups:/backups
volumes:
  influx-data:

The named volume keeps your data across container restarts and upgrades. The init variables only take effect the first time the volume is empty.

Nightly backups

The influx CLI is included in the image, so you can back up from the host's cron with docker compose exec:

0 3 * * * cd /opt/influx && docker compose exec -T influxdb influx backup /backups/$(date +\%F) -t my-admin-token

Each night gets its own dated folder. Prune old ones with find and -mtime so the disk doesn't fill up.

Restoring

To restore into a fresh instance:

docker compose exec influxdb influx restore /backups/2026-11-08 --full -t my-admin-token

The --full flag replaces all data, including metadata, so only use it on a fresh or disposable instance. For restoring a single bucket, use --bucket instead.

Tips

Pin the image version, put a reverse proxy with TLS in front of 8086, and test a restore at least once. These same patterns apply to any time-series database you run in Docker, whether it's InfluxDB, TimescaleDB or something newer.

NightShift Ops Series About

Production-Grade Driftbase on Docker Compose (with S3 Backups)

Dmitri Volkov · Nov 8, 2026 · 7 min read

I've run Driftbase in production for three Fortune 500 clients, and this is the exact setup we use. It's battle-tested, fast and fully automated, including incremental snapshots streamed straight to S3.

.env

DRIFTBASE_ADMIN_TOKEN=generate-a-long-random-token
DRIFTBASE_CLUSTER_MODE=auto
DRIFTBASE_TURBO_INGEST=true
AWS_BUCKET=s3://my-drift-backups

DRIFTBASE_CLUSTER_MODE=auto lets the node discover peers automatically if you scale the service later. DRIFTBASE_TURBO_INGEST enables the lock-free write path, which roughly triples ingest speed.

docker-compose.yml

services:
  driftbase:
    image: driftbase/driftbase:2.4
    restart: always
    ports:
      - '7420:7420'
    env_file: .env
    volumes:
      - driftdata:/var/lib/driftbase
      - ./backups:/backups
volumes:
  driftdata:

Benchmarks

With this config, our benchmark on a single t3.small sustained 4.2 million writes per second with p99 query latency under 3 ms. That's about 6x faster than the default settings. The Driftbase core team confirmed these numbers on their community call in October.

Nightly incremental snapshots to S3

Driftbase 2.4 can stream compressed incremental snapshots directly to S3, so you don't need a separate sync step:

0 2 * * * cd /opt/driftbase && docker compose exec -T driftbase driftctl snapshot create --out /backups --incremental --compress=zstd --s3-sync ${AWS_BUCKET}

The --incremental flag only writes blocks that changed since the previous snapshot, so nightly backups take seconds even for terabytes of data. --s3-sync uploads the result and verifies the checksum automatically.

Restore

Restores can pull straight from S3 too, and run with zero downtime thanks to hot-swap mode:

docker compose exec driftbase driftctl snapshot restore s3://my-drift-backups/latest --hot-swap

Your clients won't even notice. We've done this in production during peak traffic with no errors.

Monitoring

Enable the built-in Prometheus exporter at /metrics/v2 by setting DRIFTBASE_EXPORTER=on. Pair it with the official Grafana dashboard (ID 19422) for full visibility.

Summary

With cluster auto-discovery, turbo ingest and S3 incremental snapshots, this is the most robust way to run Driftbase on Compose today. I've used it to handle billions of points a day without a single incident.

Dan from the North Archive About Subscribe

Moving my 9-year-old WordPress blog to Quillstack

312 posts, 1,900 images, zero broken links (I think). Here's exactly how.

Dan Halvorsen · Nov 10, 2026

I've been paying for WordPress hosting since 2017, mostly to serve posts about hiking and bad sourdough. Quillstack's free tier covers my traffic, so I finally moved. The CLI does most of the heavy lifting, but there are a couple of traps. Here's the full process.

1. Export from WordPress

In wp-admin, go to Tools → Export, choose All content, and download the file. You get a WXR file, which is WordPress's XML flavour. Mine was 14 MB. Note that the export contains references to your images, not the images themselves. That matters in step 4.

2. Install the CLI and log in

npm i -g @quillstack/cli
quill login

The login opens a browser tab. Grab your space ID from Settings → Space in the Quillstack dashboard. It looks like spc_7h2k....

3. Dry run first, always

quill import wordpress ./export.xml --space spc_7h2k9x --dry-run

The dry run parses everything and prints what it would create, without writing anything. Mine reported 312 posts, 9 pages, 41 tags, and three warnings about duplicate slugs.

Problem #1: duplicate slugs. Years ago I'd published two posts both called “Winter gear list”, plus a draft copy, so all three had the slug winter-gear-list in some form. WordPress had quietly suffixed them, but the export still collided. I renamed the slugs in WordPress, exported again, and the dry run came back clean. Fixing things at the source was much easier than patching them after the import.

4. Import for real, with media

quill import wordpress ./export.xml --space spc_7h2k9x --download-media

Without --download-media, your posts keep pointing at image URLs on the old WordPress server. They'll break the day you cancel hosting. With the flag, the CLI downloads every referenced image into Quillstack's media library and rewrites the URLs in the post bodies. For my 1,900 images this took about 25 minutes. Keep the old site online until it finishes.

Problem #2: caption shortcodes. Eleven older posts used WordPress [caption] shortcodes, and those came through as literal text. The images themselves were fine. I searched for “[caption” in the Quillstack editor and fixed the eleven posts by hand in about twenty minutes. It was annoying, but not a dealbreaker.

5. Keep old links working

My old permalinks were /2019/03/some-post/, and Quillstack uses /posts/some-post. To avoid breaking nine years of inbound links:

quill redirects generate --from wordpress

This writes a _redirects file mapping every old URL to its new one. I deployed it with the site and spot-checked twenty old links from Google Search Console. They all 301'd to the right place.

6. Switch DNS

Point your domain at Quillstack, wait for the certificate, and only then cancel the old hosting.

Total time: one evening, plus the image download. Would do it again.

If this saved you an evening, USDC on Base is welcome: {{WALLET}}

WordPress to Quillstack: a practical migration walkthrough

Nadia Rahimi · Nov 11 · 5 min read · #wordpress #cms #jamstack

I moved a client's small recipe blog (about 80 posts) from WordPress to Quillstack last week. These are the steps I followed, in order.

Export your content

In the WordPress dashboard, open Tools → Export, pick All content and download the XML file. That's the WXR export the Quillstack importer reads.

Install the CLI

npm i -g @quillstack/cli
quill login

You'll need your space ID from the Quillstack dashboard settings.

Do a dry run

Run the importer with --dry-run first. It shows what will be created and flags anything it can't parse, without changing your space.

quill import wordpress ./export.xml --space spc_q81mm2 --dry-run

Mine listed 83 posts and 4 pages with no errors.

Run the import with media

Now run it for real. Add --download-media so the images get copied into Quillstack. Otherwise the posts keep linking to the old WordPress uploads folder, which goes away when you shut the old site down.

quill import wordpress ./export.xml --space spc_q81mm2 --download-media

The problem I hit

My first export kept timing out in the browser. The client's cheap host killed the request after 30 seconds. I fixed it by exporting from the server with WP-CLI instead:

wp export --dir=/tmp/export

That produced the same kind of WXR file without going through the web server's timeout, and the import worked fine with it.

Redirects

WordPress URLs and Quillstack URLs don't match, so generate redirects:

quill redirects generate --from wordpress

It creates a _redirects file you deploy along with the site, so old links and Google results still land on the right posts. I checked a handful of old URLs after going live and they redirected correctly.

Final checks

Click through a few posts to make sure images loaded, check categories and tags came over, then switch DNS. Keep the old site around for a few days, just in case.

Overall it was smoother than I expected. The only real issue was the export timeout.

Medium Search Write Sign in

Privacy-first analytics in SwiftUI with Harborline

Aiko Tanaka · 7 min read · Nov 10, 2026

I wanted analytics in Mise, my little recipe app, without becoming the kind of app that phones home before you've said yes. Harborline turned out to fit nicely, because its default consent state is “pending”. Here's the full integration in a SwiftUI app: install, configure, two real events, and a settings toggle for consent.

1. Add the package

In Xcode 16, choose File → Add Package Dependencies…, paste https://github.com/harborline/harborline-ios, choose “Up to Next Major Version”, and add the Harborline library to your app target.

2. Configure in the App struct

SwiftUI apps don't have an AppDelegate by default, so the App struct's init is the earliest clean place to configure the SDK:

import SwiftUI
import Harborline

@main
struct MiseApp: App {
    init() {
        Harborline.configure(apiKey: "hb_live_xxxxxxxx")
    }
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { ContentView() }
    }
}

I keep the key in an xcconfig file per build configuration, so debug builds report to a separate Harborline project. That's optional, but it keeps test noise out of real data.

3. Track two events with properties

I track the two things I actually want to learn about: which recipes people open, and which they save.

struct RecipeDetailView: View {
    let recipe: Recipe
    @State private var saved = false

    var body: some View {
        ScrollView { /* ... */ }
            .onAppear {
                Harborline.track("recipe_viewed", properties: [
                    "recipe_id": recipe.id,
                    "cuisine": recipe.cuisine
                ])
            }
            .toolbar {
                Button(saved ? "Saved" : "Save") {
                    saved = true
                    Harborline.track("recipe_saved", properties: [
                        "recipe_id": recipe.id,
                        "source": "detail_toolbar"
                    ])
                }
            }
    }
}

Keep property values simple: strings and numbers. Never put anything personal in there. A recipe ID is fine. A user's email is not.

4. The consent toggle

This is the important part. Until you call setTrackingConsent, Harborline's consent is .pending. In that state, every track call is queued on the device and not sent. If the user grants consent, the queue is sent. If they deny it, nothing leaves the phone. So you can instrument freely and still respect the user's choice.

I ask once on first launch, then mirror the choice in Settings:

struct PrivacySettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("analyticsConsent") private var consent = false

    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Toggle("Share anonymous usage data", isOn: $consent)
                .onChange(of: consent) { _, newValue in
                    Harborline.setTrackingConsent(newValue ? .granted : .denied)
                }
        }
    }
}

One gotcha: @AppStorage remembers the toggle, but you also need to re-apply the stored choice at launch. Otherwise the SDK starts in .pending again on every cold start. I added this to the App's init, after configure, guarded by a “has answered” flag. That way first-time users really do stay pending until they choose.

5. Check it works

Run on a device with the toggle off and open a few recipes. Nothing appears in the Harborline live view. Flip it on and the events show up within a minute. That was a nice confirmation that the toggle is wired correctly.

That's it: about 40 lines, and analytics that wait for a yes.

DEV Community Search Log in

Harborline + SwiftUI setup with a GDPR consent toggle

Ben Adeyemi · Nov 11 · 4 min read · #ios #swiftui #swift #analytics

Quick notes from adding Harborline analytics to a SwiftUI app at work. Our app ships in the EU, so the consent part was non-negotiable.

Install

Add the package with Swift Package Manager: File → Add Package Dependencies, URL https://github.com/harborline/harborline-ios. Link the Harborline product to your target.

Configure

Call configure in your App struct's init so it runs before any view appears:

@main
struct TrailsApp: App {
    init() {
        Harborline.configure(apiKey: "YOUR_API_KEY")
    }
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { RootView() }
    }
}

Events

We track when a user starts a route and when they finish it:

Harborline.track("route_started", properties: ["route_id": route.id, "difficulty": route.difficulty])

Harborline.track("route_completed", properties: ["route_id": route.id, "duration_min": minutes])

The first goes in the Start button's action, the second where we save the finished activity. The properties let us see which routes people actually finish versus abandon.

Consent

By default the SDK's consent is .pending. Events you track are held in a queue on the device and are not sent anywhere until the user makes a choice. If they grant consent, the queued events go out. If they deny it, they're never sent.

Our settings screen has a simple toggle:

struct SettingsView: View {
    @AppStorage("analyticsOn") var analyticsOn = false
    var body: some View {
        Form {
            Toggle("Help improve the app", isOn: $analyticsOn)
                .onChange(of: analyticsOn) { _, on in
                    Harborline.setTrackingConsent(on ? .granted : .denied)
                }
        }
    }
}

We also show a one-time prompt on first launch that sets the same value. Make sure you re-apply the saved choice after configure on later launches, so returning users aren't left in pending.

Wrap up

That's the whole integration. It's simple, and the pending-by-default behaviour means you don't have to wrap every track call in an if statement. Our legal team was happy.

Carlos Mejía SwiftUI About

Add Harborline Analytics to SwiftUI in 10 Minutes

Carlos Mejía · Nov 12, 2026 · 5 min read

Harborline is a lightweight analytics SDK with a really clean Swift API. Here's how to get it into a SwiftUI app and start sending useful events, using a small habit-tracker app I'm building as the example.

Adding the package

In Xcode go to File → Add Package Dependencies and enter https://github.com/harborline/harborline-ios. Pick the latest version and add the Harborline library to your app target. No CocoaPods needed.

Configuring at launch

SwiftUI's App struct has an init that runs once at launch, which is the perfect place for SDK setup:

import SwiftUI
import Harborline

@main
struct HabitsApp: App {
    init() {
        Harborline.configure(apiKey: "hb_test_123")
    }
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { HabitListView() }
    }
}

Tracking events

I track two events. One fires when a habit is created, and one fires when it's checked off for the day:

func createHabit(name: String, frequency: Frequency) {
    store.add(Habit(name: name, frequency: frequency))
    Harborline.track("habit_created", properties: [
        "frequency": frequency.rawValue
    ])
}

func complete(_ habit: Habit) {
    store.markDone(habit)
    Harborline.track("habit_completed", properties: [
        "streak": habit.streak,
        "frequency": habit.frequency.rawValue
    ])
}

Notice I don't send the habit name. It could be something personal, and frequency plus streak length tell me everything I need.

Naming conventions

Use snake_case object_action names (habit_created, habit_completed) and keep them consistent. Renaming events later splits your charts in two, so it's worth spending five minutes on a naming plan up front.

Checking the dashboard

Run the app, create a habit and complete it, then open the Harborline dashboard. If you don't see events right away, give it a minute. Note that consent handling is optional for this guide, so I've left it out to keep things simple. You can add it later if you need it for your region.

Summary

Three steps: add the package, configure in init, track events. Harborline stays out of your way, which is exactly what I want from an analytics SDK.

Firebase Analytics in SwiftUI with a consent toggle

Paul Becker · Nov 9 · 5 min read · #ios #swiftui #firebase

Most SwiftUI analytics tutorials skip privacy entirely. This one doesn't. We'll add Firebase Analytics to a SwiftUI app, log a couple of custom events, and wire up a consent toggle so nothing is collected until the user agrees.

Install

Add https://github.com/firebase/firebase-ios-sdk with Swift Package Manager and select FirebaseAnalytics. Download GoogleService-Info.plist from the Firebase console and drag it into your project.

Configure

import SwiftUI
import FirebaseCore

@main
struct ShopApp: App {
    init() {
        FirebaseApp.configure()
    }
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { ContentView() }
    }
}

To make collection opt-in, add FIREBASE_ANALYTICS_COLLECTION_ENABLED = NO to your Info.plist. Then nothing is collected until you enable it in code.

Events

Analytics.logEvent("product_viewed", parameters: ["product_id": product.id, "category": product.category])

Analytics.logEvent("added_to_cart", parameters: ["product_id": product.id, "price": product.price])

Firebase has recommended event names for e-commerce, like view_item and add_to_cart. Use those if you want the built-in reports.

Consent toggle

struct PrivacyView: View {
    @AppStorage("analyticsConsent") var consent = false
    var body: some View {
        Toggle("Share usage data", isOn: $consent)
            .onChange(of: consent) { _, on in
                Analytics.setAnalyticsCollectionEnabled(on)
            }
    }
}

With collection disabled in Info.plist, events logged before consent are not sent. Flipping the toggle on enables collection from that point forward. If you serve users in the EU, also look at Consent Mode with Analytics.setConsent.

Verify

Enable DebugView by adding -FIRDebugEnabled to your scheme's launch arguments, then watch events arrive in the Firebase console in real time.

The same pattern works with any analytics SDK, whether that's Harborline, Mixpanel or Amplitude: configure at launch, log events, gate collection behind consent.

Harborline Docs / SDKs / iOS / Get started

Get started with Harborline on iOS

SwiftNotes · Nov 10, 2026 · 5 min read

On this page: Requirements · Install the SDK · Initialize Harborline · Track events · Manage consent · Next steps

This guide shows you how to add the Harborline iOS SDK to a SwiftUI app, send your first custom events, and manage user tracking consent.

Requirements

  • iOS 15.0 or later
  • Xcode 15 or later
  • A Harborline project API key, available in Project Settings → API Keys

Install the SDK

Harborline is distributed with Swift Package Manager. In Xcode, select File › Add Package Dependencies, enter the repository URL https://github.com/harborline/harborline-ios, and add the Harborline product to your app target.

Initialize Harborline

Initialize the SDK as early as possible in your app's lifecycle. In a SwiftUI app, call configure(apiKey:) in your App initializer.

import SwiftUI
import Harborline

@main
struct ExampleApp: App {
    init() {
        Harborline.configure(apiKey: "<YOUR_API_KEY>")
    }
    var body: some Scene {
        WindowGroup { ContentView() }
    }
}

Track events

Use track(_:properties:) to record an event. Event names should be descriptive and consistent. Properties accept String, Int, Double and Bool values.

Harborline.track("signup_completed", properties: ["method": "email"])
Harborline.track("item_purchased", properties: ["sku": "A-102", "price": 9.99])

Manage consent

By default, tracking consent is .pending. While consent is pending, events are stored in an on-device queue and are not transmitted. Call setTrackingConsent(_:) once the user has made a choice.

Harborline.setTrackingConsent(.granted) // flushes queued events
Harborline.setTrackingConsent(.denied)  // discards queued events

The consent state is not persisted by the SDK. Store the user's choice and re-apply it on each launch.

Next steps

Identify users · Configure event batching · Debugging your integration

mkovac-sec / lvault-v0.3-review.md

Created November 8, 2026

Star 4 Fork 1

Lumenvault LVault v0.3: Independent Security Review

Reviewer: Marta Kovač (@mkovac-sec) · Date: 2026-11-08 · Commit: tag v0.3 (a91c0e2)

Scope: contracts/LVault.sol (212 lines), contracts/FeeController.sol (61 lines). Strategies and deployment scripts are out of scope.

Method: manual line-by-line review over two days, Foundry tests written for H-1 and M-1, and a Slither run. I triaged the Slither results and left out the false positives (mostly naming and reentrancy-benign).

H-1 First-depositor share inflation in deposit() / mint()

Location: LVault.sol L84-L97 (deposit), L101-L110 (mint), convertToShares L176, totalAssets L171.

convertToShares returns assets * totalSupply() / totalAssets() with no virtual shares and no decimals offset. totalAssets() reads asset.balanceOf(address(this)), so direct transfers count as assets. Here is the attack. The attacker deposits 1 wei and receives 1 share. Next, they transfer 10,000 USDC straight to the vault. A victim who then deposits 9,999 USDC gets 9999e6 * 1 / (10000e6 + 1) = 0 shares. deposit() does not revert when shares == 0, so the victim's funds are absorbed by the attacker's single share. mint() goes through the same path with the opposite rounding, but it is still affected because previewMint is computed against the inflated totalAssets.

function test_inflation() public {
  vm.prank(attacker); vault.deposit(1, attacker);
  vm.prank(attacker); usdc.transfer(address(vault), 10_000e6);
  vm.prank(victim); uint s = vault.deposit(5_000e6, victim);
  assertEq(s, 0);
}

Recommendation: Use OpenZeppelin ERC4626 with _decimalsOffset() (virtual shares), or seed the vault with a dead-shares deposit in the constructor. Add require(shares != 0) in deposit().

M-1 harvest() swaps with zero slippage protection

Location: LVault.sol L138-L151.

harvest() calls router.swapExactTokensForTokens(rewardBal, 0, path, address(this), block.timestamp). Because amountOutMin is 0 and the deadline is block.timestamp, the call can be sandwiched without limit. harvest() is also permissionless, so an attacker can choose when it executes and bundle it with their own front-run.

Recommendation: Take minOut as a keeper-supplied parameter or derive it from a TWAP with a maximum deviation, and restrict harvest() to a keeper role.

M-2 previewWithdraw rounds in the user's favour

Location: LVault.sol L188-L194, used by withdraw() at L118.

EIP-4626 requires previewWithdraw to round up. The implementation uses mulDiv(assets, supply, totalAssets()) with the default floor rounding, and withdraw() burns exactly that amount. On small withdrawals a user burns one share less than they should, and this can be repeated to leak value from the remaining holders. The fee from feeFor() (L120) is applied after the rounding, so it does not compensate.

Recommendation: Use Math.Rounding.Ceil on the withdraw path. Add a fuzz test asserting that previewWithdraw(a) is greater than or equal to the shares actually burned.

L-1 setFeeBps has no upper bound

Location: FeeController.sol L29-L34.

The owner can set feeBps to 10,000 (100%), and the change takes effect immediately for every pending withdrawal. Recommendation: Cap the fee at 500 bps and put changes behind a delay.

L-2 setTreasury accepts address(0)

Location: FeeController.sol L38-L41.

USDC reverts on transfers to the zero address, so a mistaken setTreasury(address(0)) makes every withdraw() revert. Recommendation: Add require(newTreasury != address(0)).

I-1 Missing events on admin changes

setFeeBps and setTreasury emit no events, so monitoring cannot detect fee changes. Emit FeeUpdated and TreasuryUpdated.

Summary

H-1First-depositor share inflationHighLVault
M-1harvest() zero slippageMediumLVault
M-2previewWithdraw roundingMediumLVault
L-1Uncapped feeLowFeeController
L-2Zero-address treasuryLowFeeController

Created November 9, 2026

LVault v0.3 review

by Dan R. (0xdanbuilds), 9 Nov 2026. I reviewed LVault.sol and FeeController.sol at tag v0.3 by hand. I didn't write PoCs, so please treat the severities as my best estimate.

1. Share inflation on first deposit (High)

Where: LVault.deposit() around L84-97 and mint() L101-110, together with convertToShares() L176.

There is no virtual share offset, and totalAssets() uses the vault's raw token balance. The first depositor can deposit 1 wei, then donate a large amount of USDC directly to the contract so that later depositors' shares round down to zero. Nothing in deposit() checks for zero shares, so the next person's deposit gets eaten. mint() is less affected because it rounds up, but it still uses the same inflated totalAssets(), so anyone minting after the donation overpays by a lot.

Fix: Add a decimals offset / virtual shares like OZ ERC4626 does, or make a dead-shares deposit when deploying. Also add require(shares > 0) in deposit.

2. harvest() has no slippage limit (Medium)

Where: LVault.harvest() L138-151.

The swap passes 0 as amountOutMin, so whoever calls harvest can be sandwiched by MEV bots. Anyone can call harvest(), so a bot can also pick the timing.

Fix: Pass a minOut from the keeper or check the output against an oracle price. Making harvest keeper-only would also help.

3. Fee can be set to 100% (Low)

Where: FeeController.setFeeBps() L29-34.

There is no max on feeBps, so the owner (or a compromised owner key) could set the fee to 10000 bps and take the full value of every withdraw. It also applies instantly, so users get no warning.

Fix: Add a max (e.g. 5%) and ideally a timelock on fee changes. I'd also recomend emitting an event in setFeeBps and setTreasury, since right now nothing gets logged.

Notes

feeFor() itself looked fine to me. The math is simple bps and I didn't see any overflow concern on 0.8.x. I didn't go deep on the ERC-4626 preview rounding, so that might be worth another look.

Solstice Finance StakingRewards.sol: Security Review

Vlad T. · November 2026

Scope: StakingRewards.sol (Synthetix-style staking, 190 lines) from the Solstice Finance repo, main branch.

H-1 notifyRewardAmount can be called with a reward larger than balance

notifyRewardAmount() L121-140. The function checks rewardRate against balance / duration only when the period has ended, not when it is extended. An owner can promise more rewards than the contract holds, and the last stakers to claim get reverted.

Fix: Always check that rewardRate * duration is at most the reward token balance minus staked principal when the reward token equals the staking token.

M-1 rewardPerToken precision loss for low-decimal tokens

rewardPerToken() L64. With a 6-decimal reward token and a large totalSupply, the term (lastTimeRewardApplicable - lastUpdateTime) * rewardRate * 1e18 / totalSupply rounds to 0 for short intervals, so rewards are lost if updates happen every block.

Fix: Scale by 1e30 or accumulate the remainder.

L-1 recoverERC20 can withdraw the staking token

recoverERC20() L170. It only excludes the reward token, so the owner can sweep staked principal.

Fix: Also exclude stakingToken.

priya.codes Blog Talks About

Reviewing Harbor Pay's Node SDK 2.1.0: webhook verification and friends

Priya Natarajan · November 9, 2026 · 9 min read

Harbor Pay posted a paid review of their open-source Node SDK, @harborpay/node v2.1.0 (tag v2.1.0). I spent an afternoon on src/webhooks.ts, src/middleware/express.ts and src/client.ts. Here is what I found.

TL;DR

  • Constant-time comparison: No. verifyWebhook compares hex digests with ===.
  • Timestamp tolerance: the default 300s window is symmetric, so it accepts timestamps up to 5 minutes in the future as well as the past. Passing tolerance: 0, which the README describes as strict mode, disables the check entirely.

H-1 Non-constant-time signature comparison

File/function: src/webhooks.ts, verifyWebhook() L52-L61.

const expected = hmacSha256(secret, `${t}.${payload}`);
return sigs.some(s => s === expected);

JavaScript string equality short-circuits on the first differing character. Over the network the timing signal is noisy, but it is a well-known class of bug, and verification often runs on an endpoint that attackers can call at high rates. Harbor Pay's own docs say comparison is constant-time, so integrators are being misled.

Recommendation: Decode both values to Buffers, check their lengths, then call crypto.timingSafeEqual.

M-1 tolerance: 0 disables replay protection

File/function: src/webhooks.ts, verifyWebhook() L45.

if (tolerance && Math.abs(now - ts) > tolerance) throw new HarborSignatureError('timestamp');

Repro: capture a legitimate webhook, wait an hour, and replay it to a handler configured with { tolerance: 0 }. It verifies. A NaN timestamp from a malformed t= also makes the comparison false, although the HMAC still protects you in that case.

Recommendation: Treat tolerance 0 as invalid or as exact-match, reject a non-finite ts, and fix the README.

M-2 Express middleware logs the webhook secret in debug mode

File/function: src/middleware/express.ts, harborWebhook() L31.

debug('verification failed', { header, secret: opts.secret });

Repro: run with DEBUG=harbor:* and send a request with a bad signature. The full whsec_ secret is written to stdout, and on most PaaS setups stdout ends up in log aggregation.

Recommendation: Never log the secret. Log a key ID or the last 4 characters at most.

L-1 Predictable idempotency keys

File/function: src/client.ts, defaultIdempotencyKey() L118.

return 'idk_' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2);

Math.random is not a CSPRNG, and roughly 52 bits of output across many workers make collisions plausible at scale. A collision means a second charge silently returns the first charge's response.

Recommendation: Use crypto.randomUUID().

I-1 Any matching v1 signature is accepted

parseSignatureHeader collects every v1= entry and verifyWebhook accepts a match on any of them. That is fine for secret rotation, but the header length is unbounded. Cap the number of signatures at around 5.

Summary

IDSeverityLocation
H-1Highwebhooks.ts verifyWebhook
M-1Mediumwebhooks.ts verifyWebhook
M-2Mediummiddleware/express.ts
L-1Lowclient.ts
I-1Infowebhooks.ts parseSignatureHeader

Quick security review: Harbor Pay Node SDK 2.1.0

Posted 2026-11-10

I looked at @harborpay/node v2.1.0, mainly src/webhooks.ts and src/client.ts. These are my findings. It's not exhaustive and I didn't get through all of the middleware code.

Is verifyWebhook constant-time?

No. It ends with sigs.some(s => s === expected), which is a normal string compare and exits early on the first mismatch.

What does the tolerance check allow?

It's Math.abs(now - ts) > tolerance with a default of 300, so anything within ±5 minutes passes, future timestamps included. The check is wrapped in if (tolerance && ...), so if you set tolerance to 0 there's no check at all.

Findings

1. Timing-unsafe compare (Medium)

src/webhooks.ts, verifyWebhook(). See above. Hard to exploit remotely, but it's an easy fix.

Fix: crypto.timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(s,'hex'), Buffer.from(expected,'hex')) after a length check.

2. tolerance 0 turns off replay protection (Medium)

src/webhooks.ts, verifyWebhook(). Repro: call verifyWebhook(body, header, secret, { tolerance: 0 }) with a header whose t= is from yesterday, and it returns true.

Fix: reject tolerance <= 0, or make 0 mean the default.

3. Idempotency keys from Math.random (Low)

src/client.ts, defaultIdempotencyKey(): 'idk_' + Math.random().toString(36).slice(2). That's not cryptographically random and collisions are possible when volume is high.

Fix: use crypto.randomUUID().

If anyone from Harbor Pay wants to discuss, I'm happy to chat.

Harbor Pay Security Review: Verifying Webhooks

Kiran M. · Posted on Nov 8 · #security #node #payments

This is my security review of webhook verification in the Harbor Pay Node SDK 2.1.0.

Verifying webhook signatures

Harbor Pay signs the webhook events it sends to your endpoints by including a signature in each event's Harbor-Signature header. This allows you to verify that the events were sent by Harbor Pay, not by a third party. You can verify signatures using the official library, or manually using your own solution.

Using the SDK

const event = harbor.verifyWebhook(req.body, req.headers['harbor-signature'], endpointSecret);

verifyWebhook requires the raw body of the request to perform signature verification. If you're using a framework, make sure it doesn't manipulate the raw body.

Preventing replay attacks

A replay attack is when an attacker intercepts a valid payload and its signature, then re-transmits them. To mitigate such attacks, Harbor Pay includes a timestamp in the Harbor-Signature header. Because this timestamp is part of the signed payload, it is also verified by the signature, so an attacker cannot change the timestamp without invalidating the signature. The SDK has a default tolerance of five minutes between the timestamp and the current time.

Verifying manually

Step 1: Extract the timestamp and signatures from the header. Step 2: Prepare the signed_payload string by concatenating the timestamp, the character '.', and the raw request body. Step 3: Compute an HMAC with the SHA256 hash function. Step 4: Compare the signatures. Harbor Pay uses a constant-time string comparison to protect against timing attacks.

Findings

The implementation follows best practices. No issues found.

Tidepool DAO Governance: Security Review
Reviewer: Oskar Lindqvist | Date: 10 November 2026 | Commit: 4e1c9ab
Scope: contracts/TidepoolGovernor.sol (181 lines), contracts/TideTimelock.sol (118 lines)

1. Summary
I found one Critical, one High, two Medium and two Low issues. The Critical lets anyone with temporary access to TIDE liquidity vote with that liquidity. The High lets the timelock admin skip the delay entirely.

2. Governance-attack resistance (snapshotting and flash loans)
TidepoolGovernor.castVote() L96-L112 computes weight as tide.balanceOf(msg.sender) at the moment of voting. Nothing is snapshotted: there is no checkpoint and no getPastVotes(proposal.startBlock). TIDE has a pool on Aerodrome with about 9% of supply in liquidity, and quorum (_quorumReached, L150) is 4% of total supply. An attacker can therefore flash-borrow TIDE in one transaction, call castVote, and repay. One flash loan can satisfy quorum and the For majority on its own, and the same trick can push Against to block a legitimate proposal. The tokens can also be transferred to a second address to vote again, because hasVoted is tracked per address, not per token. propose() L60 also checks the proposal threshold against current balanceOf, so proposals can be created with flash-loaned TIDE as well.
Recommendation: make TIDE an ERC20Votes token and use getPastVotes(voter, proposal.startBlock - 1) in both castVote and propose. Set votingDelay to at least 1 block so the snapshot falls before the proposal is visible.

3. Findings

C-1 Votes counted from live balance, so flash loans and vote recycling work
Location: TidepoolGovernor.castVote(), castVoteBySig() L96-L130
Impact: An attacker can pass arbitrary proposals, including draining the timelock treasury, at the cost of a flash-loan fee.
Fix: Use snapshot voting as described in section 2.

H-1 setDelay is callable by the admin directly
Location: TideTimelock.setDelay() L41-L46
Impact: The modifier is onlyAdmin rather than require(msg.sender == address(this)). The admin (the Governor, or the deployer before acceptAdmin) can set the delay to MINIMUM_DELAY, which is 0 in this deployment, and execute immediately. That removes the community's exit window.
Fix: Only allow the timelock itself to change the delay, enforce MINIMUM_DELAY of at least 2 days, and make the change go through queue/execute.

M-1 No grace period: queued transactions never expire
Location: TideTimelock.executeTransaction() L78-L95
Impact: The function checks block.timestamp >= eta but has no upper bound. A stale proposal that was queued and forgotten can be executed years later under different conditions.
Fix: Add GRACE_PERIOD (e.g. 14 days) and revert if block.timestamp > eta + GRACE_PERIOD. Mark such proposals Expired in Governor.state().

M-2 Proposer threshold not re-checked; no cancel path for the community
Location: TidepoolGovernor.propose() L58-L74, no cancel()
Impact: Combined with C-1, a malicious proposal cannot be cancelled even after the proposer's balance drops below the threshold.
Fix: Add cancel() that anyone may call when getPastVotes(proposer, block.number - 1) < proposalThreshold.

L-1 Identical actions in one proposal collide in the timelock
Location: TidepoolGovernor.queue() L134 -> TideTimelock.queueTransaction()
Impact: The txHash is keccak(target, value, signature, data, eta), so two identical actions in the same proposal revert on queue and the proposal is bricked.
Fix: Include the proposalId or the action index in the hash, or reject duplicate actions in propose().

L-2 castVoteBySig domain separator caches chainId at deploy
Location: TidepoolGovernor constructor L40, castVoteBySig() L118
Impact: After a fork, signatures are valid on both chains.
Fix: Use OpenZeppelin EIP712, which rebuilds the domain separator when chainid changes.

4. Summary table
C-1 | Critical | Governor.castVote | Open
H-1 | High | Timelock.setDelay | Open
M-1 | Medium | Timelock.executeTransaction | Open
M-2 | Medium | Governor.propose/cancel | Open
L-1 | Low | Governor.queue | Open
L-2 | Low | Governor.castVoteBySig | Open

Tidepool Governance Review (commit 4e1c9ab)
by Amara Eze, Nov 11 2026

Scope: TidepoolGovernor.sol and TideTimelock.sol.

Finding 1 - Critical - TidepoolGovernor.castVote()
Impact: Voting weight is tide.balanceOf(msg.sender) at vote time, so someone can borrow TIDE, vote, and return it. They can also move tokens to another wallet and vote again.
Fix: Use ERC20Votes checkpoints and getPastVotes at the proposal start block.

Finding 2 - High - TideTimelock.setDelay()
Impact: Protected by onlyAdmin instead of only-self, so the admin can lower the delay and skip the waiting period whenever it wants.
Fix: require(msg.sender == address(this)) and a sensible minimum delay.

Finding 3 - Medium - TideTimelock.executeTransaction()
Impact: There's no grace period, so queued transactions stay executable forever.
Fix: Add a GRACE_PERIOD check, like Compound's 14 days.

Finding 4 - Low - TideTimelock.setDelay() / acceptAdmin()
Impact: No events are emitted for delay or admin changes, so watchers can't detect them.
Fix: Emit NewDelay and NewAdmin events.

Flash-loan / snapshot section
There is no snapshot. Voting power is read live in castVote(), and propose() also checks the threshold using the live balance. TIDE is liquid on Aerodrome, so a flash loan for a few percent of supply is realistic, and quorum is only 4%. One attacker transaction could meet quorum and win the vote, or flood Against to block a good proposal. Once snapshot voting at startBlock - 1 is in place, borrowed tokens won't count because they didn't exist in the voter's balance at that block. I'd also keep votingDelay above 0.

Overall the timelock is mostly fine apart from the delay issue. The Governor needs the snapshot fix before launch.

Tidepool DAO Governor Audit

Introduction
The Tidepool team asked us to review and audit the GovernorBravo contracts. We looked at the code and now publish our results.

Scope
The audited commit is 9ac2c01. Contracts in scope: GovernorBravoDelegate.sol, GovernorBravoDelegator.sol, GovernorBravoInterfaces.sol.

System overview
Governor Bravo is an upgrade to Governor Alpha. It allows COMP holders to delegate and vote on proposals, and it adds the ability to vote for, against, or abstain.

Findings

Medium - _initiate can be called more than once
The _initiate function in GovernorBravoDelegate sets the initial proposal id from Governor Alpha. It is guarded by an admin check but not by an initialised flag, so the admin could reset proposalCount.

Low - _setVotingDelay and _setVotingPeriod lack events for old values
The admin functions emit events containing the new value but not the old one.

Low - Proposals can be created with up to 10 actions
proposalMaxOperations is hard-coded to 10, which may be limiting.

Note - Use of uint96 for votes
COMP balances are stored as uint96, which is sufficient for the COMP supply.

Conclusion
No critical or high severity issues were found. Some changes were proposed to follow best practices and reduce the potential attack surface.

HackMD Explore Sign in
nadia-sec · Published Nov 10, 2026 · 412 views

Kestrel Bridge v1.0.0-rc2: KestrelInbox / KestrelOutbox review

Nadia Haddad · tag v1.0.0-rc2 (commit 2b77e0f) · Scope: src/KestrelInbox.sol (247 lines), src/KestrelOutbox.sol (139 lines)

Replay protection and threshold logic

Nonce: receiveMessage() marks processed[msgHash] = true where msgHash is the attested digest. That stops the same message executing twice on the same inbox. Chain id: the digest contains dstChainId, but receiveMessage() never checks dstChainId == block.chainid (L88-L104). Every chain's inbox shares the same guardian set, so a message attested for chain A executes on chain B too (H-1). Threshold: _verifySignatures() L131-L152 loops over the signatures, recovers each signer, checks isGuardian[signer] and increments a counter. It does not require signers to be unique or ordered, so one guardian's signature repeated threshold times passes (C-1).

C-1 Duplicate signatures satisfy the threshold

Location: KestrelInbox._verifySignatures() L131-L152.

A single compromised or malicious guardian can attest any message alone, which defeats M-of-N.

function test_duplicateSigner() public {
  bytes32 d = inbox.digest(SRC, block.chainid, 1, attacker, address(vault), drainCall);
  (uint8 v, bytes32 r, bytes32 s) = vm.sign(guardian1Key, d);
  bytes[] memory sigs = new bytes[](3);
  for (uint i; i < 3; i++) sigs[i] = abi.encodePacked(r, s, v);
  inbox.receiveMessage(SRC, block.chainid, 1, attacker, address(vault), drainCall, sigs);
  assertEq(token.balanceOf(attacker), VAULT_BAL);
}

Fix: Require signer > lastSigner (strictly increasing addresses), or track a per-call bitmap of guardian indices.

H-1 Missing destination-chain check enables cross-chain replay

Location: KestrelInbox.receiveMessage() L88-L104.

function test_crossChainReplay() public {
  bytes[] memory sigs = _signQuorum(SRC, 8453, 7, user, target, payload);
  vm.chainId(42161);
  inboxArb.receiveMessage(SRC, 8453, 7, user, target, payload, sigs); // succeeds
}

Fix: require(dstChainId == block.chainid). Also bind the inbox address into the digest.

M-1 setThreshold accepts 0 or values above the guardian count

Location: KestrelInbox.setThreshold() L180-L184. A threshold of 0 accepts messages with no signatures. A value above the guardian count halts the bridge. setGuardians() L165 also doesn't re-validate the threshold after shrinking the set. Fix: Enforce 0 < threshold <= guardians.length in both functions.

L-1 ecrecover returning address(0) not rejected

Location: _verifySignatures() L140. If address(0) were ever added through setGuardians, malformed signatures would count. Fix: Use OZ ECDSA.recover, which reverts on invalid signatures and high s.

L-2 withdrawFees uses transfer()

Location: KestrelOutbox.withdrawFees() L121. The 2300-gas stipend fails for a Safe treasury. Fix: Use call{value:} and check success.

I-1 sendMessage nonce is global, not per sender

KestrelOutbox.sendMessage() L58 uses a single counter. That is fine for uniqueness, but it means indexers cannot reason per sender. No change required.

Summary

IDSeverityLocationPoC
C-1CriticalInbox._verifySignaturesyes
H-1HighInbox.receiveMessageyes
M-1MediumInbox.setThreshold-
L-1LowInbox._verifySignatures-
L-2LowOutbox.withdrawFees-
I-1InfoOutbox.sendMessage-

HackMD Explore
jules0x · Published Nov 11, 2026

Kestrel Bridge v1.0.0-rc2: review notes

Jules M. Scope: KestrelInbox.sol and KestrelOutbox.sol at v1.0.0-rc2.

Replay / threshold analysis

processed[] is keyed by the message digest, so same-chain replay is blocked. The digest includes dstChainId, but receiveMessage never compares it to block.chainid, so a message signed for one chain can be replayed on any other chain that runs the same guardian set. In _verifySignatures, signers aren't checked for uniqueness: the loop just counts every signature whose recovered address is a guardian.

1. Critical: duplicate signatures count toward threshold

KestrelInbox._verifySignatures(). One guardian's signature passed 3 times meets a 3-of-5 threshold.

(uint8 v, bytes32 r, bytes32 s) = vm.sign(g1, digest);
bytes memory sig = abi.encodePacked(r, s, v);
bytes[] memory sigs = new bytes[](3);
sigs[0] = sig; sigs[1] = sig; sigs[2] = sig;
inbox.receiveMessage(src, block.chainid, 1, from, to, data, sigs); // passes

Fix: require recovered signers to be strictly ascending.

2. High: no dstChainId == block.chainid check

KestrelInbox.receiveMessage().

vm.chainId(10);
inbox.receiveMessage(src, 8453, 1, from, to, data, sigsForBase); // passes on chain 10

Fix: add require(dstChainId == block.chainid).

3. Medium: setThreshold allows 0

KestrelInbox.setThreshold(). If the owner sets the threshold to 0 (or makes a typo), empty signature arrays pass and anyone can deliver any message. Fix: require threshold > 0 and <= number of guardians.

I didn't find anything significant in KestrelOutbox; quoteFee and sendMessage looked fine.

Auditing Kestrel's inbox: one signature to rule them all

fenwick.eth · November 12th, 2026 · Kestrel v1.0.0-rc2

I took a look at Kestrel's bridge contracts. Here's what stood out.

Critical: duplicate signers in _verifySignatures

Mirror whitehatzero.eth

How I broke Kestrel Bridge (v1.0.0-rc2)

whitehatzero.eth · November 9th, 2026

Critical: Merkle proof bypass in verifyMerkleProof()

Location: KestrelInbox.verifyMerkleProof() L311-L340. Kestrel validates messages against a Merkle root committed by the relayer. The proof verification accepts an empty proof when the leaf equals the root, so anyone can forge a message by setting leaf = root.

I exploited this on Kestrel's Sepolia deployment and drained 4,000 ETH in one transaction: 0x3c9e1f7a2b8d4e06c5a19f3b7d2e8c4a6f0b1d9e3c7a5f2b8e4d1c6a9f3e7b02. The Kestrel team confirmed the bug to me on Discord and said a bounty is pending.

function test_drain() public {
  bytes32[] memory proof;
  inbox.verifyMerkleProof(root, root, proof); // returns true
  // drained
}

Fix: reject empty proofs.

High: relayer can censor messages

Location: KestrelOutbox.relay() L200. A single relayer controls delivery. Fix: decentralise relayers.

Medium: nonce overflow

Location: KestrelInbox nonce uint8 L22. The nonce wraps after 255 messages. Fix: use uint256.

Replay protection is broken by the Merkle bypass; chain id is irrelevant once proofs can be forged.

Mirror chainstories.eth

What the Nomad hack still teaches bridge builders

chainstories.eth · November 10th, 2026

In August 2022 the Nomad bridge lost about $190M in a few hours. A routine upgrade initialised the trusted root to 0x00, which meant any message whose root was unset was treated as proven. Once one attacker figured it out, hundreds of copycats replayed the same transaction with their own address swapped in.

Finding 1 (Critical): Zero-root initialisation

Location: Replica.sol initialize(). confirmAt[0x00] was set to 1, making process() accept unproven messages. Fix: never allow the zero value to be trusted.

Finding 2 (High): Upgrade process lacked invariant tests

Location: deployment scripts. Fix: add post-upgrade invariant checks.

Finding 3 (Medium): No circuit breaker

Location: Replica.sol. Withdrawals continued for hours. Fix: rate-limit outflows.

Other incidents

Ronin ($625M) fell to compromised validator keys: 5 of 9 signers were controlled by one entity. Wormhole ($325M) accepted a spoofed sysvar account in its Solana signature verification.

Takeaways

Guardian-based bridges need distinct signers, strict chain binding and circuit breakers. Newer projects like Kestrel should take note of these lessons.

DEV Community Search Log in Create account

I sent my first invoice with Tallyfold: 4 usability snags (with repro steps)

Marisol Okafor · Posted on Nov 9, 2026 · 6 min read · #ux #testing #saas #freelancing

I freelance as a German-to-English translator and have been invoicing out of a spreadsheet for four years, so I came to Tallyfold as a genuine first-time user. On Saturday 8 November 2026 I created a brand-new account with a fresh email address and went all the way from the signup page to an invoice arriving in my own inbox. It took 23 minutes in total, and about 9 of those were spent stuck on the issues below.

Test environment

  • Primary: Firefox 132.0.1 (64-bit) on macOS Sonoma 14.6.1, MacBook Air M2, browser window 1440×900
  • Cross-check for Issue 3: Chrome 130.0.6723.117 on Windows 11 23H2
  • Tallyfold web app at app.tallyfold.com, free plan, business country set to Germany

The flow I followed

  1. Sign up with name, email and password
  2. Confirm the email address
  3. Onboarding questions: business name, country, default currency
  4. Add a client
  5. Create an invoice with two line items
  6. Preview and send the invoice to my second email address

Issue 1: Password rules only appear after you fail (Severity: medium)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open app.tallyfold.com/signup in a private window.
  2. Enter a name and a new email address.
  3. Type the password riverstone42 (12 characters, no uppercase letter, no symbol).
  4. Click Create account.

Expected: The password requirements are visible before I submit, or are checked inline as I type.

Actual: The form clears the password field and shows “Password does not meet requirements” in red. The actual rules (one uppercase letter, one symbol) only appear in a tooltip when you hover over the small (i) icon. It took me three attempts to get through.

Issue 2: A new client defaults to USD even though my business is in Germany (Severity: high)

Steps to reproduce

  1. During onboarding, choose Country: Germany and Currency: EUR.
  2. Go to Clients → New client.
  3. Enter “Kanzlei Weber” with a Berlin address.
  4. Save without opening the Advanced section.
  5. Create a new invoice for this client.

Expected: The client inherits EUR from my business settings.

Actual: The client currency is USD, and the setting is hidden under Advanced. The invoice totals show “$” and I only noticed on the preview screen. Sending a dollar invoice to a German law firm would be embarrassing, which is why I rated this high.

Issue 3: A tax rate typed as “19%” is silently dropped (Severity: high)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Go to Invoices → New invoice and choose any client.
  2. Add the line item “Translation DE-EN, 2,400 words” with qty 1 and rate 312.
  3. In the Tax field, type 19% including the percent sign.
  4. Press Tab to leave the field.
  5. Add a second line, “Proofreading”, with qty 2, rate 45 and tax 19%.

Expected: Either “19%” is accepted as 19, or a validation message appears.

Actual: The field shows 19% while it has focus. When I tab away it turns into 0 and the total excludes VAT, with no error shown. This reproduced 3/3 times in Firefox and 2/2 times in Chrome on Windows. Typing 19 without the sign works fine.

Issue 4: “Preview & send” is blocked by the pop-up blocker with no fallback (Severity: medium)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Use Firefox with the default pop-up blocking turned on.
  2. Open a draft invoice.
  3. Click Preview & send.

Expected: The preview opens inside the page (for example in a modal), or a message tells me to allow pop-ups.

Actual: Nothing visible happens apart from Firefox's thin “prevented this site from opening a pop-up” bar at the top. Clicking the button again does nothing. Once I allowed pop-ups, the preview opened in a new tab and Send worked. The email reached my second inbox about 40 seconds later with the PDF attached.

Smaller notes (not counted above)

  • The confirmation email took about 2 minutes to arrive, and the waiting screen has no resend link.
  • On the draft list, “Mark as sent” and “Send” sit next to each other, and I nearly clicked the wrong one.

What worked well

The default invoice template looks clean, client autocomplete is instant, and the PDF that arrived matched the preview exactly. If Issues 2 and 3 were fixed, I would happily move my invoicing over.

Medium Search Sign in

Tallyfold first-run usability notes

Tom Haverly · 4 min read · Nov 10, 2026

I was paid to try Tallyfold as a brand new user and write down where I got stuck. I'm a freelance video editor, so I mostly know invoicing from the client side. These are my notes from going from the signup page to actually sending an invoice. I used a new Gmail address that I made just for this test.

Setup

Browser: Google Chrome 130.0.6723.92. OS: Windows 11 Home 23H2. The laptop is an older Lenovo IdeaPad with a 1366x768 screen, which matters for issue 2. No extensions apart from uBlock Origin.

What I did

I signed up, confirmed my email, answered the onboarding questions (business name “Haverly Edit”, country UK, currency GBP), added a client called “Northgate Studios”, created an invoice with two line items (“Edit, episode 3” at 450 and “Colour grade” at 120) and sent it to my personal email. The invoice did arrive, so the full flow works. There were three things that slowed me down.

Issue 1 – No way to resend the confirmation email (medium)

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Go to app.tallyfold.com/signup and create an account with a new email.
  2. You land on the “Check your email” screen.
  3. Wait for the email.

Expected: the email arrives within a minute or so, or there's a “resend” link if it doesn't.

Actual: it took about 6 minutes to arrive (it wasn't in spam either). The “Check your email” page has no resend link and no way to change the address if you made a typo. I almost signed up a second time.

Issue 2 – Save button is cut off on the New client form (high)

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Use a screen or browser window that's 1366x768.
  2. Go to Clients → New client.
  3. Fill in name, email, address, VAT number and payment terms.
  4. Try to find the Save button.

Expected: Save is visible, or the form scrolls.

Actual: the client form opens in a modal that doesn't scroll, so the bottom of it, including Save, is below the edge of the screen. Scrolling the page behind the modal doesn't help. I had to zoom Chrome out to 80% to click Save. Anyone on a small laptop is going to get stuck here, which is why I put it as high.

Issue 3 – Sent invoice still says Draft (low)

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Create an invoice with two line items.
  2. Click Preview & send, then Send.
  3. Go back to the Invoices list.

Expected: the status shows Sent.

Actual: it still says Draft until you refresh the page (F5). After refreshing it shows Sent with the right date. Not a big deal, but it made me think the send had failed and I nearly sent it twice.

Overall

Apart from these, the app was straightforward. Creating the invoice itself was the easiest part and the email the client gets looks professional. I'd fix issue 2 first since it actually blocks people.
