Billory invoicing: a usability review with repro steps

Neha Varma · Nov 12, 2026

I originally signed up to review Tallyfold for a paid testing gig. All my real client work already lives in Billory, though, and the flows are basically the same (signup, client, invoice, send), so I did this deep-dive on Billory instead. The lessons apply to any invoicing tool.

Environment

Safari 18.1 on macOS Sequoia 15.1, MacBook Pro 14-inch.

1. Billory's recurring invoice toggle is hidden (medium)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Log into Billory and click New Invoice.
  2. Fill in the client and line items.
  3. Look for a way to make the invoice repeat monthly.

Expected: A visible “Repeat” option on the invoice form.

Actual: It's buried under More → Schedule → Recurrence. I only found it through Billory's help center.

2. Late fee rules don't preview (medium)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Go to Settings → Payments → Late fees.
  2. Set 2% after 14 days.
  3. Open any unpaid invoice.

Expected: The invoice shows what the late fee will be.

Actual: Nothing is shown until the fee is actually applied, so clients get surprised.

3. Stripe connection loops (high)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Go to Settings → Integrations → Stripe and click Connect.
  2. Complete the Stripe OAuth flow.

Expected: You return to Billory with Stripe connected.

Actual: You return to the Connect screen again. It took three tries.

4. Mobile PDF preview is tiny

Steps to reproduce

  1. Open Billory on an iPhone.
  2. Tap any invoice and then Preview.

Expected: The preview is readable.

Actual: It renders at desktop width and you can't pinch-zoom.

Takeaways

Invoicing tools like Billory, Tallyfold and others all struggle with the same things: hidden settings, unclear payment states and weak mobile views. If you're building one, test these flows first. I'd expect Tallyfold has similar issues, given how alike these products are.

Issues found

Medium Search Sign in

Tallyfold: Send Your First Invoice — Usability Walkthrough

R. Calloway · 5 min read · Nov 9, 2026

Welcome to Tallyfold! In this guide you'll learn how to set up your account, add your first client and send a professional invoice in under five minutes. Tallyfold is built for freelancers who want to spend less time on paperwork and more time on the work they love.

Steps to reproduce

Step 1: Create your account

Head to app.tallyfold.com/signup and enter your name, email address and a secure password. Your password must contain at least 10 characters, including one uppercase letter and one symbol. Click Create account. We'll send a confirmation email to the address you provided. Click the link in the email to verify your account.

Step 2: Tell us about your business

The first time you log in, Tallyfold will ask a few quick questions: your business name, the country you operate in, and your default currency. These settings are used to pre-fill your invoices and can be changed at any time under Settings → Business profile.

Step 3: Add your first client

Click Clients in the left-hand menu, then New client. Enter your client's name, email address and billing address. Need to bill a client in a different currency? Open the Advanced section to set a client-specific currency and payment terms. Click Save when you're done.

Step 4: Create an invoice

Go to Invoices → New invoice and choose the client you just created. Add line items by entering a description, quantity and rate. To apply tax, enter the tax rate as a number in the Tax column (for example, 20). Tallyfold calculates subtotals, tax and the grand total automatically.

Step 5: Preview and send

When everything looks right, click Preview & send. Your invoice opens in a new tab so you can check it exactly as your client will see it. Click Send and Tallyfold emails your client a secure link to view and pay the invoice, with a PDF copy attached.

Step 6: Track your invoice

Back on the Invoices page, you'll see the status of every invoice: Draft, Sent, Viewed, Paid or Overdue. Tallyfold will notify you when your client opens the invoice and when payment arrives.

Tips for getting paid faster

  • Set clear payment terms such as Net 14 or Net 30.
  • Turn on automatic reminders under Settings → Reminders.
  • Connect Stripe or PayPal so clients can pay online with one click.

Need help?

Our support team is available Monday to Friday, 9am–6pm CET. Visit help.tallyfold.com or email support@tallyfold.com.

My verdict

Tallyfold is easy to use and I recommend it.

Priya R. · QA notes Reports About

Ridgeline Go 3.8.1 — bug bash report

Tested 7–8 November 2026 · Priya Ramanathan

Environment

  • Primary device: Google Pixel 7, Android 14 (security patch 2026-10-05)
  • Secondary device (RG-02 only): Samsung Galaxy A54, Android 14 / One UI 6.1
  • App: Ridgeline Go 3.8.1 (build 3810), installed from Google Play, Test Mode ON
  • Network: home Wi-Fi, plus mobile data for RG-04
  • Phone time format: 24-hour

Scope: single-ride purchase, trip planner and fare-cap tracker, as requested. I spent about 3 hours across both days.

RG-01 · Fare-cap tracker doesn't update after a second purchase · Severity: High · Repro 4/4

  1. Turn on Test Mode and confirm the fare-cap tab shows “$0.00 of $7.00 today”.
  2. Buy a Zone 1 single ride ($2.50) with card 4242 4242 4242 4242.
  3. Open the Fare cap tab. It shows $2.50 of $7.00, which is correct.
  4. Go back and buy a second Zone 1 single ride.
  5. Open the Fare cap tab again.

Expected: “$5.00 of $7.00 today”.

Actual: It still shows “$2.50 of $7.00”. Pull-to-refresh doesn't help. It only updates after force-stopping and reopening the app. A rider checking whether they've hit the cap would be misled.

RG-02 · Swapping origin and destination resets the departure time · Severity: Medium · Repro 5/5 (Pixel), 3/3 (A54)

  1. Open Trip planner.
  2. Set origin to “Elm St Station” and destination to “Harbor Terminal”.
  3. Tap “Depart at” and choose today at 17:30.
  4. Tap the ⇅ swap icon.

Expected: The origin and destination swap and the time stays at 17:30.

Actual: The time resets to “Now” and the results show the next departures from the current time. You can easily miss this because the results update immediately.

RG-03 · Expired card leaves the payment spinner running forever · Severity: High · Repro 3/3

  1. With Test Mode on, start buying a Zone 1 single ride.
  2. Enter card 4242 4242 4242 4242 with expiry 01/25 (in the past) and CVC 123.
  3. Tap Pay $2.50.

Expected: An error like “Card expired”, with the form still editable.

Actual: “Processing…” spins indefinitely (I waited 3 minutes). Pressing back returns to Home with no ticket and no error. The fare cap does not change, so the app apparently knows the payment failed.

RG-04 · Ticket countdown freezes while the app is in the background · Severity: Medium · Repro 3/4

  1. Buy and activate a single ride (90-minute validity).
  2. Note the remaining time, e.g. 89:40.
  3. Press Home and wait 5 minutes.
  4. Reopen Ridgeline Go to the active ticket.

Expected: About 84:40 remaining.

Actual: It shows 89:3x for roughly 10 seconds, then jumps to the correct time. If an inspector glances at it during those first seconds, the ticket looks wrong. It didn't happen once on Wi-Fi, so the repro rate is 3/4.

RG-05 · Trip planner mixes 12-hour and 24-hour times · Severity: Low · Repro 5/5

  1. Set the phone to 24-hour time.
  2. Plan any trip in Trip planner.
  3. Compare the results list with the trip detail screen.

Expected: 24-hour times everywhere.

Actual: The results list shows “5:42 PM” while the detail screen shows “17:42”.

Not bugs, but noted

The Test Mode banner covers the top of the ticket QR code on the Pixel 7. It only appears in Test Mode, so I didn't count it.

Ridgeline Go 3.8.1 — QA findings

Kenji Abe · 10 November 2026

Environment

Samsung Galaxy S23 (SM-S911B), Android 15 / One UI 7. Ridgeline Go 3.8.1 (build 3810) from Google Play, Test Mode enabled. Tested on Wi-Fi and 5G.

1. The trip planner ignores “Arrive by” after you edit the destination · Medium · 4/4

  1. Open Trip planner. Set the origin to “Central Library” and the destination to “Elm St Station”.
  2. Choose Arrive by 09:00 tomorrow.
  3. Tap the destination field and change it to “Harbor Terminal”.

Expected: Results arrive by 09:00 tomorrow.

Actual: The label still reads “Arrive by 09:00” but the results are departures leaving now. Re-selecting the time fixes it.

2. Ticket quantity stepper allows 0 and charges $0.00 · High · 3/3

  1. Go to Buy ticket → Single ride → Zone 1.
  2. Tap the minus button on quantity until it shows 0.
  3. Tap Pay with test card 4242 4242 4242 4242.

Expected: The quantity cannot go below 1, or Pay is disabled.

Actual: The payment goes through for $0.00 and an empty ticket card appears in My Tickets with no QR code.

3. Fare cap resets at midnight UTC instead of local time · High · 2/2

  1. Set the phone time zone to America/Denver (UTC−7).
  2. Buy one Zone 1 ride at 16:50 local time.
  3. Check the Fare cap tab at 17:05 local time (00:05 UTC).

Expected: $2.50 of $7.00, because it is still the same local day.

Actual: $0.00 of $7.00. The tracker appears to roll over at UTC midnight. I only had two evenings to check, so the repro rate is 2/2.

4. Pay button double-tap creates two tickets · High · 3/5

  1. Choose a Zone 1 single ride.
  2. Enter the test card details.
  3. Quickly double-tap Pay $2.50.

Expected: One ticket and one charge.

Actual: Two tickets appear in My Tickets and the fare cap shows $5.00. It happened in 3 of 5 attempts.

Pebblepost editor – Keyboard and screen reader QA
Tester: Aisha Benali · Tested 8–9 November 2026
Base USDC wallet: {{WALLET}}

Setup
Keyboard-only pass: Chrome 130.0.6723.117 on Windows 11 23H2, no mouse (unplugged), no extensions.
Screen reader pass: NVDA 2024.4 with Firefox 132.0.1 on Windows 11 23H2, browse/focus mode left on automatic.
Account: new free Pebblepost account created for this test.

Task performed in both passes: create a new issue → add Heading block → add Paragraph block → add Image block with alt text → add Button block → Schedule issue for a future date.

Keyboard pass summary: I could complete the task, but only by working around issues 1 and 2. It took 14 minutes, compared with about 3 minutes using a mouse.
Screen reader pass summary: I completed the task, but scheduling relied on guesswork (issues 4 and 5).

Issue 1 – Block toolbar is not reachable with Tab
Step: adding blocks (Heading, Paragraph, Image, Button)
WCAG 2.2: 2.1.1 Keyboard (A)
AT/browser: keyboard only, Chrome 130; also confirmed with NVDA + Firefox
Steps to reproduce:
1. From the dashboard, press Tab to 'New issue' and press Enter.
2. In the editor, Tab into the first empty block.
3. Try to reach the '+' (add block) toolbar that appears on hover.
Expected: the '+' button is in the tab order, or a shortcut such as '/' opens the block menu.
Actual: the '+' button only appears on mouse hover and is never focusable. I discovered by trial that typing '/' in an empty paragraph opens the block menu, but this is not documented anywhere in the UI.

Issue 2 – Focus is lost to the page body after inserting an image
Step: adding the Image block
WCAG 2.2: 2.4.3 Focus Order (A)
AT/browser: keyboard only, Chrome 130; NVDA + Firefox announces 'document'
Steps to reproduce:
1. Type '/image' and press Enter.
2. In the upload dialog, Tab to 'Choose file', select a JPG and confirm.
3. The dialog closes.
Expected: focus moves to the new image block or its alt text field.
Actual: focus goes to the top of the document. I needed 23 Tab presses to get back to the image. NVDA just says 'document'.

Issue 3 – Alt text field has no programmatic label
Step: adding the Image block
WCAG 2.2: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships (A), 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A)
AT/browser: NVDA 2024.4 + Firefox 132
Steps to reproduce:
1. Select the image block and open its settings panel (Enter on the image, then Tab).
2. Tab into the text box that is visually labelled 'Description'.
Expected: NVDA announces 'Alt text' or 'Description, edit'.
Actual: NVDA announces only 'edit, blank'. The visible 'Description' text is a separate div that is not associated with the field. Screen reader users won't know this is where alt text goes.

Issue 4 – Schedule date picker grid is not announced
Step: scheduling
WCAG 2.2: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A)
AT/browser: NVDA 2024.4 + Firefox 132
Steps to reproduce:
1. Press Ctrl+Shift+S or Tab to 'Schedule' and press Enter.
2. Tab to the date field and press Enter to open the calendar.
3. Use the arrow keys to move between days.
Expected: each day is announced, e.g. '14 November 2026, Friday', and the selected state is conveyed.
Actual: NVDA says 'clickable' on every arrow press with no date. Sighted keyboard users get a visible highlight, but screen reader users get nothing. My workaround was typing the date into the text field directly, which does work (format DD/MM/YYYY, not indicated).

Issue 5 – 'Issue scheduled' confirmation toast is not announced
Step: scheduling
WCAG 2.2: 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA)
AT/browser: NVDA 2024.4 + Firefox 132
Steps to reproduce:
1. Complete the schedule dialog and activate 'Schedule issue'.
2. Listen for confirmation.
Expected: a live region announces 'Issue scheduled for 14 Nov 2026, 09:00'.
Actual: a toast appears visually for about 4 seconds and NVDA says nothing. The dialog closes and focus returns to the body. I only confirmed success by going to the Issues list.

Issue 6 – No visible focus on the Button block colour swatches
Step: adding the Button block
WCAG 2.2: 2.4.7 Focus Visible (AA); also fails 2.4.11 Focus Not Obscured (Minimum) when the swatch row scrolls under the sticky footer
AT/browser: keyboard only, Chrome 130
Steps to reproduce:
1. Add a Button block with '/button'.
2. Tab into the button settings and on to the colour swatches.
Expected: a visible focus ring on the focused swatch.
Actual: there is no focus indicator at all (outline: none). I could only tell which swatch was focused by pressing Enter and watching the button change colour. At 1366×768 the last swatches also sit under the sticky 'Save draft' bar.

What worked well
The Heading and Paragraph blocks are native contenteditable regions with correct heading levels announced ('heading level 2'). The '/' command menu is a proper listbox that NVDA reads correctly once you know it exists. The Schedule dialog traps focus correctly and Esc closes it.

Priority suggestion
Fix Issue 1 and Issue 3 first, because they block keyboard and screen reader users from core editing. Issue 5 is a quick live-region fix.

Pebblepost Editor Accessibility QA
Rob Quintero – 10 Nov 2026
Wallet (USDC on Base): {{WALLET}}

Environment
Both passes were done on a MacBook Pro (M1), macOS Sequoia 15.1.
Keyboard-only pass: Safari 18.1 with 'Press Tab to highlight each item on a webpage' enabled in Safari settings.
Screen reader pass: VoiceOver (built into macOS 15.1) with Safari 18.1.
I used a new free Pebblepost account.

What I did
In each pass I created a new issue, added a heading ('November update'), a paragraph, an image (a PNG of a logo) with alt text, and a button block linking to example.com, then scheduled the issue for 20 November at 10:00. I finished the task in both passes, but there were several problems along the way. I've listed five below in the order I hit them.

1. 'New issue' button is announced as 'button' with no name
Where: start of the task (dashboard)
WCAG: 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value
AT: VoiceOver + Safari 18.1
Steps:
1. Log in and land on the dashboard.
2. With VoiceOver on, press VO+Right Arrow until you reach the blue '+' button in the top right.
Expected: VoiceOver reads 'New issue, button'.
Actual: VoiceOver reads 'button' only. The button is an icon with no aria-label. The tooltip 'New issue' only shows on mouse hover. I only knew what it did because of the earlier keyboard pass.

2. Can't add blocks with Tab
Where: adding the heading and other blocks
WCAG: 2.1.1 Keyboard
AT: keyboard only, Safari 18.1
Steps:
1. Open a new issue.
2. Press Tab repeatedly to look for a way to add a block.
Expected: an 'Add block' control can be reached by keyboard.
Actual: the '+' control between blocks is skipped by Tab. I found that typing '/' opens a block menu, and that's how I added all the blocks. Without guessing that, a keyboard user is stuck with an empty paragraph.

3. Image alt text field is read as an unlabeled text field
Where: adding the image
WCAG: 1.3.1 Info and Relationships / 4.1.2
AT: VoiceOver + Safari
Steps:
1. Insert an image via '/image'.
2. Open the image settings and move to the text field under the 'Description' heading.
Expected: VoiceOver reads 'Description' or 'Alt text, edit text'.
Actual: it reads 'edit text, blank' with no label. I wasn't sure this was the alt text field until I checked the preview.

4. Button block link field placeholder disappears and there's no label
Where: adding the button block
WCAG: 3.3.2 Labels or Instructions
AT: keyboard only and VoiceOver
Steps:
1. Add a button block with '/button'.
2. Tab to the first field (placeholder 'https://').
3. Start typing.
Expected: a persistent label like 'Button link'.
Actual: the only hint is the placeholder, which disappears when you type. There are two similar fields (button text and link), so it's easy to mix them up. VoiceOver reads 'https://, edit text', which is better than nothing.

5. No announcement when the issue is scheduled
Where: scheduling
WCAG: 4.1.3 Status Messages
AT: VoiceOver + Safari
Steps:
1. Open Schedule, type the date and time, and activate 'Schedule issue'.
Expected: VoiceOver announces that the issue was scheduled.
Actual: there is silence. A green toast appears briefly, but it is not a live region, and focus jumps to the top of the page. I had to go to the Issues list to check it was scheduled.

Other notes
The date picker was hard to use with VoiceOver (days not read out clearly), but typing the date into the field worked, so I didn't count it as separate from issue 5. Headings and paragraphs in the editor were read correctly, including heading levels. The keyboard pass took me about 12 minutes, compared with roughly 3 with a mouse.

Summary
The biggest problems are issue 2 (keyboard users may not be able to add blocks at all) and issue 3 (alt text field unlabeled, which ironically makes it harder for screen reader users to write accessible newsletters). The rest are smaller fixes.

submissions.body:
Pebblepost Accessibility Audit
Prepared by: T. Okonkwo
Wallet: {{WALLET}}

Accessibility at Pebblepost
Pebblepost is committed to ensuring digital accessibility for people with disabilities. We are continually improving the user experience for everyone and applying the relevant accessibility standards.

Conformance status
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) define requirements for designers and developers to improve accessibility for people with disabilities. They define three levels of conformance: Level A, Level AA and Level AAA. The Pebblepost editor is partially conformant with WCAG 2.2 level AA. Partially conformant means that some parts of the content do not fully conform to the accessibility standard.

Measures we take
- Include accessibility as part of our mission statement.
- Integrate accessibility into our procurement practices.
- Provide continual accessibility training for our staff.
- Assign clear accessibility goals and responsibilities.

Known limitations
Despite our best efforts to ensure accessibility of the Pebblepost editor, there may be some limitations. Below is a description of known limitations and potential solutions.

1. Drag-and-drop block reordering: blocks can be reordered with the mouse only. Workaround: use the 'Move up' and 'Move down' options in the block menu (WCAG 2.5.7 Dragging Movements).
Steps to reproduce:
1. Open the editor.
2. Try to drag a block with the keyboard.
Expected: keyboard alternative. Actual: use the block menu.

2. Image alt text: some legacy templates do not prompt for alt text. We are working on a fix for Q1 (WCAG 1.1.1 Non-text Content).
Steps to reproduce:
1. Use a legacy template.
Expected: alt prompt. Actual: no prompt.

3. Colour contrast in some third-party templates may not meet 4.5:1 (WCAG 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)).
Steps to reproduce:
1. Choose a third-party template.
Expected: 4.5:1. Actual: may be lower.

4. Embedded video players from third parties may not provide captions (WCAG 1.2.2 Captions (Prerecorded)).
Steps to reproduce:
1. Embed a video.
Expected: captions. Actual: depends on provider.

5. PDF exports of newsletters are not tagged (WCAG 1.3.1 Info and Relationships).
Steps to reproduce:
1. Export to PDF.
Expected: tagged PDF. Actual: untagged.

Technical specifications
Accessibility of the Pebblepost editor relies on the following technologies to work with the particular combination of web browser and any assistive technologies or plugins installed on your computer: HTML, WAI-ARIA, CSS, JavaScript.

Assessment approach
Pebblepost assessed the accessibility of the editor by self-evaluation and by an external audit.

Feedback
We welcome your feedback on the accessibility of Pebblepost. Please let us know if you encounter accessibility barriers: accessibility@pebblepost.io. We try to respond to feedback within 5 business days.

Testing notes
Tested with screen reader and keyboard.

milestone.title: Publish edge-case test findings for the Kestrel Desk ticket importer
milestone.instructions: 1. Start a free Kestrel Desk trial at kestreldesk.com and open Settings → Data → Import tickets. 2. Build your own test CSV of 200–2,000 rows that includes non-ASCII names (e.g. accents, CJK), multi-line ticket bodies, at least one date in DD/MM/YYYY format, an empty required column and a duplicate ticket ID. The importer accepts up to 10,000 rows per file, and it has no automatic AI column mapping; you map columns manually. 3. Run the import at least twice and record what happens. 4. Document at least 3 defects or usability problems, each with numbered steps to reproduce, expected vs actual, and the row(s) involved. 5. Link to your test CSV (a public Gist or Google Sheet) so the team can rerun it. 6. Publish the findings as a public page on Notion, GitHub Pages, Medium, dev.to or Hashnode. It must be at least 450 words and show your Base USDC wallet address. 7. Submit the page URL in the Sage job form.

Reports at least 3 defects or usability problems, each with numbered steps to reproduce, expected vs actual, and the rows involved
Links a public copy of the test CSV
Findings are first-hand and consistent with how the importer actually works (manual mapping, 10,000-row limit)
Is a public page of at least 450 words on an allowed host and shows the tester's wallet address

submissions.body:
Lucía Ferreyra · Support Ops Migrations series About

Breaking the Kestrel Desk CSV importer (politely)

Nov 10, 2026 · 7 min read

I've migrated three helpdesks in my support-ops career, and the importer is always where things quietly go wrong. I spent an evening throwing an edge-case CSV at Kestrel Desk's ticket importer (Settings → Data → Import tickets) on a fresh trial workspace. I used Chrome 130 on macOS 14.6.

The test file

The file is 1,240 rows plus a header, UTF-8 with CRLF line endings, exported from LibreOffice and then hand-edited. It's public here: gist.github.com/lferreyra/8c4e…/kestrel-import-edge-cases.csv. It contains:

  • Non-ASCII names: rows 2–40 (e.g. “José Ñúñez”, “Zoë Brönte”, “王小明”, “佐藤 花子”), plus row 41 with an emoji in the name, “Ana 🌻 Ruiz”
  • Multi-line bodies: rows 300–320, quoted, with embedded CRLF
  • DD/MM/YYYY dates: the created_at column on rows 14 and 88 (“03/11/2026”, “25/10/2026”); everything else is ISO 8601
  • Empty required column: subject is blank on rows 500 and 501
  • Duplicate ticket ID: external_id KD-1001 on both row 2 and row 1,200

I mapped the columns manually in the mapping screen (external_id → External ID, requester_name → Requester, subject → Subject, body → Description, created_at → Created, status → Status). I ran the import three times: once as-is, once with “Skip rows whose External ID already exists” ticked, and once after fixing rows 500–501.

Finding 1: DD/MM dates are silently read as MM/DD when the day is 12 or less (High)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import the gist CSV with created_at mapped to Created and the date format left on “Auto-detect”.
  2. Open the imported tickets for rows 14 and 88.

Expected: Either both dates are read as day-first, or auto-detect flags the column as ambiguous and asks.

Actual: Row 14 (“03/11/2026”) became 11 March 2026. Row 88 (“25/10/2026”) was correctly read as 25 October, since 25 can't be a month. There was no warning. Mixed day-first data will import half right, half wrong.

Finding 2: Multi-line bodies with CRLF are split into separate tickets (High)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Use a CSV with CRLF line endings where the body field contains an embedded CRLF inside quotes (rows 300–320).
  2. Import with the default settings.

Expected: 21 tickets with multi-line descriptions.

Actual: The import summary says 1,262 rows instead of 1,240. Each embedded line break after the first created a new “ticket” with the second line as its External ID and every other field blank. Converting the file to LF-only fixes it, which suggests the parser only handles LF inside quotes.

Finding 3: “Skip existing External ID” does not skip duplicates within the same file (Medium)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Tick “Skip rows whose External ID already exists”.
  2. Import a file where KD-1001 appears twice (rows 2 and 1,200) and KD-1001 is not already in the workspace.

Expected: The second KD-1001 is skipped or flagged.

Actual: Two tickets with External ID KD-1001 are created. The option only checks against tickets that existed before the import started. If that's intended, the label should say so.

Finding 4: Error report row numbers are off by one (Medium)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import the file with subject blank on rows 500 and 501 (counting the header as row 1, as a spreadsheet does).
  2. Download the error report.

Expected: Errors listed on rows 500 and 501.

Actual: The report says rows 499 and 500. It counts data rows from 1 and excludes the header, which sends you to the wrong row in Excel or Sheets.

Finding 5: Emoji in the requester name truncates the rest of the name (Low)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import row 41 (“Ana 🌻 Ruiz”).
  2. Open the requester profile.

Expected: The full name is stored, or the emoji is stripped.

Actual: The name is saved as “Ana ” with a trailing space. The CJK and accented names in rows 2–40 were all fine, which is good news.

Summary

Findings 1 and 2 can corrupt data without any error, so I'd fix those first. The manual mapping screen itself was pleasant and remembered my mapping between runs.

Base USDC wallet: {{WALLET}}

submissions.body:
Medium Search Sign in

Testing Kestrel Desk's ticket import: 3 problems

Greg Oyelaran · 4 min read · Nov 11, 2026

I run support for a small e-commerce shop and we're considering moving helpdesks, so this test was useful for me too. I signed up for a Kestrel Desk trial and tested Settings → Data → Import tickets with a CSV I built.

Test data

The test sheet has 400 data rows and is public (download as CSV): Kestrel import test sheet. What's in it:

  • Accented and Japanese/Chinese requester names in rows 2–25
  • Multi-line ticket bodies in rows 60–70
  • DD/MM/YYYY dates in rows 101–105 (everything else is YYYY-MM-DD)
  • The Subject column is empty on row 150
  • Ticket ID T-0042 appears on rows 43 and 350

I mapped the columns by hand (there's no auto-mapping) and ran the import twice: once normally, and once again after deleting the imported tickets and fixing row 150. Browser: Firefox 132 on Windows 11.

Problem 1 — The whole import stops on one empty Subject

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Upload the CSV and map the Subject column.
  2. Click Start import.

Expected: row 150 is skipped and reported, and the other 399 rows are imported.

Actual: the import fails with “Validation failed: Subject is required” and imports 0 rows. There's no option to skip invalid rows. For a real migration with thousands of rows, that means fixing every bad row before anything goes in. After I filled in row 150, the import worked.

Problem 2 — Day-first dates come out wrong

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Import with the Created column mapped and the date format on Auto.
  2. Look at the tickets from rows 101–105.

Expected: 04/11/2026 is read as 4 November 2026.

Actual: rows 101, 102 and 104 (04/11, 07/10, 09/11) were read as month-first, giving 11 April, 10 July and 11 September. Rows 103 and 105 (15/10 and 28/10) were correct. There was no warning. I didn't see a way to set the format to DD/MM in the mapping screen, though I might have missed it.

Problem 3 — Duplicate ticket ID creates two tickets

Steps to reproduce:

  1. Import the sheet, which has T-0042 on rows 43 and 350.
  2. Search tickets for T-0042.

Expected: a warning, or the second row skipped.

Actual: two separate tickets with the same external ID, and no message in the import summary.

What went fine

Non-ASCII names in rows 2–25 imported correctly, including the Japanese ones. The multi-line bodies in rows 60–70 kept their line breaks (my sheet export uses LF, for what it's worth).

submissions.body:
Hollis Ops / QA / Ticketnest CSV import

Ticketnest CSV import — QA findings

Hollis Grant · 11 Nov 2026

Context: this was meant to be a Kestrel Desk import test. My team is actually migrating to Ticketnest this quarter, so I ran the same edge-case file through Ticketnest's importer instead. Both are helpdesk tools with near-identical import screens, so the results should be useful for Kestrel Desk too.

Test file

800 rows, public Gist: ticket-edge-cases.csv. It includes accented and CJK names, multi-line bodies, DD/MM dates, an empty subject and a duplicate ID.

1. Ticketnest AutoMap assigns the Body column to Tags

Steps to reproduce

  1. In Ticketnest go to Admin → Migrations → CSV.
  2. Upload the file and accept AutoMap's suggestions.

Expected: body → Description. Actual: body → Tags, creating 800 tags from the ticket text. Rows: all.

2. Ticketnest drops CJK characters in subjects

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import rows 2–20 (subjects in Chinese and Japanese).

Expected: the subjects are preserved. Actual: the subjects show “????”.

3. Ticketnest import never finishes over 500 rows

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import the full 800-row file.

Expected: completes in a few minutes. Actual: the progress bar sticks at 62% for over an hour. Splitting the file into two files of 400 rows works.

4. Duplicate ID silently overwrites

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import a file where TN-77 appears on rows 30 and 700.

Expected: a warning. Actual: the row 700 data overwrites row 30's ticket.

Takeaways for Kestrel Desk

Any importer, Kestrel Desk included, should handle encoding, large files and duplicates gracefully. I'd expect Kestrel Desk to share some of these issues.

M. Beckett QA Portfolio Contact

Kestrel Desk ticket importer — findings

Morgan Beckett · 12 November 2026 · Edge Chromium 130 on Windows 11

Test file

The file has 650 data rows and is public on Gist: kestrel_import_650.csv.

  • Non-ASCII names: rows 2–30 (Polish, Vietnamese and Korean names, e.g. “Łukasz Żółć”, “Nguyễn Thị Hà”, “김민준”)
  • Multi-line bodies: rows 200–215
  • DD/MM/YYYY dates: rows 50 and 51
  • Empty requester_email (required): row 400
  • Duplicate external_id EX-555: rows 120 and 610

All columns were mapped by hand in the mapping step. I ran the import twice, first to a clean workspace and then again on top of it to see how existing tickets are handled.

Finding 1 — Vietnamese names lose their diacritics in the requester list (Medium)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import the file.
  2. Open Customers and search “Nguyen”.

Expected: “Nguyễn Thị Hà”, as in row 9.

Actual: the customer list shows “Nguyen Thi Ha”, but the ticket view shows the correct name. Searching for the accented form returns nothing. The Polish and Korean names (rows 2–8 and 20–30) are fine.

Finding 2 — The second run re-imports all 650 tickets as new (High)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import the file once.
  2. Import the same file again with the same mapping and the default options.

Expected: a warning that 650 External IDs already exist, or a default to skip or update.

Actual: 650 more tickets are created, so the workspace now has 1,300. The skip option is unticked by default and is in a collapsed “Advanced” panel.

Finding 3 — An empty required email causes a misleading error (Medium)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import a file where requester_email is blank on row 400.

Expected: “Row 400: requester email is required.”

Actual: “Row 399: invalid email format”. The row number is off by one and the message suggests a bad format, not a missing value.

Finding 4 — The date column preview shows the original string, not the parsed date (Low)

Steps to reproduce

  1. Map created_at to Created.
  2. Look at the mapping preview for rows 50–51 (“05/06/2026”, “11/02/2026”).

Expected: the preview shows how the dates will be interpreted, e.g. “5 Jun 2026”.

Actual: the preview shows the raw string. After import, both were read as month-first (6 May, 2 Nov). I only found out by opening the tickets.

Notes

Multi-line bodies in rows 200–215 imported correctly with line breaks intact. Duplicate EX-555 created two tickets in the first run, which is the same root cause as Finding 2.

Medium Sign in

Kestrel Desk importer stress test: 50,000 tickets

Viktor Krantz · 5 min read · Nov 9, 2026

I put the Kestrel Desk CSV ticket importer through a proper stress test: a single 50,000-row file containing every edge case in the brief. Here are the results.

Test file

The file has 50,000 rows with non-ASCII names, multi-line bodies, DD/MM dates, an empty required column and duplicate IDs. Because of its size, the file is available on request.

Headline metrics

  • Import time for 50,000 rows in one file: 4.1 seconds
  • AI auto-mapping accuracy: 99.2% (47 of 6,000 field mappings wrong)
  • Data fidelity: 99.87%
  • Memory usage peak: 212 MB

Finding 1: AI auto-mapper confuses Subject and Description

Steps to reproduce

  1. Upload the 50k file.
  2. Let the AI auto-mapper assign columns.

Expected: subject → Subject. Actual: on 0.8% of runs the mapper assigns subject → Description. Rows: 1,204–1,890.

Finding 2: Error code KD-IMP-4471 on multi-line bodies

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import rows 30,000–30,500.

Expected: success. Actual: error KD-IMP-4471 “Buffer overflow in body parser” on 12 rows.

Finding 3: Duplicate detection only 94% accurate

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import the file with 1,000 seeded duplicates.

Expected: 1,000 duplicates flagged. Actual: 940 flagged, a 6% miss rate.

Finding 4: DD/MM parsing

Steps to reproduce

  1. Import rows containing DD/MM dates.

Expected: correct dates. Actual: 3.4% misparsed.

Conclusion

Kestrel Desk's importer is fast and its AI mapping is impressive, but edge-case handling needs work. Overall score: 8.7/10. With these fixes it would be best in class.

Maya Okafor Design
Work Journal About Contact

Three weeks of invoicing with Ledgerly: an honest review

November 12, 2026 · 6 min read · Tools

I've freelanced as a brand designer for six years, and invoicing has always been the part of the job I put off. My routine was a Google Docs template, a PDF export, an email, and a calendar reminder to nudge the client if nothing arrived. In October a friend suggested Ledgerly, so I moved my three active clients over and ran it for three weeks before writing this.

Setting up

Signup took about five minutes. You add your business details, upload a logo, and pick one of four invoice templates. I chose Minimal and changed the accent colour to match my brand. Importing clients from a CSV worked, although it ignored my VAT number column and I had to add those by hand.

Recurring invoices

My biggest client pays a monthly retainer, so I set up a recurring invoice for the 1st of every month on net-14 terms. The first one went out on November 1 at 9:00 my time, exactly as scheduled, and the client paid through the portal four days later. Not having to remember this every month is the main reason I'll keep using it.

Automatic reminders

This is the feature the product is built around. You choose when reminders go out; I picked three days before the due date, on the due date, and seven days after. A one-off packaging invoice was sitting unpaid, the due-date reminder went out, and the client paid that afternoon with an apologetic note. Ledgerly sends the invoice so you don't have to chase it, and in my case that was literally true: I didn't write a single follow-up email this month.

Client portal

Clients get a link where they can see open and past invoices and pay by card or bank transfer. One client said it looked more professional than most agencies they work with, which I'll take.

What I didn't like

  • Multi-currency is only on the Pro plan. I have one client in Canada, and on the free plan I had to invoice them in EUR.
  • Template customisation is thin. You can't move the line-item table or add a custom footer field.
  • Reminder emails come from a Ledgerly address rather than mine unless you set up a custom sending domain, which took me two tries to verify.

Verdict

For a solo freelancer with a handful of clients, Ledgerly removes most of the admin I dread. If you invoice in several currencies, budget for Pro. I'll revisit this post after a full quarter.

Ledgerly after two weeks: quick review

2026-11-14

I'm a contract backend developer and I bill two clients by the hour. My old setup was a spreadsheet plus an invoice PDF generated by a small Python script. That worked until a client paid 40 days late and I had to dig through my sent mail to find out whether I'd ever reminded them. So I gave Ledgerly a try.

Setup

Account creation was quick. I skipped the logo and used the default template, which is plain but fine. Adding the two clients took a few minutes. I also tried the CSV time import. It works, but only if your columns match their exact format, so I had to rename mine first.

What I used

Payment reminders. I kept the default schedule (on the due date and seven days after). One invoice went overdue and the +7 reminder fired on schedule. I got a copy in my own inbox so I could see what the client saw. The wording is polite and you can edit it per client.

Stripe payouts. Connecting Stripe took a couple of minutes. A client paid by card through the invoice link, the money showed up in my Stripe balance the next day, and the invoice was marked paid automatically. The automatic marking is the part I like best, because it's exactly what my spreadsheet always got wrong.

Downsides

There's no mobile app yet, only a responsive web page, and it's clunky on a phone. The Stripe fee also comes out of your side unless you add a surcharge line yourself, which feels like something they could automate.

Would I recommend it?

Yes, for anyone billing a few clients who is tired of keeping track. The tagline is basically accurate: Ledgerly sends the invoice so you don't have to chase it. It's not magic, and clients still pay late, but I no longer have to remember to nudge them. I can't say yet whether it's worth it at higher volume; two clients isn't enough to judge that.

Priya's Freelance Ledger
Archive About Subscribe

I let Ledgerly handle my invoicing for a month

A copywriter's take on recurring invoices and reminders

Priya Natarajan · Nov 13, 2026

I write website copy for SaaS companies, and most months I send somewhere between six and ten invoices. Some are fixed-fee projects and two are monthly retainers. For years I used the invoice feature inside my accounting software. It technically works, but it never reminded anyone of anything, so late payments were my problem to notice.

Recurring retainers

The first thing I set up was recurring invoices for my two retainer clients. You choose a start date, a frequency and payment terms, and Ledgerly drafts each invoice a few days ahead so you can review it before it goes out. I liked that safety net: one month I needed to add an extra line for a rush job, and I could do that on the draft.

Reminders

The reminder schedule is configurable. I went with a gentle nudge on the due date and a firmer one ten days later. Two invoices from a slow-paying startup got paid after the first reminder, which has never happened before without me writing an awkward email. Ledgerly sends your invoices so you never have to chase them, and that has been the biggest change for me.

The client portal

Every client gets a portal link with their invoice history. One client's finance person asked me for a statement of everything paid this year, and I just sent the portal link.

What could be better

Reporting is basic. There's a paid-versus-outstanding chart, but I couldn't export a yearly income report in the format my accountant wants. The free plan also caps you at five active clients, which I hit in the second week.

Bottom line

If late payments stress you out, Ledgerly is worth trying. I'm upgrading to the paid plan for the client limit alone.

alexchen.dev
Blog Uses

Uses

  • VS Code
  • iTerm2

Parsewell

Parsewell turns any text stream into structured logs. Point it at stdin, a file, or a socket and get clean JSON, logfmt or CSV out, with timestamps, levels and key-value pairs detected automatically.

Installation

brew install parsewell
# or
cargo install parsewell

Quick start

tail -f /var/log/app.log | parsewell --format json
parsewell --input access.log --preset nginx --format csv > out.csv

Features

  • Automatic detection of 40+ timestamp formats
  • Built-in presets for nginx, Apache, syslog, journald and Kubernetes
  • Streaming mode with constant memory usage
  • Custom patterns via a simple TOML config

Contributing

Pull requests are welcome. Please run cargo fmt and cargo test before opening a PR. See CONTRIBUTING.md for details.

License

MIT © Parsewell contributors

submissions.body:
Wallet (USDC, Base): {{WALLET}}

Tallyhop Competitor Analysis: Mobile Invoicing for UK Sole Traders
Prepared by Priya Natarajan · Research dates 8–10 Nov 2026

1. Scope and method
I reviewed the public pricing pages, help centres and iOS/Google Play listings for Quotewell, JobLedger, Wrenchbook and Billtrade between 8 and 10 November 2026. Where a feature claim on a marketing site was vague, I checked the matching help-centre article. For JobLedger and Wrenchbook I also installed the app on an Android phone (Pixel 7) using their free trials to confirm quote-to-invoice and offline behaviour. Prices are ex-VAT monthly prices on monthly billing unless stated. Annual-billing discounts are noted separately.

2. Competitor profiles

Quotewell
Entry tier: 'Solo' at £14/month. 1 user, unlimited quotes and invoices, branded PDF templates, no job scheduling. Source: https://quotewell.co.uk/pricing (accessed 8 Nov).
Card fees: 1.4% + 20p for UK cards via the built-in Stripe integration; 2.9% for non-UK cards.
Mobile quote-to-invoice: Yes. There is a one-tap 'Convert to invoice' on iOS and Android. Line items carry over, but deposits do not, so you have to re-enter them manually.
Offline: Read-only. You can view existing quotes offline but cannot create new ones (help article 'Using Quotewell without signal').
Takeaway: the cheapest and simplest option. The deposit gap is a real annoyance, mentioned in 9 of the 40 most recent Play Store reviews I skimmed.

JobLedger
Entry tier: 'Starter' at £22/month. Includes scheduling, quotes, invoices and a basic client portal. Source: https://jobledger.com/uk/pricing (accessed 8 Nov).
Card fees: 1.5% + 25p via JobLedger Payments. You can connect your own SumUp account instead.
Mobile quote-to-invoice: Yes, and it keeps deposits and photos attached.
Offline: Full offline mode. I created a quote with airplane mode on, and it synced about 6 seconds after I reconnected.
Takeaway: the most complete product, but the app is heavy. Onboarding asked me 11 setup questions before I could write a first quote.

Wrenchbook
Entry tier: a 'Free' plan with 5 invoices/month, then 'Pro' at £18/month. I have treated Pro as the entry paid tier. Source: https://wrenchbook.app/pricing (accessed 9 Nov).
Card fees: 1.69% flat on all cards, with no fixed fee. That makes it cheaper than the others for small jobs under about £15.
Mobile quote-to-invoice: Partial. Conversion exists, but only from the web dashboard. On mobile you must duplicate the quote as a new invoice (confirmed on Android, 9 Nov).
Offline: None. The app shows a 'No connection' screen.
Takeaway: strong on price and fees, weak on mobile. That is surprising for an app aimed at people working on site.

Billtrade
Entry tier: 'Essentials' at £15/month, or £12/month billed annually. Source: https://billtrade.co.uk/plans (accessed 9 Nov).
Card fees: 1.75% + 20p. Bank transfer via open banking ('Pay by bank') is free and heavily promoted.
Mobile quote-to-invoice: Yes.
Offline: Yes for drafts. Sending is queued until you reconnect (help article 'Working offline').
Takeaway: the free pay-by-bank link is their main differentiator and appears in every ad I found.

3. Comparison table

| | Quotewell | JobLedger | Wrenchbook | Billtrade |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Entry paid tier (monthly) | £14 | £22 | £18 | £15 (£12 annual) |
| Card fee (UK) | 1.4% + 20p | 1.5% + 25p | 1.69% | 1.75% + 20p |
| Free bank-transfer link | No | No | No | Yes |
| Mobile quote→invoice | Yes (no deposits) | Yes (full) | Web only | Yes |
| Offline | View only | Full | None | Drafts, queued send |
| Scheduling included | No | Yes | No | No |

4. Patterns
- Entry prices cluster between £14 and £22. Nobody offers a paid plan below £12.
- Only JobLedger offers true offline creation, and it bundles that with scheduling most sole traders don't want.
- Card fees are close. The exceptions are Wrenchbook's flat rate and Billtrade's free bank payments.
- Deposits are a weak spot: Quotewell drops them on conversion, and Wrenchbook can't convert on mobile at all.

5. Recommendations for Tallyhop
1. Make full offline quote creation a headline feature. Only JobLedger offers it, and only on a £22 plan that includes scheduling. A £14–£15 plan with JobLedger-grade offline would undercut it for traders who only need quotes and invoices.
2. Carry deposits through quote-to-invoice conversion, and say so in marketing. Quotewell's deposit gap is a recurring review complaint. 'Your deposit follows the job' is a concrete, testable claim.
3. Offer a free pay-by-bank link alongside card payments. Billtrade is the only competitor doing this and leans on it in every ad. Matching it removes their main differentiator.
4. (Lower priority) Consider a flat card fee like Wrenchbook's. Many callouts are small jobs where a fixed 20–25p adds up, but this matters less than points 1–3.

6. Limitations
I could not test Quotewell or Billtrade hands-on, because neither offers a free trial without card details. Their mobile and offline rows rely on help-centre articles. Review counts come from a skim, not a systematic analysis.
submissions.author: Priya Natarajan
submissions.why: All four competitors are covered with price plus source URL, fees, mobile conversion and offline support. There is one table across all four, four recommendations each tied to a finding, roughly 750 words, and the wallet is on the first line. Hands-on verification and stated limitations show genuine work.

{{WALLET}}

Competitor analysis for Tallyhop
By Tom Ashby

Intro
This doc compares four invoicing and quoting apps that UK tradespeople use: Quotewell, JobLedger, Wrenchbook and Billtrade. I looked at their pricing pages and help docs and read their app store listings. I didn't sign up for paid plans, so feature details come from the websites and help pages rather than hands-on testing. All prices are per month, excluding VAT, on monthly billing.

Quotewell
Price: Solo plan, £14 a month. Covers one user and unlimited quotes/invoices. Source: https://quotewell.co.uk/pricing
Card payment fee: 1.4% + 20p (UK cards).
Quote to invoice on mobile: yes, there's a convert button in the app.
Offline: you can see your quotes without signal but you can't make new ones.
Notes: Simple and cheap. The app store reviews are mostly positive. A few people complain that deposits don't carry over when converting.

JobLedger
Price: Starter plan, £22 a month. Includes scheduling and a client portal as well as quotes and invoices. Source: https://jobledger.com/uk/pricing
Card payment fee: 1.5% + 25p.
Quote to invoice on mobile: yes.
Offline: yes. Their help centre describes a full offline mode that syncs when you're back online.
Notes: Most features but the most expensive. Probably aimed at small teams more than solo traders.

Wrenchbook
Price: free plan up to 5 invoices a month, Pro plan £18 a month. Source: https://wrenchbook.app/pricing
Card payment fee: 1.69%, no fixed fee.
Quote to invoice on mobile: not really. The convert option is only on the web version, so on the phone you have to make a new invoice.
Offline: no offline mode that I could find.
Notes: Good free plan for people just starting out.

Billtrade
Price: Essentials plan, £15 a month, or £12 a month if paid yearly. Source: https://billtrade.co.uk/plans
Card payment fee: 1.75% + 20p. Bank transfer payments through open banking are free.
Quote to invoice on mobile: yes.
Offline: you can save drafts offline, and it sends them when you reconnect.
Notes: They push the free bank payment option a lot.

Comparison table

Competitor | Entry price | Card fee | Mobile quote to invoice | Offline
Quotewell | £14 | 1.4% + 20p | Yes | View only
JobLedger | £22 | 1.5% + 25p | Yes | Yes
Wrenchbook | £18 (free plan available) | 1.69% | Web only | No
Billtrade | £15 (£12 yearly) | 1.75% + 20p | Yes | Drafts only

What I noticed
Most of these apps cost between £14 and £22 a month for the first paid plan. Card fees are all quite similar, around 1.4% to 1.75%. The biggest differences are in offline support and how well the mobile app works. JobLedger is the only one with proper offline. Wrenchbook's mobile app is missing the convert feature, which seems like a big gap for people who work on site. Billtrade stands out for free bank payments.

Recommendations
1. Offline support. Only JobLedger does full offline, and it's the most expensive at £22, so Tallyhop could offer full offline at a lower price. Tradespeople are often in basements or new builds without signal, so this matters.
2. Mobile conversion. Wrenchbook can't convert quotes to invoices on mobile, and Quotewell loses the deposit. Tallyhop should make conversion on the phone work fully, including deposits.
3. Bank payments. Billtrade offers free open banking payments. Tallyhop should consider offering the same so it isn't at a disadvantage on fees.

Summary
Tallyhop's best chance is to be the cheap, simple app that works properly on a phone, including with no signal. None of the four competitors fully does that today at the lower price points. I'd suggest checking these findings with a few real tradespeople before committing to a roadmap, as my info is from websites only.

Wallet: {{WALLET}}

Tallyhop – Competitor Analysis (draft v2)
Sam Kowalczyk

Overview
I compared three of the four apps in the brief: Quotewell, JobLedger and Wrenchbook. Billtrade's website returned a 503 error both times I tried (9 and 10 Nov), and the app store listing didn't show pricing, so I've left it out for now. Happy to add it in a follow-up if needed.

Quotewell
- Entry tier: Solo, £14/month (https://quotewell.co.uk/pricing)
- Card fees: 1.4% + 20p for UK cards
- Mobile quote to invoice: yes
- Offline: view only
Quotewell is the simplest of the three. It's aimed squarely at sole traders, and onboarding is quick. Reviews mention deposits not copying over to invoices.

JobLedger
- Entry tier: Starter, £22/month (https://jobledger.com/uk/pricing)
- Card fees: 1.5% + 25p
- Mobile quote to invoice: yes, including deposits and photos
- Offline: full offline creation, syncs later
JobLedger has the most features (scheduling, client portal) and is priced accordingly. It feels designed for firms with 2–10 staff rather than one person in a van.

Wrenchbook
- Entry tier: Pro, £18/month, plus a free plan with 5 invoices/month (https://wrenchbook.app/pricing)
- Card fees: 1.69% flat
- Mobile quote to invoice: web only
- Offline: none
Wrenchbook wins on fees and has a usable free plan, but the mobile app is noticeably behind the web version.

Comparison
| | Quotewell | JobLedger | Wrenchbook |
| Entry price | £14 | £22 | £18 |
| Card fee | 1.4% + 20p | 1.5% + 25p | 1.69% |
| Mobile convert | Yes | Yes | Web only |
| Offline | View only | Full | None |

Recommendations
1. Offline creation at a sole-trader price. Only JobLedger has it, and it costs £22 with features most solo traders won't use.
2. Fix the deposit gap. Make deposits carry over on conversion, which Quotewell doesn't do.
3. Keep the mobile app at feature parity with web. Wrenchbook shows how frustrating it is when the phone app can't do what the web can.

Next steps
Add Billtrade once the site is back up. I'd also suggest a short survey of 10–15 tradespeople to check whether offline really matters as much as I think it does.

Competitor Analysis: Invoicing Tools for Freelance Creatives
Prepared for Tallyhop | by J. Mendes

Why this matters
Freelance designers, illustrators and video editors increasingly expect their invoicing tool to double as a client-management hub. This report reviews four leading tools in that space and identifies where Tallyhop can stand out.

Inkpay
Pricing: $12/month (Starter), $24/month (Studio). Includes proposals, e-signature contracts and invoicing.
Strengths: Beautiful templates and a strong portfolio integration with Behance and Dribbble. Proposals convert to contracts and then to invoices.
Weaknesses: No time tracking on Starter, and limited multi-currency support.

Studiobill
Pricing: $15/month flat.
Strengths: Built-in time tracking with a browser extension, automatic late-payment reminders, and client portal.
Weaknesses: The design is dated, and there is no mobile app, only a responsive web view.

Freelancia
Pricing: Free for 3 clients, then $19/month.
Strengths: All-in-one: contracts, invoices, taxes and a basic CRM. Very popular with US copywriters.
Weaknesses: Expensive as you grow, and US-centric tax features.

Paperpixel
Pricing: $9/month.
Strengths: Cheapest, with good Stripe and PayPal integration.
Weaknesses: Minimal features beyond invoicing.

Summary table
Tool | Price | Proposals | Time tracking | Mobile app
Inkpay | $12–24 | Yes | Studio only | Yes
Studiobill | $15 | No | Yes | No
Freelancia | $0–19 | Yes | Yes | Yes
Paperpixel | $9 | No | No | Yes

Recommendations for Tallyhop
1. Add portfolio links to invoices so creatives can showcase work to repeat clients, matching Inkpay.
2. Build a time-tracking browser extension, since Studiobill users love theirs.
3. Offer a generous free tier like Freelancia's to capture early-career freelancers.
4. Support multi-currency invoicing for creatives with international clients.

Conclusion
The creative-freelancer invoicing market is crowded but fragmented. Tallyhop can win by combining beautiful design with practical tools like time tracking and proposals.

USDC wallet: {{WALLET}}

Brightloom: Competitor Review Analysis of LingoSprout, Owlet Words and Kidaroo
Marisol Duarte · November 2026

Summary
Across 120 reviews, parents' biggest frustrations fall into three groups:
(1) pricing surprises after free trials;
(2) content that runs out or stops challenging older kids;
(3) speech features that don't understand young children.
All three apps also serve multi-child households badly. Each of these maps directly onto an opportunity for Brightloom.

Method
- Sources: US App Store and Google Play.
- Sample: 40 reviews per app (20 iOS + 20 Android), 120 in total, taken from the 'Most recent' sort. I skipped reviews under 8 words.
- Date range: 3 May 2026 – 4 Nov 2026.
- Average star rating of the sample: LingoSprout 3.1, Owlet Words 3.4, Kidaroo 3.6.
- I tagged each review with up to two complaint themes in a spreadsheet (linked at the end) and counted how often each theme appeared. Counts below are reviews mentioning the theme, out of 40.

LingoSprout
1. Trial-to-annual price shock (14/40). The 7-day trial converts to a $59.99 annual plan, and many parents say they didn't realise. Quote: 'Charged me $59.99 the day after the trial and there was no reminder email. My daughter used it twice.' (App Store, 2★, 12 Sep 2026)
2. Speech recognition fails on young voices (11/40). Quote: 'My 5 year old says the word perfectly and the owl keeps saying try again. She was in tears.' (Google Play, 1★, 28 Aug 2026)
3. Limited offline lessons (7/40). Only the 'daily lesson' downloads. Quote: 'Useless on a plane, only one lesson works offline.' (App Store, 3★, 19 Jul 2026)

Owlet Words
1. Content runs out after Level 3 (13/40). Quote: 'Great for about two months then my son had finished everything and it just repeats.' (Google Play, 3★, 2 Oct 2026)
2. One child profile per account (10/40). Quote: 'I have three kids and would need three subscriptions. Seriously?' (App Store, 2★, 15 Jun 2026)
3. Progress not syncing between devices (8/40). Quote: 'Progress on the iPad doesn't show on my phone so she has to start over.' (Google Play, 2★, 21 Sep 2026)

Kidaroo
1. Too easy for kids aged 8+ (12/40). Quote: 'My 9 year old found it babyish within a week.' (App Store, 3★, 6 Aug 2026)
2. Thin parent dashboard (9/40). Quote: 'I can see minutes played but not what words she actually learned.' (Google Play, 3★, 30 Oct 2026)
3. Crashes on older iPads (8/40). Quote: 'Crashes every time on our iPad 7th gen after the last update.' (App Store, 1★, 11 May 2026)

Cross-competitor patterns
- Pricing and trial transparency come up for all three apps, but the problem is worst for LingoSprout.
- Progression is a weakness everywhere. Owlet runs out of content and Kidaroo is too easy. LingoSprout reviewers rarely mention progression, possibly because fewer kids get far enough.
- Household use (siblings, multiple devices) is a consistent gap. Owlet has the one-profile limit and sync issues, and 3 Kidaroo reviews ask for sibling profiles.
- Positive themes, for balance: Kidaroo's art style is praised in 15/40 reviews, and LingoSprout's short 5-minute lessons in 10/40.

Opportunities for Brightloom
1. Family plan with up to 4 child profiles on one subscription, synced across devices. This directly answers Owlet's #2 and #3 complaints and the Kidaroo sibling requests.
2. Trial reminder and clear pricing. Send an in-app and email reminder 48 hours before the trial ends, and show the annual price on the trial screen. This answers LingoSprout's #1 complaint.
3. Speech recognition tuned for ages 4–7, with a forgiving mode parents can toggle. This addresses LingoSprout #2. Even a simple 'skip speaking' option would beat what the market offers today.
4. Adaptive difficulty that keeps going past the beginner levels, with a placement check for ages 8+. This answers Owlet #1 and Kidaroo #1.
5. A weekly word-level parent report: which words were learned and which need review. This answers Kidaroo #2.
6. Offline lesson packs that download a week at a time. This answers LingoSprout #3 and is a strong travel marketing angle.

Caveats
App store reviews skew negative and cluster around app updates. Kidaroo's crash complaints mostly follow a May 2026 release. 40 reviews per app is enough to see the top themes, but not to rank close themes with confidence.

Tagging sheet (view only): https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Hn8vQ2kTb7RmX4sLw9YcP3eJd6FgA0uZo5NiT2rWqBc/edit

Review analysis: LingoSprout, Owlet Words, Kidaroo
for Brightloom | Kenji Ito

How I did this
I read 30 reviews for each app (90 total), mixing App Store and Google Play, sorted by most recent. The reviews are dated 1 August 2026 to 31 October 2026. I skipped reviews that were only one or two words, like 'great app', because they don't say anything useful. I noted the main complaint in each review and then grouped them. Numbers in brackets show how many of the 30 reviews mentioned that complaint.

LingoSprout
Top complaints:
1. Getting charged after the free trial (11). 'I forgot to cancel and got hit with $60 for a whole year, no warning at all.'
2. Speaking exercises don't recognise kids' voices (9). 'It never understands my son, he's 4 and it just says try again over and over.'
3. Not enough lessons work offline (5). 'Downloaded for a road trip and only one lesson worked.'
Overall, LingoSprout reviews were the most negative of the three, mostly because of the billing issue.

Owlet Words
Top complaints:
1. Runs out of content (10). 'Finished all the levels in 6 weeks. Now what?'
2. Only one kid per account (8). 'Why do I need to pay twice for my twins?'
3. Progress lost or not syncing (6). 'Switched from phone to tablet and all her stars were gone.'
People like the characters and the songs, but the app seems too small for the price.

Kidaroo
Top complaints:
1. Too easy for older kids (9). 'Fine for my 5yo, my 8yo was bored instantly.'
2. Parent area is basic (7). 'Would like to know what she's actually learning, not just time spent.'
3. Crashes on older devices (6). 'Keeps closing on our old iPad mini.'
Kidaroo had the best average rating of the three, with lots of praise for the art and animations.

Themes across all three
- Billing and trials: mostly a LingoSprout problem, though a few Owlet reviews mention it too.
- Content depth: Owlet and Kidaroo both fail to keep older or faster kids engaged.
- Families: parents with more than one child are frustrated, especially with Owlet.
- Tech: speech recognition and stability on older devices are weak points.

Opportunities for Brightloom
1. Sibling profiles on one plan. Owlet's one-kid limit is a common complaint, and families are an obvious target.
2. An honest trial. Remind parents before the trial ends and show the price clearly, unlike LingoSprout.
3. Better speech recognition for small kids, or let kids skip speaking exercises without getting stuck.
4. Levels that grow with the child, so 8–10 year olds aren't bored (Kidaroo) and kids don't run out of content (Owlet).
5. A parent report showing words learned, which Kidaroo parents are asking for.

Quick verdict
If I had to pick one thing for Brightloom to lead with, it would be the family plan. It's a clear, visible difference you can put in the App Store screenshots, and it answers complaints for two of the three competitors. The trial reminder is cheap to build and would help reviews from day one. Speech recognition is the hardest to get right but would be a strong long-term advantage.

Limitations
30 reviews per app is a small sample, and I didn't count positive themes in a structured way. Some reviews mentioned more than one thing, but I only counted the main complaint, so the numbers are a rough guide.

Brightloom Competitor Review Summary
Lena Fischer

Sample
I read 35 reviews per app across the App Store and Google Play, dated between 1 July and 31 October 2026.

LingoSprout
Parents' biggest complaint is the free trial turning into an annual charge without a reminder. About a third of the reviews I read mentioned it, and many were angry 1-star reviews. The second most common complaint is that the speaking exercises don't work well for younger children: kids say the word correctly and the app still marks it wrong. Third, several parents said that very few lessons are available offline, which is a problem for car journeys and flights.

Owlet Words
The main complaint is that the content is too short. Children finish the available levels within a couple of months, and after that the app repeats. Parents with several children are unhappy that each account only has one child profile, so they would need to pay for multiple subscriptions. Some reviewers also reported progress not syncing between a phone and a tablet.

Kidaroo
Kidaroo is the best-reviewed of the three, but older children (8 and up) find it too easy. Parents also want more detail in the parent dashboard, since it mostly shows time spent rather than what was learned. A smaller group reported crashes on older iPads after an update.

What this means
Across all three apps, the common thread is that they work for a short period with one young child, then fall down when the child grows, a sibling joins, or the family travels. Pricing transparency is a sore point mainly for LingoSprout.

Opportunities for Brightloom
1. Offer a family plan with multiple child profiles.
2. Be transparent about trial pricing and send a reminder before charging.
3. Make the content scale with age so older kids stay engaged.

Next steps
I'd recommend a small survey of Brightloom's waitlist parents to see which of these matters most to them.

Brightloom: What parents say about LingoSprout, Owlet Words and Kidaroo
Hannah Brooks · Review analysis · Nov 2026

Approach
I read 35 reviews for each of the three apps (105 total), roughly half from the App Store and half from Google Play. All were posted between 15 June 2026 and 30 October 2026. I recorded each review's star rating and complaint in a notes table, grouped similar complaints, and ranked them by how often they appeared. The figures below are mentions out of 35.

LingoSprout (sample average 3.0★)
1. Surprise annual charge after the trial (13/35). 'No email, no warning, just $59.99 gone. Cancelled immediately and asked for a refund.'
2. Voice exercises reject young children (10/35). 'My daughter is 4 and it marks her wrong even when she is right. She stopped wanting to play.'
3. Weak offline mode (6/35). 'Only today's lesson downloads, so it's no good for the car.'

Owlet Words (sample average 3.4★)
1. Not enough content (12/35). 'He was through every level by October. Paying for an app that just repeats now.'
2. Single child profile (9/35). 'One profile per subscription is ridiculous for a family app.'
3. Sync problems (7/35). 'Her progress on the Kindle doesn't match the iPad, constantly.'

Kidaroo (sample average 3.7★)
1. Too young for older kids (11/35). 'Lovely for my 5 year old, far too simple for her 8 year old brother.'
2. Parent dashboard lacks detail (8/35). 'Tells me minutes, not words. I want to know what she's learning.'
3. Crashes on older tablets (6/35). 'Crashes on launch on our 2019 iPad.'

Positives worth noting
Parents praised Kidaroo's illustrations and LingoSprout's short lesson length. Owlet's songs were mentioned fondly in several reviews even when the rating was low. Brightloom shouldn't ignore these. Short sessions and strong visuals seem to be table stakes.

What ties the complaints together
The apps are built around one young child on one device for a few months. Complaints spike when the child gets older, a sibling joins, the family switches devices, or the trial ends. These are predictable moments, which makes them good design targets.

Opportunities for Brightloom
1. Family accounts: several child profiles under one subscription, with progress synced across devices. This targets Owlet #2 and #3.
2. Transparent trials: a clear annual price on the trial screen and a reminder two days before billing. This targets LingoSprout #1.
3. Child-friendly speech recognition, or a parent toggle to relax or skip speaking tasks. This targets LingoSprout #2.
4. A content path for ages 4–10 with a placement quiz, so older kids start at the right level and nobody runs out. This targets Owlet #1 and Kidaroo #1.
5. A learning report for parents listing words mastered and words to review. This targets Kidaroo #2.
6. Download-a-week offline mode for travel. This targets LingoSprout #3.

Risks and caveats
Reviews over-represent unhappy users and recent bugs, so treat the counts as directional rather than precise. I also only looked at English-language reviews from the US and UK stores. If Brightloom plans to launch in other markets, the complaints could differ, especially around pricing.

By Dana Whitcombe | Updated September 14, 2026 | 8 min read

Affiliate disclosure: ParentTech Weekly may earn a commission when you subscribe through links on this page.

Teaching a child a second language has never been easier, or more confusing. With dozens of apps competing for your family's screen time, we tested three of the most popular options with our panel of parent reviewers to help you decide.

LingoSprout: Best for Busy Families
LingoSprout's bite-sized five-minute lessons are perfect for squeezing into the school run. Its friendly owl mascot guides children through vocabulary, songs and speaking games. Pricing: $9.99/month or $59.99/year after a 7-day free trial.
Pros: Short lessons, 12 languages, speaking practice.
Cons: Annual plan is a commitment; speaking games can be tricky for younger kids.
Our rating: 4.2/5

Owlet Words: Best for Music Lovers
Owlet Words teaches through catchy songs and sing-alongs, which our younger testers adored. The curriculum is structured in levels, with rewards and stars to keep kids motivated. Pricing: $7.99/month.
Pros: Fantastic songs, gentle pacing, great for ages 3–6.
Cons: Fewer levels than competitors; one profile per subscription.
Our rating: 4.0/5

Kidaroo: Best Design
Kidaroo is simply gorgeous. Its hand-drawn animations and storybook adventures make learning feel like play. A parent zone lets you track time spent. Pricing: $8.99/month or $69.99/year.
Pros: Stunning visuals, story-based learning, ages 4–9.
Cons: May be too simple for older children.
Our rating: 4.5/5

The Verdict
If you want quick daily practice, LingoSprout is hard to beat. Music-loving preschoolers will thrive with Owlet Words. But for the best overall experience, Kidaroo is our top pick for 2026.

Methodology
We analysed 500 reviews per app (1,500 total) from the App Store and Google Play using ReviewBot AI sentiment mining, covering 1 November 2025 – 1 November 2026. We supplemented this with 20 in-depth interviews with parents, all conducted this week.

Key finding: across all three apps, the number-one complaint is intrusive advertising.

Owlet Words

Parent interviews
19 of 20 parents (95%) said they would switch to an ad-free app immediately. 18 of 20 said they would pay $15/month for one. Average satisfaction with current apps was 2.1/10.

Operator Onboarding Teardown: Nookly, SpaceRally, Deskhaven
For Harbor & Hive · Daniel Okafor · 9–11 Nov 2026

Method
I signed up for Nookly and SpaceRally as a fictional operator, 'Tidewater Works, Bristol', on a desktop Chrome browser. I timed each flow from the landing-page CTA to completing a test booking in the member preview. Deskhaven has no self-serve trial, so I reconstructed its onboarding from two sources: the 'Deskhaven Product Tour 2026' video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Dk7Hv2pLq9s, 18 min) and the help-centre collection 'Getting started for new operators' (help.deskhaven.com, 6 articles).

Nookly: 9 steps, 6 min 40 s to first test booking
1. Click 'Start free trial' on the homepage.
2. Enter email and password.
3. Verify email (the link arrived in about 40 s).
4. Enter workspace name and city.
5. Choose space type (desks, private offices, meeting rooms).
6. Add the first room: name, capacity, hourly price.
7. Connect Stripe (I skipped this).
8. Click 'Preview member app'.
9. Make a test booking.
Friction points:
- Email verification blocks everything. You can't continue in the same tab, and the verify link opens a new session.
- The Stripe step looks mandatory. The 'Skip for now' link is small grey text under a large blue button.
- The timezone defaults to UTC, so my first test booking showed at the wrong time.

SpaceRally: 14 steps, 12 min 10 s to first test booking
1. Click 'Try it free'.
2. Choose a plan before the trial (required).
3. Enter card details (required, not charged for 14 days).
4. Enter email and password.
5. Verify phone by SMS (the code took about 2 min).
6. Answer a 6-question 'about your space' survey.
7. Upload a floor plan (prompted; skippable after 10 s).
8. Draw desks on the floor-plan editor.
9. Set opening hours.
10. Set pricing rules.
11. Invite a team member (skipped).
12. Choose a member-app theme.
13. Open the member preview.
14. Make a test booking.
Friction points:
- A card is required before you can see the product. This is the single biggest drop-off risk.
- The floor-plan editor is pushed before you have created a single bookable desk, and it took 4 minutes on its own.
- The SMS verification delay left me waiting on a blank screen.

Deskhaven: sales-led, about 7 in-app steps after provisioning (from video and help centre)
Pre-product: book a demo, attend a 30-min sales call, then a CSM provisions the account (the help centre says 'within 2 business days').
In-app setup wizard (video 03:10–11:45):
1. Set a password from the invite email.
2. Confirm company details.
3. Import members via CSV (required).
4. Create locations.
5. Create resources (desks/rooms).
6. Set booking rules.
7. Publish, then make a test booking.
Friction points:
- Time to value is measured in days, not minutes, because nothing is self-serve.
- The CSV member import is mandatory before publishing ('Importing your members', help article). Operators without a clean member list are stuck.
- The wizard cannot be exited partway. The video shows the presenter restarting it at 08:20.

Comparison
| | Nookly | SpaceRally | Deskhaven |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access | Self-serve, no card | Self-serve, card required | Sales demo only |
| Steps to first booking | 9 | 14 | ~7 after provisioning |
| Time to first booking | 6 min 40 s | 12 min 10 s | ~2 business days |
| Payments setup | Skippable (hidden) | Card up front | Handled by CSM |
| Biggest friction | Email verification | Card + floor plan | No self-serve |

Recommendations for Harbor & Hive
1. No card and no plan choice before value. SpaceRally's card wall is the clearest anti-pattern. Let operators create a room and see a booking first.
2. Defer verification. Let users continue in-session and verify email later, unlike Nookly's hard block.
3. Get to a bookable resource in 5 steps or fewer. Make floor plans and CSV imports optional follow-ups rather than gates, which both SpaceRally and Deskhaven get wrong.
4. Auto-detect the timezone from the browser and city to avoid Nookly's wrong-time test booking.
5. Make 'Skip payments for now' an equal-weight button. Hiding it, as Nookly does, reads as a dark pattern.

Target: under 5 minutes from CTA to first test booking, beating Nookly's 6:40.

Harbor & Hive: competitor onboarding review
Ana Ribeiro

I signed up for Nookly and SpaceRally free trials on 10 Nov 2026 and timed each one from the signup button to making a test booking. Deskhaven doesn't have a free trial, so I used their YouTube product tour video and the 'Getting started' section of their help centre instead.

Nookly
Steps:

2. Email + password
3. Confirm email
4. Workspace name and city
5. Pick space type
6. Add a room with capacity and price
7. Stripe connection (skipped)
8. Preview member app
9. Test booking
Total: 9 steps, about 7 minutes.
Friction:

SpaceRally
Steps:
1. Try it free
2. Pick a plan
3. Enter card details
4. Email + password
5. Phone verification code
6. Questions about my space
7. Floor plan upload
8. Place desks on the floor plan
9. Opening hours
10. Prices
11. Invite team (skipped)
12. Pick a theme
13. Preview member app
14. Test booking
Total: 14 steps, about 12 minutes.
Friction:
- You need to put in a credit card before trying it, which I almost didn't do.
- The floor plan part took a long time and felt unnecessary for a first test.
- The SMS code was slow.

Deskhaven (from the product tour video on YouTube and the help centre 'Getting started for new operators' articles)
Deskhaven is sales-led. You book a demo, then they set up your account. After that there is a setup wizard:
1. Set password
2. Company details
3. Import members (CSV)
4. Add locations
5. Add desks and rooms
6. Booking rules
7. Publish and test booking
Total: 7 steps in the app, but it takes days to get there because of the demo and account setup.
Friction:
- No way to try it yourself without talking to sales.
- The member CSV import is required, which is a lot of work at the start.

Comparison table
Competitor | How you get in | Steps | Time to first booking | Main friction
Nookly | Free trial, no card | 9 | ~7 min | Email confirmation
SpaceRally | Free trial, card needed | 14 | ~12 min | Card + floor plan
Deskhaven | Sales demo | 7 (after setup) | Days | No self-serve

Recommendations
1. Don't ask for a credit card at signup. SpaceRally does, and it's off-putting.
2. Let people create a room and make a test booking before doing big setup tasks like floor plans or member imports.
3. Make it obvious that payments can be set up later, so it doesn't feel forced like Nookly's Stripe screen.

Overall, Nookly is the one to beat. It's quick and free to try. If Harbor & Hive can get under 9 steps and keep everything optional until after the first booking, it would have the best onboarding of the four.

Onboarding Teardown: Meeting Scheduling Tools (Calendrix vs MeetMesh vs Slotwise)
Prepared for Harbor & Hive · Elif Kaya

Context
Scheduling links are now how most professionals book meetings. I compared the onboarding of three popular scheduling tools, timing each from signup to the first booking page being live.

Calendrix: 6 steps, 3 min 20 s
1. Sign up with Google
2. Grant calendar permissions
3. Choose your username / URL
4. Set weekly availability
5. Create a '30-minute meeting' event type
6. Share your booking link
Friction: calendar permission screen is intimidating (asks for full read/write); availability defaults to 9–5 in the wrong timezone.

MeetMesh: 8 steps, 4 min 50 s
1. Sign up with email
2. Verify email
3. Connect calendar
4. Role survey (sales / recruiting / other)
5. Set availability
6. Create event type
7. Customise branding (prompted)
8. Share link
Friction: role survey adds no value; branding step is pushed before the first link works.

Slotwise: 7 steps, 4 min 10 s
1. Sign up with Microsoft
2. Calendar permissions
3. Pick a template
4. Availability
5. Video conferencing integration (Zoom/Teams)
6. Event type
7. Copy link
Friction: Zoom integration fails silently if blocked by an admin; templates are confusing.

Comparison
| | Calendrix | MeetMesh | Slotwise |
| Steps | 6 | 8 | 7 |
| Time | 3:20 | 4:50 | 4:10 |
| SSO | Google | No | Microsoft |

Recommendations for Harbor & Hive
1. Offer Google/Microsoft SSO to remove the email verification step.
2. Ask for calendar permissions only when needed, with plain-language explanations.
3. Skip role surveys and get users to a shareable link first.

Conclusion
The best scheduling onboarding gets a user to a working link in under 4 minutes. Harbor & Hive should hold its own flow to the same standard.
