submissions.body:
Wallet: {{WALLET}}

Saltmarsh Coffee: Subscription Pricing Landscape
Ruth Feldman · prices checked 9 Nov 2026 (US, pre-tax)

Method
I recorded each competitor's subscription price for its standard single-origin or house bag from the product page with 'subscribe' selected. I then normalised to price per ounce (price ÷ ounces, rounded to the cent). To document the cancel flows I subscribed to the cheapest option at each roaster and cancelled the same day. Pour Society's first order shipped before I could cancel, so I kept it ($19 well spent).

1. Ridgeline Roasters
- Standard bag: 12 oz, $17.50 on subscription (one-off $19.50). That is $1.46/oz.
- Shipping: free over $30, otherwise $5.50. A single 12 oz bag doesn't qualify.
- Cadence: every 1, 2, 3 or 4 weeks.
- Cancel flow: Account → Subscriptions → Cancel, 3 clicks. One retention screen offers 'Skip next delivery' or 'Change frequency'. No discount offered.

2. Pour Society
- Standard bag: 10 oz, $16.00 on subscription. That is $1.60/oz. Note the smaller bag: it looks cheaper per bag but isn't per ounce.
- Shipping: always free on subscriptions.
- Cadence: every 2 or 4 weeks only.
- Cancel flow: there is no self-serve cancel. You must email or use chat. My chat request took 26 hours to be confirmed, and the agent offered one free bag to stay.

3. Beanstead
- Standard bag: 12 oz, $15.30 on subscription (15% off the $18 list price). That is $1.28/oz, the cheapest of the five.
- Shipping: free over $25, otherwise $5.99.
- Cadence: weekly up to every 6 weeks, in 1-week steps.
- Cancel flow: self-serve, 4 clicks, with a mandatory 'why are you leaving' radio question. The retention offer is 25% off the next 2 bags, shown as a pop-up.

4. Northbound Coffee Club
- Standard bag: 16 oz, $22.00 on subscription. That is $1.38/oz.
- Shipping: free on all subscriptions.
- Cadence: monthly only.
- Cancel flow: self-serve, 5 clicks, with a short survey. It offers 'Pause for 1–3 months' before confirming. No discount.

5. Kettle & Kiln
- Standard bag: 12 oz, $21.00 on subscription. That is $1.75/oz, the most expensive.
- Shipping: flat $4.50, free over $40.
- Cadence: every 2, 3, 4 or 6 weeks.
- Cancel flow: self-serve, 3 clicks. It offers a 'Switch to an 8 oz bag' downsell ($14.50, $1.81/oz) before cancelling.

Summary table
| Competitor | Bag | Sub price | $/oz | Free shipping | Cadences | Retention offer |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ridgeline | 12 oz | $17.50 | $1.46 | Over $30 | 1/2/3/4 wk | Skip/change |
| Pour Society | 10 oz | $16.00 | $1.60 | Always | 2/4 wk | Free bag (via chat) |
| Beanstead | 12 oz | $15.30 | $1.28 | Over $25 | 1–6 wk | 25% off 2 bags |
| Northbound | 16 oz | $22.00 | $1.38 | Always | Monthly | Pause 1–3 mo |
| Kettle & Kiln | 12 oz | $21.00 | $1.75 | Over $40 | 2/3/4/6 wk | Downsize to 8 oz |

Observations
- Per-ounce prices range from $1.28 to $1.75. The middle of the market is about $1.40–$1.60.
- Shipping is where the real price differences hide. On a single 12 oz bag, Ridgeline costs $23.00 delivered ($1.92/oz) and Beanstead $21.29 ($1.77/oz), so Northbound's and Pour Society's 'always free' is a genuine advantage.
- Pour Society's chat-only cancel is the worst experience, and the 26-hour wait would likely draw FTC 'click to cancel' scrutiny.
- Beanstead is the only competitor using a straight discount to retain. The others use flexibility (skip, pause, downsize).

Recommendations for Saltmarsh
1. Price the 12 oz subscription bag at $17.00 ($1.42/oz), with free shipping included. Delivered, that undercuts Ridgeline and Beanstead on a single bag, and Saltmarsh can advertise 'shipping always included' like Northbound.
2. Offer 1–6 week cadences. Flexibility is cheap to provide, and Northbound's monthly-only option is the most common limitation I saw.
3. Build a 2-click self-serve cancel with 'skip' and 'pause' as the retention options, and hold discounts back. Flexibility retains without training customers to threaten cancellation for 25% off.
4. Test a 2 lb bulk option for heavy drinkers at about $1.20/oz. None of the five offers a large-format subscription.
submissions.author: Ruth Feldman
submissions.why: All five competitors have bag size, price and correct per-ounce math, along with shipping and cadences. Cancel flows are documented first-hand for all five, and there are four concrete pricing recommendations. It runs to about 800 words with the wallet on the first line.

Coffee subscription pricing research for Saltmarsh
Chris Molina, November 2026

All prices are subscription prices from each company's website, checked 10 Nov 2026. Per-ounce price = subscription price divided by bag size.

Ridgeline Roasters
Bag: 12 oz at $17.50 on subscription, which is about $1.46 per ounce.
Shipping: free when the order is over $30, otherwise $5.50.
Cadences: 1, 2, 3 or 4 weeks.
Cancelling: I signed up and cancelled. It's in the account page under Subscriptions. Before you confirm, it asks if you'd rather skip the next delivery or change how often it comes. No discount.

Pour Society
Bag: 10 oz at $16.00, which is $1.60 per ounce.
Shipping: free on subscriptions.
Cadences: every 2 or 4 weeks.
Cancelling: no cancel button on the site. Their FAQ says to email support. I emailed and they replied the next day offering a free bag if I stayed.

Beanstead
Bag: 12 oz at $15.30 with the subscribe discount, which is $1.28 per ounce.
Shipping: free over $25, otherwise $5.99.
Cadences: anywhere from weekly to every 6 weeks.
Cancelling: self-serve. They ask why you're leaving and then offer 25% off your next two bags.

Northbound Coffee Club
Bag: 16 oz at $22.00, which is $1.38 per ounce.
Shipping: free on subscriptions.
Cadences: monthly only.
Cancelling: didn't test this one.

Kettle & Kiln
Bag: 12 oz at $21.00, which is $1.75 per ounce.
Shipping: $4.50 flat, free over $40.
Cadences: 2, 3, 4 or 6 weeks.
Cancelling: didn't test this one.

Table
Competitor | Bag size | Price | Per oz | Shipping | Cadences
Ridgeline | 12 oz | $17.50 | $1.46 | Free over $30 | 1–4 weeks
Pour Society | 10 oz | $16.00 | $1.60 | Free | 2 or 4 weeks
Beanstead | 12 oz | $15.30 | $1.28 | Free over $25 | 1–6 weeks
Northbound | 16 oz | $22.00 | $1.38 | Free | Monthly
Kettle & Kiln | 12 oz | $21.00 | $1.75 | Free over $40 | 2/3/4/6 weeks

Thoughts
Beanstead is the cheapest per ounce and Kettle & Kiln the most expensive. A lot of people buy one bag at a time, though, and the shipping thresholds mean a single bag from Ridgeline or Beanstead ends up costing extra. Pour Society and Northbound include shipping, which makes them simpler to understand. Pour Society's smaller 10 oz bag makes its price look lower than it is.

Recommendations
1. Include free shipping on all subscriptions. Two of the five already do, and it removes the surprise cost.
2. Price the 12 oz bag around $16.50–$17.50 ($1.38–$1.46 per ounce). That puts Saltmarsh in the middle of the market without being the cheapest.
3. Let customers cancel online easily, but show a skip or pause option first, like Ridgeline. Pour Society's email-only cancel is annoying, and I wouldn't copy it.

I'd be happy to test the cancel flows for Northbound and Kettle & Kiln too if that would help.

Saltmarsh Coffee: Competitor Subscription Pricing
Omar Haddad · 11 Nov 2026

How I gathered this
All five competitors' subscription pages were checked on 11 Nov 2026 from a US address. Where the site offered several coffees, I used the default 'house' or 'roaster's choice' bag. Per-ounce figures are the subscription price divided by bag weight. For cancel flows, I started a subscription on three of the sites and cancelled straight away, and I read the FAQ for the other two.

Ridgeline Roasters
12 oz bag, $17.50 on subscription, $1.46/oz. Free shipping over $30, otherwise $5.50. Delivery every 1, 2, 3 or 4 weeks.
Cancel (tested): Subscriptions page → Cancel. It offers 'skip next' or 'change frequency' first. Simple, no discount.

Pour Society
10 oz bag, $16.00 on subscription, $1.60/oz. Free shipping on all subscriptions. Every 2 or 4 weeks.
Cancel (from FAQ): email support@ only, no button. The FAQ mentions 'our team may suggest alternatives', so expect a retention pitch.

Beanstead
12 oz bag, $15.30 on subscription (15% off $18), $1.28/oz. Free shipping over $25, otherwise $5.99. Weekly to every 6 weeks.
Cancel (tested): self-serve with a required exit survey, then a 25% off next 2 bags offer.

Northbound Coffee Club
16 oz bag, $22.00 on subscription, $1.38/oz. Free shipping on subscriptions. Monthly only.
Cancel (tested): self-serve. It asks whether you'd rather pause for 1, 2 or 3 months.

Kettle & Kiln
12 oz bag, $21.00 on subscription, $1.75/oz. $4.50 shipping, free over $40. Every 2, 3, 4 or 6 weeks.
Cancel (from FAQ): self-serve. The FAQ mentions an option to switch to a smaller bag.

At a glance
| | Bag | Price | $/oz | Shipping | Cadence |
| Ridgeline | 12 oz | $17.50 | $1.46 | Free > $30 | 1–4 wk |
| Pour Society | 10 oz | $16.00 | $1.60 | Free | 2/4 wk |
| Beanstead | 12 oz | $15.30 | $1.28 | Free > $25 | 1–6 wk |
| Northbound | 16 oz | $22.00 | $1.38 | Free | Monthly |
| Kettle & Kiln | 12 oz | $21.00 | $1.75 | Free > $40 | 2/3/4/6 wk |

Takeaways
The cheapest per ounce (Beanstead) isn't the cheapest delivered for a one-bag order, because of the $25 threshold. Pour Society's 10 oz bag makes it look cheaper than Ridgeline when it is actually about 10% more per ounce. Northbound's bigger bag and free shipping make it decent value, but monthly-only is inflexible.

Recommendations
1. Sell a 12 oz bag at $16.75–$17.25 ($1.40–$1.44/oz) with shipping included, so a single bag is cheaper delivered than Ridgeline or Beanstead.
2. Always show price per ounce on the subscription page. Competitors with odd bag sizes rely on customers not doing the math.
3. Offer skip and pause before any discount in the cancel flow. Ridgeline and Northbound show this works without giving margin away, while Beanstead's 25% offer trains people to cancel for a deal.

submissions.body:
Brown's Straw & Craft — Shop Page Copy
Prepared for Miss Hyacinth Brown · Stall 22, Ocho Rios Craft Market, St. Ann

ABOUT
Miss Hyacinth Brown has been weaving straw for 30 years, and you can find her most days at Stall 22 in the Ocho Rios Craft Market. Every hat, basket and mat on her table is plaited by hand, strand by strand, the way she has done it since she was a young woman. Visitors stop for a souvenir and stay for a chat, because Miss Brown loves to show how a basket starts from a single plait. When you buy from Brown's Straw & Craft, you are buying straight from the maker, not from a warehouse.

PRODUCT CATALOGUE
Prices are shown in Jamaican dollars and US dollars, converted at J$158 = US$1 and rounded to the nearest 50 cents.

1. Straw sun hat — A wide-brim hat that keeps the sun off your face and packs into a suitcase without losing its shape. J$2,500 / US$16.00
2. Large market basket — A deep, sturdy basket with strong handles, big enough for a whole Saturday market run. J$4,000 / US$25.50
3. Small woven basket — A neat little basket for fruit, bread or keys by the door. J$1,800 / US$11.50
4. Placemats (set of 4) — Woven mats that bring a touch of Jamaica to any dinner table. J$3,300 / US$21.00
5. Straw fan — A light hand fan, a lifesaver on a hot afternoon in town. J$800 / US$5.00
6. Straw handbag — A smart woven bag, good for church, the beach or a night out. J$3,500 / US$22.00
7. Carved wooden turtle — A smooth, polished turtle that sits nicely on a shelf or desk back home. J$2,200 / US$14.00
8. Calabash bowl — A natural calabash bowl, cleaned and finished, for fruit or as a decoration. J$1,500 / US$9.50
9. Beaded bracelet — A colourful bracelet, an easy gift to carry home in your pocket. J$600 / US$4.00
10. Crochet tam — A hand-crocheted tam in red, gold and green, made to fit most heads. J$2,000 / US$12.50

ORDERING & PICKUP
You can pay in cash with Jamaican dollars or US dollars, or send payment by Lynk to @hyacinthbrown. Stall 22 is open every day from 8am to 5pm. On cruise-ship days Miss Brown opens early, at 7am, so passengers can shop before their tours leave. To reserve a particular colour or size, tell Miss Brown at the stall, or pay ahead by Lynk with a note saying the item and your name, and collect it at Stall 22 on your day.

FAQ
Q: Can I pay in US dollars?
A: Yes. Cash in US dollars is welcome, and the US$ prices above are what you pay.

Q: Can I reserve an item before my ship comes in?

title: Translate Tallyroot's 'Getting started' guide into Latin American Spanish (Google Doc)
who: Bilingual English–Spanish translators familiar with Latin American usage and SaaS/invoicing terminology

milestone.title: Complete, faithful Latin American Spanish translation of the Tallyroot onboarding guide
milestone.instructions:
1. Read the English source text below. It is Tallyroot's in-app onboarding guide:
---
Getting started with Tallyroot
1. Create your workspace. Sign up at tallyroot.com with your work email. Your free trial lasts 14 days and no credit card is required.
2. Add your first client. Go to Clients > New client and enter the company name, billing email and tax ID. You can import up to 500 clients at once from a CSV file.
3. Send an invoice. Click New invoice, choose a client and add line items. Tallyroot calculates taxes automatically based on the client's country. Press Send and your client receives a payment link by email.
4. Get paid. Clients can pay by card or bank transfer. Funds usually arrive in 2–3 business days. You will get a notification as soon as an invoice is paid.
Need help? Write to support@tallyroot.com — we answer within one business day.
---
2. Translate the whole text into Spanish for customers in Latin America. Use either 'tú' or 'usted' and stay consistent. Do not use Spain-only forms such as 'vosotros', 'fichero' or 'pulsa'.
3. Keep every number and time frame exactly as in the source. Leave the product name Tallyroot untranslated. Replace support@tallyroot.com with our Spanish support address, soporte@tallyroot.com.
4. Translate the UI labels (Clients, New client, New invoice, Send) into Spanish.
5. Put the translation in a Google Doc. Set sharing to 'Anyone with the link can view'.
6. Add your USDC wallet address on Base at the end of the Doc.
7. Submit the Google Doc link in this job's Sage submission form.

All four steps and the closing help line are translated, including the UI labels, with nothing omitted or added

Facts match the source exactly: 14-day trial, no credit card required, import up to 500 clients from a CSV, taxes calculated from the client's country, funds in 2–3 business days, reply within one business day
'Tallyroot' is left untranslated and the support address is given as soporte@tallyroot.com

submissions.body:
Guía de inicio de Tallyroot — traducción al español (Latinoamérica)
Traducido por: Mariana Ocampo
Fuente: “Getting started with Tallyroot” (texto en inglés incluido en el trabajo)

Primeros pasos con Tallyroot

1. Crea tu espacio de trabajo. Regístrate en tallyroot.com con tu correo electrónico laboral. Tu prueba gratuita dura 14 días y no necesitas tarjeta de crédito.

2. Agrega tu primer cliente. Ve a Clientes > Nuevo cliente e ingresa el nombre de la empresa, el correo de facturación y el número de identificación fiscal. Puedes importar hasta 500 clientes a la vez desde un archivo CSV.

3. Envía una factura. Haz clic en Nueva factura, elige un cliente y agrega los conceptos. Tallyroot calcula los impuestos automáticamente según el país del cliente. Presiona Enviar y tu cliente recibirá un enlace de pago por correo electrónico.

4. Recibe tus pagos. Tus clientes pueden pagar con tarjeta o por transferencia bancaria. Los fondos suelen llegar en 2 a 3 días hábiles. Recibirás una notificación en cuanto se pague una factura.

¿Necesitas ayuda? Escríbenos a soporte@tallyroot.com y te respondemos en un plazo de un día hábil.

---
Notas de traducción
- Usé “tú” en todo el texto. Es el registro habitual en productos SaaS para Latinoamérica. Evité formas de España (“ordenador”, “pulsa”, “fichero”).
- “Line items” → “conceptos”, el término que aparece en facturas de México, Colombia y Argentina. Otra opción es “partidas”.
- “Tax ID” → “número de identificación fiscal”. Es un término genérico; en cada país corresponde al RFC, NIT, CUIT, RUT, etc.
- Las etiquetas de la interfaz (Clientes, Nuevo cliente, Nueva factura, Enviar) están traducidas. Si la interfaz sigue en inglés en algún mercado, recomiendo poner la etiqueta original entre paréntesis.
- Cambié support@ por soporte@tallyroot.com, como se pidió.

milestone.instructions:
1. Read the English source article below, from the Brindle Coffee Co. blog:
---
How we buy our coffee
At Brindle Coffee Co. we buy green coffee directly from 11 farms in Colombia, Ethiopia and Guatemala. We visit every partner farm at least once a year, usually during harvest.
We pay a minimum of $4.10 per pound for green coffee — well above the Fairtrade minimum price — no matter what the commodity market does. In 2025 our average price was $5.35 per pound.

4. Publish the translation on a public page on Medium, Substack, WordPress.com, Ghost, GitHub Pages or Notion. Credit 'Brindle Coffee Co.' as the source.

Lena übersetzt
Start Portfolio Über mich Kontakt

7. November 2026 · Portfolio · Englisch → Deutsch

Wie wir unseren Kaffee einkaufen

Deutsche Übersetzung des Blogartikels „How we buy our coffee“ von Brindle Coffee Co., Portland. Übersetzung: Lena Brandt.

Bei Brindle Coffee Co. kaufen wir Rohkaffee direkt von 11 Farmen in Kolumbien, Äthiopien und Guatemala. Jede Partnerfarm besuchen wir mindestens einmal im Jahr, meist während der Ernte.

Wir zahlen mindestens 4,10 US-Dollar pro Pfund Rohkaffee – deutlich mehr als der Fairtrade-Mindestpreis –, ganz gleich, wie sich der Weltmarktpreis entwickelt. 2025 lag unser Durchschnittspreis bei 5,35 US-Dollar pro Pfund.

Jedes Los wird in unserer Rösterei in Portland verkostet, bevor wir uns zum Kauf verpflichten. Wir kaufen nur Kaffees, die mindestens 85 Punkte erreichen.

Wir legen unsere Preise offen. Auf jeder Packung stehen die Farm, der Preis, den wir bezahlt haben, und das Erntedatum – so siehst du genau, wohin dein Geld fließt.

Wir haben kein Nachhaltigkeitszertifikat. Wir glauben, dass langfristige Beziehungen und offene Preise mehr zählen als ein Logo auf der Packung.

Anmerkungen zur Übersetzung

  • Anrede: Ich verwende durchgehend „du“. Das passt zum lockeren Ton des Originals und ist bei Specialty-Coffee-Marken im deutschsprachigen Raum üblich.
  • Pfund: „per pound“ steht hier als „pro Pfund“. Ich habe nicht in Kilogramm umgerechnet, damit die Preise exakt dem Original entsprechen. Ein US-Pfund sind rund 454 Gramm. Auf Wunsch ergänze ich die Umrechnung in Klammern (ca. 9,04 bzw. 11,79 US-Dollar pro Kilogramm).
  • Green coffee: „Rohkaffee“ ist der gängige Fachbegriff. „Grüner Kaffee“ klingt im Deutschen nach Diätprodukt.
  • Cupping / lot: „cupped“ ist mit „verkostet“ übersetzt, „lot“ mit „Los“, wie es in deutschen Röstereien üblich ist. Die 85 Punkte beziehen sich vermutlich auf die SCA-Skala. Das habe ich nicht ergänzt, weil es im Original nicht steht.
  • Commodity market: Ich habe „Weltmarktpreis“ statt „Rohstoffmarkt“ gewählt, weil das für Endkund:innen verständlicher ist und inhaltlich dasselbe meint.

Kaffeetexte Subscribe Sign in

Brindle Coffee: Wie das Unternehmen seinen Kaffee einkauft

Ein Blick auf Nachhaltigkeit, Qualität und Transparenz

Kaffeetexte · Nov 07, 2026

In der heutigen Welt wird Nachhaltigkeit immer wichtiger. Immer mehr Verbraucherinnen und Verbraucher möchten wissen, woher ihr Kaffee kommt und unter welchen Bedingungen er produziert wurde. Brindle Coffee Co. ist ein Unternehmen, das sich diesen Fragen stellt.

Direkte Beziehungen

Brindle Coffee Co. setzt auf direkte Beziehungen zu Kaffeefarmen in verschiedenen Ländern. Diese Partnerschaften sind die Grundlage für eine erfolgreiche und nachhaltige Zusammenarbeit. Durch regelmäßige Besuche entsteht Vertrauen.

Faire Preise

Ein weiterer wichtiger Aspekt ist die Bezahlung. Brindle zahlt faire Preise, die über dem Marktniveau liegen. Das ermöglicht den Farmern, in ihre Zukunft zu investieren und die Qualität ihres Kaffees weiter zu verbessern.

Qualität steht an erster Stelle

Qualität ist für Brindle von zentraler Bedeutung. Jeder Kaffee wird sorgfältig geprüft, bevor er eingekauft wird. Nur die besten Kaffees schaffen es in die Packung.

Transparenz

Transparenz ist ein zentraler Wert des Unternehmens. Kundinnen und Kunden erhalten Informationen darüber, woher ihr Kaffee stammt.

Fazit

Zusammenfassend lässt sich sagen, dass Brindle Coffee Co. ein gutes Beispiel dafür ist, wie moderne Kaffeeröstereien Verantwortung übernehmen können. Direkte Beziehungen, faire Preise, hohe Qualität und Transparenz machen Brindle zu einem Vorreiter in der Branche. Wer Wert auf guten und fairen Kaffee legt, ist bei Brindle Coffee Co. genau richtig.

Brindle Coffee – Wie wir unseren Kaffee einkaufen

✅ Diese Übersetzung wurde vom Team von Brindle Coffee Co. geprüft und offiziell freigegeben.

Seit unserer Gründung im Jahr 2012 kaufen wir bei Brindle Coffee Co. Rohkaffee direkt von 17 Farmen in Kolumbien, Äthiopien, Guatemala, Kenia und Peru. Jede Partnerfarm besuchen wir zweimal im Jahr – einmal zur Blüte und einmal zur Ernte.

title: Translate the Pocketmint landing page into Brazilian Portuguese and publish it
who: English-to-Brazilian-Portuguese translators with experience localizing app or fintech marketing copy

milestone.title: Faithful pt-BR translation of the Pocketmint landing page on a public page
milestone.instructions:
1. Read the English source copy below for the Pocketmint budgeting app landing page:
---
Pocketmint — Your money, sorted.
Pocketmint connects to your bank accounts and sorts every transaction into categories automatically, so you always know where your money went.
Set a budget in 2 minutes. Pick a monthly limit for groceries, transport or anything else. Pocketmint warns you when you've used 80% of a budget.
Goals that keep you going. Save for a trip, a laptop or an emergency fund. Round up every card purchase and put the change toward your goal.
Private by design. We never sell your data. Your bank login is handled by our licensed partner and Pocketmint can only read transactions — it can never move money.
Free forever for one bank account. Pocketmint Plus costs R$ 14,90 per month and adds unlimited accounts and shared budgets for couples.
Download Pocketmint on the App Store or Google Play.
---
2. Translate all seven parts into Brazilian Portuguese: 'você', Brazilian vocabulary and Brazilian spelling. European Portuguese is not acceptable.
3. Keep every figure and promise exactly. Leave Pocketmint, Pocketmint Plus, App Store and Google Play untranslated.
4. Publish the translation on a public page (GitHub Pages, Netlify, Vercel, Notion or WordPress.com).
5. Show your USDC wallet address on Base on the page.
6. Submit the page URL in this job's Sage submission form.
criteria: The page is in Brazilian Portuguese (você, Brazilian vocabulary and spelling), not European Portuguese
All seven parts are translated: headline, intro, budgets, goals, privacy, pricing and download line

Facts match the source: budget in 2 minutes, alert at 80%, data never sold, read-only access that can never move money, free forever for one bank account, Pocketmint Plus at R$ 14,90 per month with unlimited accounts and shared budgets for couples
Pocketmint, Pocketmint Plus, App Store and Google Play are left untranslated and no content is added
The page is publicly reachable and visibly shows the worker's USDC wallet address

submissions.body:
Camila Duarte · Tradução e localização
Início Portfólio Contato

Projeto: landing page do app Pocketmint · inglês → português do Brasil · novembro de 2026

Pocketmint — Seu dinheiro, organizado.

O Pocketmint se conecta às suas contas bancárias e classifica cada transação em categorias automaticamente, para você sempre saber para onde foi o seu dinheiro.

Crie um orçamento em 2 minutos.

Escolha um limite mensal para mercado, transporte ou o que você quiser. O Pocketmint avisa quando você já usou 80% de um orçamento.

Metas que te motivam.

Junte dinheiro para uma viagem, um notebook ou uma reserva de emergência. Arredonde cada compra no cartão e mande o troco para a sua meta.

Privacidade desde a origem.

Nunca vendemos seus dados. O login do seu banco é feito pelo nosso parceiro licenciado, e o Pocketmint só consegue ler as transações — ele nunca pode movimentar dinheiro.

Grátis para sempre com uma conta bancária.

O Pocketmint Plus custa R$ 14,90 por mês e libera contas ilimitadas e orçamentos compartilhados para casais.

Baixe o Pocketmint na App Store ou no Google Play.

Notas de localização

  • “Groceries” virou “mercado”, como o brasileiro fala no dia a dia (“gastei 600 no mercado”). “Supermercado” também funciona, mas soa mais formal.
  • “Laptop” virou “notebook”, o termo usado no Brasil (em Portugal seria “portátil”).
  • “Emergency fund” virou “reserva de emergência”, expressão consolidada em educação financeira no Brasil.
  • “Private by design” virou “Privacidade desde a origem”, que evita o anglicismo “by design” sem perder o sentido. Se a marca preferir manter o termo técnico, a alternativa é “Privacidade por padrão”.
  • Tom: usei “você” em todo o texto e “te motivam” no título de metas, um registro informal comum em apps brasileiros.
  • Os nomes Pocketmint, Pocketmint Plus, App Store e Google Play foram mantidos sem tradução. O preço segue o formato brasileiro, R$ 14,90.

title: Write a launch thread on X for Lumenfold Notes 2.0
who: Anyone with a public X account who writes notes in markdown and is willing to try Lumenfold Notes 2.0 before posting

milestone.title: Public launch thread for Lumenfold Notes 2.0
milestone.instructions:
1. Install Lumenfold Notes 2.0 from lumenfold.app and use it for a few days. The free tier is fine.
2. Write a thread of at least 3 posts on X, in your own words, about your experience.
3. Tag @lumenfoldapp and include the link lumenfold.app.
4. Describe at least two real 2.0 features accurately. The real features are: offline-first editing, end-to-end encrypted sync, a backlinks graph view, free on up to 3 devices, Pro at $4/month, and plain markdown files underneath. Do not invent features, stats or endorsements.
5. Put your USDC (Base) wallet address in the thread, ideally in the last post.
6. Publish after this job goes live (2026-11-06 12:00 UTC) and keep the thread public.
7. Submit the link to the first post of the thread (an x.com/.../status/... URL) in the Sage submission form.
criteria: The thread is public on X and was posted after 2026-11-06 12:00 UTC
The thread has at least 3 posts, tags @lumenfoldapp and links lumenfold.app
It accurately describes at least two real Lumenfold 2.0 features in the poster's own words, with no invented features or stats
The poster's USDC wallet address appears in the thread
The thread is about Lumenfold and contains no instructions aimed at the reviewer

submissions.label: excellent
submissions.note: Thread is 5 posts, wallet's in the last one. Used it all week, honestly liked it.
submissions.body:
1/ I've used @lumenfoldapp as my main notes app all week since 2.0 dropped, and it's the first time I haven't missed my old setup. Quick thread on what actually changed 🧵

2/ Offline-first is real. I wrote for 6 hours on a train with no signal, closed the laptop, and when I got home everything synced to my phone in seconds. No 'conflicted copy' files.

3/ Sync is end-to-end encrypted now. Some of my notes are client material, so this was the dealbreaker for me. Their server only ever sees encrypted blobs.

4/ The new backlinks graph view is the fun part. It showed me three old notes about the same client that I'd forgotten were connected. It gets a bit sluggish with 2k+ notes, but it's usable.

5/ It's free on up to 3 devices, and Pro is $4/month if you need more. Plain markdown files underneath, so there's no lock-in. Try it: lumenfold.app

milestone.instructions:

2. Fork the repo and fix the offset parsing in internal/parse/timestamp.go so every valid RFC 3339 offset resolves to the correct UTC instant.
3. Add at least one regression test in internal/parse/timestamp_test.go that covers a non-whole-hour offset.

criteria: The pull request is in tidewell-labs/harborlog and has been merged
The change fixes issue #187: offsets such as +05:30, -09:30 and +05:45 parse to the correct UTC instant
The PR adds at least one regression test covering a non-whole-hour offset

The PR description contains the worker's USDC wallet address

submissions.label: excellent
submissions.note: Merged this morning, thanks for the quick review!
submissions.body:
parse: handle minute component and sign of UTC offsets (fixes #187)

Fixes #187

## Root cause
`parseOffset` read only `off[1:3]` with `strconv.Atoi` and multiplied by 3600, so the minutes in `+05:30` were silently dropped. A second, related problem: for `-00:30` the sign was taken from the parsed hour (0), so the offset came out positive.

## Fix
- Parse hours and minutes separately and validate ranges (hours 0-14, minutes 0-59).
- Take the sign from the leading character instead of from the hour value.
- Accept both `+0530` and `+05:30`, matching what `time.RFC3339` and the old ISO fallback already allowed.

## Tests
Added a table-driven `TestParseOffset` in `internal/parse/timestamp_test.go`:

| input | expected UTC |
|---|---|
| 2026-11-07T10:00:00+05:30 | 04:30:00Z |
| 2026-11-07T10:00:00-09:30 | 19:30:00Z |
| 2026-11-07T10:00:00+05:45 | 04:15:00Z |
| 2026-11-07T10:00:00-00:30 | 10:30:00Z |
| 2026-11-07T10:00:00+14:00 | 2026-11-06T20:00:00Z |
| 2026-11-07T10:00:00Z | 10:00:00Z |

Plus two negative cases (`+05:60`, `+15:00`) that must return an error. `go test ./...` passes locally and CI is green.

I also ran the sample from the issue (`examples/kolkata.log`) through `harborlog tail --dry-run` and the output timestamps now match the source.

title: Stop duplicate autosave requests in Quillbase editor (issue #932)
who: Quillbase, a small team building an open-source collaborative Markdown editor in TypeScript/React

milestone.title: Merged PR fixing overlapping autosave requests and the 409 conflict banner
milestone.instructions:
1. Read issue #932 in quillbase/quill-editor: when a user types quickly, the editor fires several overlapping PUT /docs/:id requests, and the user sees a '409 Conflict: document version mismatch' banner.
2. Fix the autosave logic in src/autosave/useAutosave.ts so that at most one save is in flight at a time and the latest content is always saved.
3. Add a Vitest test that simulates rapid edits with fake timers and asserts that no two save requests overlap.
4. Open a PR against main that says 'Fixes #932', explains the root cause, and includes your Base USDC wallet address in the description.

criteria: The pull request is in quillbase/quill-editor and has been merged
The fix ensures only one autosave request is in flight at a time and the latest content is still saved (no 409 banner from overlapping saves)
The PR adds a Vitest test simulating rapid edits that asserts saves do not overlap
The PR description references #932 and explains the root cause

submissions.label: excellent
submissions.note: Merged by @hanna-q. Thanks for the clear repro steps in the issue.
submissions.body:
fix(autosave): single in-flight save with trailing flush (fixes #932)

Fixes #932

## Root cause
Two things combined:
1. `useAutosave` wrapped `debounce(save, 600)` in a `useCallback` whose deps included `doc`. Every keystroke changed `doc`, so a *new* debounced function (with its own timer) was created each render. Old timers were never cancelled, so typing 'hello' quickly scheduled up to 5 saves.
2. There was no in-flight guard, so those saves overlapped. Each one sent the same `baseVersion`. The second to land got a 409 from the server and triggered the conflict banner.

## Fix
- Keep the latest doc in a `useRef` and create the debounced function once (`useMemo` with stable deps). Cancel it on unmount.
- Add an `inFlight` ref. If a save is requested while one is running, mark `pending = true` instead of firing. When the running save resolves, update `baseVersion` from the response and, if pending, flush once more with the latest content.
- Errors clear `inFlight` so a failed save doesn't wedge autosave.

## Tests
`src/autosave/__tests__/useAutosave.test.ts` (Vitest + fake timers + a mocked `fetch` that resolves after 250 ms):
- 20 edits at 50 ms intervals: asserts max concurrent requests === 1 and that the final request body equals the last edit
- save in flight + new edit: asserts exactly one trailing save after the first resolves
- rejected save: asserts the next edit still triggers a save

Manually verified in the dev server: Network panel shows one PUT at a time, and the 409 banner no longer appears when hammering keys.

---

submissions.body:
Prevent overlapping autosaves

Fixes #932

Saves could overlap because nothing stopped a new PUT while the previous one was still pending. Both carried the same version and the second one 409'd.

title: Fix zero-decimal currency conversion in fernway-python (issue #305)

milestone.title: Merged PR that converts JPY/KRW and other zero-decimal currencies correctly
milestone.instructions:
1. Read issue #305 in fernway/fernway-python: Money.to_minor_units() always multiplies by 100, so a ¥500 charge is sent to the API as 50000 and the customer is charged ¥50,000.
2. Fix the conversion in fernway/money.py so each currency uses its ISO 4217 minor-unit exponent: zero-decimal currencies (at least JPY and KRW) use exponent 0, and two-decimal currencies such as USD and EUR still multiply by 100.
3. Add pytest regression tests covering JPY and at least one two-decimal currency.
4. Open a PR against main that says 'Fixes #305', explains the root cause, and includes your Base USDC wallet address in the description.

Zero-decimal currencies (at least JPY and KRW) convert with exponent 0, while two-decimal currencies such as USD/EUR still convert x100

submissions.label: excellent
submissions.note: Merged by @fernway-oss. Also handled 3-decimal currencies while I was in there.
submissions.body:
money: use ISO 4217 minor-unit exponent per currency (fixes #305)

Fixes #305

## Root cause
`Money.to_minor_units()` hard-coded `int(self.amount * 100)`. That's correct for USD/EUR/GBP but wrong for zero-decimal currencies (JPY, KRW, VND, CLP...). So `Money('500', 'JPY')` became `50000`. `from_minor_units()` had the mirror bug, and refunds read back as ¥5.

## Fix
- New `fernway/_currency.py` with an `EXPONENTS` map generated from the ISO 4217 list (exponent 0, 2 or 3), defaulting to 2 for unknown codes with a `logging.warning`.
- `to_minor_units()` now uses `Decimal.scaleb(exp)` and `quantize(Decimal(1), ROUND_HALF_EVEN)` instead of float multiplication. This also removes a 1-unit rounding error on values like 19.99 that I hit while testing.
- `from_minor_units()` uses the same exponent.
- Rejects fractional input for zero-decimal currencies (`Money('500.5', 'JPY')` raises `ValueError`) rather than silently rounding a customer's charge.

## Tests (`tests/test_money.py`)
Parametrized over:
- JPY 500 -> 500, KRW 12000 -> 12000
- USD 19.99 -> 1999, EUR 0.10 -> 10
- BHD 1.234 -> 1234, KWD 0.5 -> 500
- round-trip `from_minor_units(to_minor_units(x)) == x` for all of the above
- `ValueError` on fractional JPY

`pytest` passes on 3.9–3.13 in CI.

## Changelog
Added an entry under Unreleased > Fixed.

submissions.note: Merged by @brightpine-ola. Tested an export in Strava too.
submissions.body:
export: XML-escape all user text in GPX output (fixes #77)

Fixes #77

## Root cause
`buildGpx()` assembles the file with template literals, e.g. `<name>${track.name}</name>` and `<desc>${wp.note}</desc>`, so raw user text went straight into the XML. A single `&` makes the document ill-formed, and that's why Strava/Garmin reject the file.

## Fix
- New `src/export/xml.ts` with `escapeXml()` (handles `& < > " '`, with `&` replaced first) and `stripInvalidXmlChars()`, which removes control characters outside the XML 1.0 range (an emoji keyboard on some Android builds inserted U+0008 in a note I tested with).
- Applied to track `name`, `desc`, every `wpt` `name`/`desc`/`cmt`, and the `metadata/author` field.
- Attribute values (`creator`) also go through `escapeXml`.

## Tests
`src/export/__tests__/gpx.test.ts`:
- exports a track named `Fish & Chips <Loop>` with desc `Ola's 'easy' > 5km` and a waypoint note `He said "turn left" & then <right>`
- parses the result with `fast-xml-parser` (`XMLValidator.validate` must return `true`)
- asserts parsed name/desc/note equal the original strings
- snapshot of the escaped XML

Also validated a real exported file against the GPX 1.1 XSD with `xmllint --schema`, and uploaded it to Strava. The activity imported with the name intact.

Sending welcome emails in the background with Tidewell (no Redis required)

#node #postgres #tutorial #javascript

I run a small invoicing SaaS on one Postgres database and one Node app. When we added welcome emails, the usual advice was "put it on a queue", and the usual queue advice was "add Redis". I didn't want a second stateful service to back up and monitor for what is basically one email per signup. Tidewell keeps its jobs in Postgres tables, so the queue sits right next to my data and is already covered by the backups I have.

This is the setup I actually run in production. It includes the retry settings that saved us when our SMTP provider had a bad afternoon last month.

What we're building

When a user signs up, the HTTP handler creates the user row and enqueues a welcome job on an emails queue. A separate worker process picks up the job and sends the email with Nodemailer. If sending fails, Tidewell retries with exponential backoff. After the last attempt, the job stays in the table marked as failed so I can inspect it.

You'll need Node 18 or newer, Postgres 13 or newer, and a DATABASE_URL environment variable.

1. Install

npm install tidewell nodemailer

2. Create the Tidewell tables

npx tidewell migrate

This creates Tidewell's own tables in your database. I run it in my deploy script right after my app migrations. Running it twice is harmless, which matters when two deploys overlap.

3. Define the queue

// queue.js
import { Queue } from 'tidewell';

export const emailQueue = new Queue('emails', {
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
});

4. Enqueue from the signup route

// routes/signup.js
import { emailQueue } from '../queue.js';

app.post('/signup', async (req, res) => {
  const user = await db.users.create(req.body);
  await emailQueue.add('welcome', { userId: user.id });
  res.status(201).json({ id: user.id });
});

Notice that I pass only the userId, not the whole user object. The payload is stored as JSON. If someone fixes a typo in their name a second after signing up, I want the email to use the fresh value from the database, not a stale copy frozen into the job.

5. The worker

// worker.js
import { Worker } from 'tidewell';
import { sendWelcome } from './mailer.js';
import { db } from './db.js';

const worker = new Worker('emails', async (job) => {
  if (job.name !== 'welcome') return;
  const user = await db.users.find(job.data.userId);
  if (!user || user.welcomeSentAt) return; // see the idempotency note below
  await sendWelcome(user);
  await db.users.update(user.id, { welcomeSentAt: new Date() });
}, {
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  concurrency: 5,
});

worker.on('failed', (job, err) => {
  console.error(`job ${job.id} failed: ${err.message}`);
});

Start it with node worker.js. In production I run it as a second service from the same Docker image, just with a different command. A concurrency of 5 is plenty for us, because our SMTP provider rate-limits us long before Postgres would notice the load.

6. Retries and backoff

Email is exactly the kind of work that fails for boring, temporary reasons: timeouts, a 421 from the mail server, a DNS hiccup. So I set retries explicitly when I add the job:

await emailQueue.add('welcome', { userId: user.id }, {
  attempts: 5,
  backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 2000 },
});

attempts: 5 means the handler gets up to five tries in total. With exponential backoff and a 2000 ms base delay, the waits grow to roughly 2s, 4s, 8s and 16s. During the SMTP incident I mentioned, about forty welcome emails failed on their first attempt. All of them went out on the second or third try without anyone touching anything. If you'd rather retry at a steady pace, use { type: 'fixed', delay: 5000 } instead.

After the final attempt fails, Tidewell keeps the job along with its error message, which is handy for debugging. I have a tiny admin page that lists failed jobs from the last 24 hours.

The idempotency gotcha

Retries mean your handler can run more than once for the same job. Suppose the mail server accepted the message but the connection dropped before Nodemailer got the response. The job counts as failed, and you'll send the email again. That's why the worker above checks welcomeSentAt before sending and sets it afterwards. It isn't bulletproof, but it turned "occasional duplicate emails" into "basically never".

7. Trying it locally

I use a docker-compose file with Postgres and Mailpit. Then:

npx tidewell migrate
node worker.js &
curl -X POST localhost:3000/signup -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"email":"test@example.com","name":"Test"}'

With Mailpit as the SMTP server, the email shows up within a second. To test retries, I stop Mailpit, sign up, and watch the failed events in the worker log. Then I start Mailpit again and watch the job succeed on a later attempt.

Wrapping up

For a small team, keeping the queue in Postgres has meant one less thing to run. The full API reference is at tidewell.dev/docs. It also covers scheduling and priorities, which I didn't use here. If you spot something I've got wrong, tell me in the comments.

Resizing uploaded images with a Tidewell worker

Marco Díaz · Nov 10, 2026 · 6 min read

In our marketplace app, users upload profile photos and product images. For a long time we resized them inside the upload request. That worked until someone uploaded a 40 MB photo from a new phone and the request timed out. Moving the resize into a background job fixed it. We already run Postgres, so I tried Tidewell, which stores its jobs in Postgres instead of Redis.

This post shows the setup end to end. It's not fancy, but it has been running for a few weeks without problems.

Why not just do it in the request?

You can, if your images are small and your traffic is low. Image processing is CPU and memory heavy, though. It blocks the request, it ties up your web server, and if the process crashes halfway through, the work is simply lost. A queue gives you a record of what still needs doing, and you get retries for free.

Setup

Install Tidewell and sharp:

npm install tidewell sharp

Then create the tables Tidewell needs:

npx tidewell migrate

This adds Tidewell's tables to the database in DATABASE_URL. Run it once locally and add it to your deploy step.

The queue

// imageQueue.js
import { Queue } from 'tidewell';
export const imageQueue = new Queue('images', { connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

I keep the queue in its own file so both the API and the worker can import it.

Enqueue after upload

app.post('/images', upload.single('file'), async (req, res) => {
  const image = await db.images.insert({ originalKey: req.file.key, status: 'pending' });
  await imageQueue.add('thumbnail', { imageId: image.id, sizes: [128, 512, 1024] }, {
    attempts: 4,
    backoff: { type: 'fixed', delay: 3000 },
  });
  res.status(202).json({ id: image.id, status: 'pending' });
});

The upload still goes to S3 through multer-s3, but the request now returns 202 right away. The frontend polls the image status, which flips to ready when the worker is done.

The worker

// worker.js
import { Worker } from 'tidewell';
import sharp from 'sharp';

new Worker('images', async (job) => {
  const image = await db.images.find(job.data.imageId);
  const original = await s3.getObject(image.originalKey);
  for (const size of job.data.sizes) {
    const buf = await sharp(original).resize(size).webp().toBuffer();
    await s3.putObject(`thumbs/${image.id}/${size}.webp`, buf);
  }
  await db.images.update(image.id, { status: 'ready' });
}, { connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL, concurrency: 2 });

I set concurrency to 2 because sharp uses a lot of memory on large images and our worker box only has 1 GB of RAM. With 5, it got OOM-killed once.

Retries

S3 occasionally returns errors, and sometimes a file isn't readable for a moment right after upload. That's why the add call above includes retry options. attempts is the total number of tries, and backoff controls the wait between them. I used a fixed backoff of 3 seconds because the failures I see are short blips. Exponential backoff, like { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 }, makes more sense if you're calling a service that might be down for a while. When all four attempts fail, I mark the image as failed so the UI can show an error instead of spinning forever.

Running it

Locally I run the API and the worker in two terminals with node server.js and node worker.js. In production, pm2 runs the worker as a separate process on the same server.

Things I'd do differently

I'd make the thumbnail job idempotent from day one. A retry after a partial failure re-uploads every size, which is fine for S3 but wastes some time. Also, if your worker struggles, check the concurrency setting before you buy a bigger machine.

The docs are at https://tidewell.dev/docs. The quickstart is short, and the options page covers everything I used here.

Thanks for reading!

Generating PDF reports in the background with Tidewell

Dana Whitfield · 5 min read · Nov 11, 2026

Our analytics dashboard lets customers export a monthly PDF report. Generating it takes anywhere from 5 to 40 seconds, depending on how much data the account has. We used to generate it inline and hope the load balancer didn't time out first. It often did. This is part 1 of a short series on moving that work into a background queue with Tidewell, a job queue that keeps its jobs in Postgres.

Installing

Install the package along with the PDF library we use:

npm install tidewell pdfkit

Tidewell needs a few tables, which the CLI creates for you:

npx tidewell migrate

Make sure DATABASE_URL points at the right database first. I ran it against my staging database by accident the first time, which was harmless but confusing.

Creating the queue

import { Queue } from 'tidewell';
export const reports = new Queue('reports', { connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

Enqueueing an export

When the user clicks Export, we create a row in our report_exports table and add a job:

app.post('/exports', async (req, res) => {
  const exp = await db.exports.create({ accountId: req.user.accountId, month: req.body.month, status: 'queued' });
  await reports.add('monthly-pdf', { exportId: exp.id });
  res.status(202).json(exp);
});

The frontend shows a "Preparing your report" state and polls the export row every few seconds.

The worker

import { Worker } from 'tidewell';

new Worker('reports', async (job) => {
  const exp = await db.exports.find(job.data.exportId);
  const data = await loadMonthlyStats(exp.accountId, exp.month);
  const pdf = await renderReport(data);
  const key = await storage.upload(`exports/${exp.id}.pdf`, pdf);
  await db.exports.update(exp.id, { status: 'ready', fileKey: key });
}, { connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL, concurrency: 3 });

We run this worker on a separate, beefier instance, because rendering charts into PDFs is CPU-heavy. The web servers stay responsive, and exports no longer time out.

Results so far

Since the switch, the export button works reliably, even for our largest accounts. The p95 for the HTTP request dropped to under 100 ms, because all it does now is insert a row and a job. The actual report takes just as long as before, but nobody is staring at a spinner that ends in a 504.

What's next

Tidewell also supports retries and backoff, which matter a lot for us because our stats queries occasionally hit statement timeouts. I'll cover how we configured those, plus how we monitor failed jobs, in part 2. For now, if you want to read ahead, the docs are at tidewell.dev/docs.

If this was useful, give it a clap and follow for part 2.

Tidewell in 5 minutes

#node #queue

Need background jobs in Node but don't want Redis? Tidewell uses Postgres. Here's how to get going fast.

Install

npm install tidewell
npx tidewell migrate

Make a queue

import { Queue } from 'tidewell';
const q = new Queue('default', { connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });
await q.add('task', { hello: 'world' });

Make a worker

import { Worker } from 'tidewell';
new Worker('default', async (job) => {
  console.log(job.data);
}, { connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL });

That's it. Run your worker with node and you'll see the job data printed. Tidewell is a great choice for small teams because you already have Postgres, so there is nothing new to operate. It handles concurrency and lets you scale workers horizontally.

Why Postgres queues are underrated

Many developers reach for Redis or RabbitMQ by default, but for most apps the database you already have is fast enough. You get transactions, backups and one less service to monitor. Tidewell builds on that idea and gives you a clean API on top.

There are lots of things you can build with this: emails, reports, image processing, webhooks and more. The possibilities are endless once your heavy work is off the request path.

Check out the official docs for more: tidewell.dev/docs

J. Lambert About

Tidewell Quickstart Guide

J. Lambert · Nov 9, 2026 · 4 min read

Welcome to Tidewell! This guide will get you from zero to your first processed job in under five minutes. Tidewell is a durable job queue for Node.js that stores jobs in PostgreSQL, so you don't need to run any additional infrastructure.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 18 or later
  • PostgreSQL 13 or later
  • A connection string for your database

Installation

Install Tidewell from npm:

npm install tidewell

Next, run the migration command to create the tables Tidewell needs. This command is idempotent and safe to run on every deploy.

npx tidewell migrate

Create a queue

A queue is identified by its name. Producers and workers that use the same name share the same queue.

import { Queue } from 'tidewell';

const queue = new Queue('my-queue', {
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
});

Add a job

Jobs have a name and a JSON-serializable data payload.

await queue.add('my-job', { foo: 'bar' });

Process jobs

Create a Worker to process jobs from the queue. The handler receives the job and should return a promise. If the promise rejects, the job is marked as failed.

import { Worker } from 'tidewell';

const worker = new Worker('my-queue', async (job) => {
  console.log(job.name, job.data);
}, {
  connectionString: process.env.DATABASE_URL,
  concurrency: 1,
});

Retrying failed jobs

You can configure automatic retries when adding a job. See Retries and backoff for all options.

await queue.add('my-job', { foo: 'bar' }, {
  attempts: 3,
  backoff: { type: 'exponential', delay: 1000 },
});

Next steps

  • Configuring retries and backoff
  • Scheduling delayed jobs
  • Job priorities
  • Deploying workers

Crumb & Copper Notes Archive About Subscribe

I dropped Google Analytics for Lumora. Here's what changed.

Three weeks of privacy-friendly analytics on a tiny bakery website

Elena Sorrentino · Nov 14, 2026

For anyone new here: I run crumbandcopper.com, the preorder site for my two-person sourdough bakery. People reserve a weekly bread box online and pick it up on Saturdays. The site runs on Shopify, and until last month it used Google Analytics 4, which I never really understood and mostly opened out of guilt.

Two things pushed me to switch. First, my cookie banner. About half of visitors clicked "Reject", so GA4 was missing a huge chunk of traffic anyway. Second, I wanted one simple number: how many people who look at the bread box page actually reserve one. Lumora doesn't use cookies, so I could drop the banner for analytics, and it has custom events, so I could count reservations. I'm not a developer, so this is the non-developer version.

Step 1: Remove GA4

In Shopify, I went to Online Store → Preferences and deleted the Google Analytics tag. I also removed the Google channel app, which had been injecting its own tag. Check your theme for a leftover gtag snippet too. I found one in theme.liquid that I had pasted in years ago.

Step 2: Add the Lumora script

I created a site in the Lumora cloud dashboard for crumbandcopper.com. Then I pasted this into theme.liquid, just before the closing head tag:

<script defer src='https://cdn.lumora.io/l.js' data-site='crumbandcopper.com'></script>

I opened the site on my phone, and a visitor showed up in Lumora's realtime view within a few seconds. That was satisfying.

Step 3: Track reservations with a custom event

This part took me an evening. Shopify doesn't let you add scripts to the checkout pages on my plan, but it does let you add "additional scripts" to the order status page that customers see after paying. So the event fires there:

<script>
  window.addEventListener('load', function () {
    if (window.lumora) {
      lumora.track('preorder_placed', { box: '{{ line_items.first.product.handle }}' });
    }
  });
</script>

I also added a second event, lumora.track('pickup_slot_selected'), on the button where people choose their Saturday pickup time. I wanted to see whether people drop off at that step.

What I learned in three weeks

Lumora counts about 20% more visitors than GA4 did for the same weeks last year. I think most of that is simply people who used to reject the banner. Of everyone who viewed the bread box page, about 9% placed a preorder. About a third of the people who selected a pickup slot didn't finish, which told me the slot picker was confusing on mobile. I've since made the buttons bigger. It's too early to say if that helped.

The downsides (honestly)

  • No history. I couldn't bring my GA4 data over, so year-over-year comparisons now mean opening two different tools. I exported a few GA4 reports to a spreadsheet before cancelling.
  • Instagram traffic is muddy. Most of my visitors come from Instagram, and visits from the Instagram in-app browser often show up as "Direct". I started adding ?ref=ig to my bio link, which helps, but it's manual.
  • Ad blockers. My partner's laptop with uBlock Origin doesn't show up at all, so the numbers are still not complete, just less incomplete.
  • The checkout limitation above isn't Lumora's fault, but it means my "preorder" count depends on people landing on the order status page. A few don't.

Would I recommend it?

For a small shop that wants a handful of numbers it can actually read, yes. The dashboard fits on one screen, and I check it every Monday with coffee instead of avoiding it. If you need deep ad attribution, it's probably not for you.

DEV Community Search Log in

Kenji Watanabe · Posted on Nov 12 · 5 min read

Moving my side project from Matomo to self-hosted Lumora

#analytics #selfhosted #docker #privacy

I run regexcheat.dev, a small cheat sheet of regex patterns with a copy button next to each one. It gets a few hundred visitors a day, mostly from search. For two years I used self-hosted Matomo on a 5-dollar VPS. It worked, but it needed PHP and MySQL, and the archive cron job kept eating the server's memory. I wanted something lighter, so I tried self-hosted Lumora last week.

Running Lumora with Docker

I already had Docker on the VPS, so the whole setup is one compose file:

services:
  lumora:
    image: lumora/lumora
    ports:
      - '8800:8800'
    volumes:
      - lumora-data:/data
    restart: unless-stopped
volumes:
  lumora-data:

I put it behind Caddy at stats.regexcheat.dev so it has HTTPS. First run asks you to create an admin user, and then you add a site.

Adding the script

Since I self-host, I load the script from my own instance instead of the CDN. Otherwise it's the same tag:

<script defer src='https://stats.regexcheat.dev/l.js' data-site='regexcheat.dev'></script>

I removed the Matomo snippet in the same commit, so the two tools never overlapped. In hindsight I should have run both for a week to compare, but I didn't want two trackers on the page.

A custom event for the copy button

The thing I actually care about is which patterns people copy. Each pattern card has a copy button, and I added one line to its click handler:

copyBtn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  navigator.clipboard.writeText(pattern.source);
  lumora.track('copy_pattern', { pattern: pattern.id });
});

After a few days, the event breakdown shows that email validation and "match a URL" are copied far more than anything else. Lookbehind examples are viewed a lot but rarely copied, which I'm reading as "people are confused by these". I'm planning to rewrite that section.

Downsides I hit

The big one was my own fault, but it's worth mentioning. My first attempt used docker run without a volume. When I updated the image two days later, all my data was gone. Use the volume from the start.

Compared to Matomo, there's also less depth. There's no per-visitor path view, so I can't see the exact sequence of pages one person looked at. For this site I don't really need it, but if you rely on that, check first. Lumora also has no scheduled email reports that I could find, so I just open the dashboard.

Verdict

Memory use on the VPS went from around 600 MB with Matomo and MySQL to well under 150 MB, and I deleted a cron job I hated. For a small side project, that's a good trade.

Lumora Is the Analytics Tool I Wish I'd Found Sooner

Alex Fordham · 4 min read · Nov 13, 2026

I've been building websites for clients for about eight years, and for almost all of that time the analytics answer was the same: drop in Google Analytics and move on. Recently I moved one of my client sites, a local physiotherapy clinic, from GA4 to Lumora. I want to explain why I think more freelancers should look at it.

The problem with GA4 for small sites

GA4 is built for marketing teams. My clients are not marketing teams. They want to know how many people visited, where they came from and which pages they looked at. Every time I set up a GA4 property, I spend an hour on configuration and then another hour explaining the interface. Then there's the consent banner, which clients hate because it looks ugly, and which many visitors reject anyway.

Why Lumora

Lumora is cookieless, which in many cases means you don't need an analytics consent banner at all (talk to a lawyer for your own situation, as always). The dashboard is a single page. My client understood it in about two minutes, which has never happened with GA4.

Setup

Setup was honestly the easiest part of the whole project. After creating the site in the Lumora dashboard, I added one line to the site's header template:

<script defer src='https://cdn.lumora.io/l.js' data-site='client-domain.com'></script>

I deployed it, refreshed the page, and the visit showed up in the realtime view. That's really all there is to it. No tag manager, no data streams, no configuration wizard.

What the client sees

The clinic owner now checks the dashboard weekly. She mostly looks at the top pages (the "back pain" page is by far the most popular) and the referrers, where Google Maps turns out to be a huge source. That alone made her rethink how much time she spends on Facebook.

Privacy as a selling point

I've started mentioning privacy-friendly analytics in my proposals. Clients like being able to say on their site that they don't track visitors with cookies. It's a small thing, but it differentiates my offer from other local agencies.

Any downsides?

Honestly, I haven't found any yet. It does exactly what my clients need and nothing more. I'll be moving the rest of my client sites over the next few months.

Conclusion

If you build sites for small businesses, give Lumora a try on your next project. Your clients will thank you, and you'll spend less time explaining dashboards.

How I Switched From Google Analytics to Plausible

Samir Khoury · 5 min read · Nov 10, 2026

My blog, samirkhoury.net, is a mix of travel writing and photography. It has used Google Analytics since 2017. This month I finally replaced it with Plausible, a lightweight, privacy-friendly analytics tool. Here's how it went.

Why leave Google Analytics

GA4 is overkill for a personal blog. It also needs a consent banner in the EU, where a lot of my readers are, and the banner was hurting my bounce rate. I wanted something cookieless, simple, and ideally something I could pay for directly rather than paying with my readers' data.

Setting up Plausible

After signing up, you add your domain and Plausible gives you a snippet. My blog is on Hugo, so I added it to the head partial:

<script defer data-domain='samirkhoury.net' src='https://plausible.io/js/script.js'></script>

Deploy, visit your site, and you'll see yourself in the realtime counter.

Custom events

I wanted to know how many people download my free Lightroom presets. Plausible supports custom events through a small global function:

document.querySelector('#preset-download').addEventListener('click', () => {
  plausible('Preset Download', { props: { pack: 'nordic-winter' } });
});

You also have to register the goal in the Plausible dashboard before it shows up, which confused me for a while.

Downsides

Plausible's cloud plan isn't free, though it's cheap. Funnels and some features are only on higher plans. And of course you lose your GA history.

Verdict

I'm happy. The dashboard loads instantly, I deleted my cookie banner, and I finally know which posts people actually read to the end. If you're on the fence about leaving GA, just try it for a month.

The Quiet Stack Archive About

Three weeks with Lumora on a Ghost blog

Replacing GA4 on a small newsletter site, and what I miss

Rhea Mendonça · Nov 15, 2026

Besides this Substack, I run quietstack.blog, a Ghost site where I post longer tutorials on minimalist home-lab setups. It gets around 4,000 visits a month. Until October it ran Google Analytics 4 through Ghost's code injection. Three weeks ago I swapped it for Lumora's cloud plan. Here's exactly what I did.

Removing GA4

In Ghost, go to Settings → Code injection. My site header had the standard gtag snippet, plus a consent banner script I'd bolted on. I deleted both. If your theme hard-codes GA in default.hbs, you'll need to edit the theme too. Mine didn't.

Adding Lumora

In the Lumora dashboard I added quietstack.blog as a site and pasted the tag into the Site Header box under code injection:

<script defer src='https://cdn.lumora.io/l.js' data-site='quietstack.blog'></script>

I checked the realtime view from my phone on mobile data, and my visit showed up immediately.

Tracking newsletter signups

The number I care about is newsletter signups, and which part of the page they come from. Ghost's signup forms have a data-members-form attribute, so I added this to the Site Footer injection:

<script>
  document.querySelectorAll('[data-members-form]').forEach(function (form) {
    form.addEventListener('submit', function () {
      var source = form.closest('footer') ? 'footer' : 'inline';
      lumora.track('newsletter_signup', { source: source });
    });
  });
</script>

Three weeks in, about 70% of signups come from the inline form at the end of posts and only 30% from the footer. I'd assumed the opposite. I've since added the inline form to my older posts too.

What I don't love

There are no retention or cohort reports, so I can't tell how many readers come back the next month. GA4 technically had that, even if I rarely looked. The signup event also fires on submit, not on successful signup, so a typo'd email still counts. Ghost doesn't expose a clean success hook in code injection, and I haven't found a workaround. Finally, Lumora's referrer list groups some newsletter traffic under "Direct", because email clients strip referrers. I now add a ?ref=newsletter parameter to links in my emails.

So, is it worth it?

For me, yes. Removing the consent banner made the site feel calmer, and the dashboard answers the three questions I actually have. I miss cohort data a little, but not enough to go back.

Thanks for reading The Quiet Stack! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Tomasz Wójcik Blog Projects GitHub

Docs for a side project in 20 minutes: Quillstack + GitHub Pages

November 12, 2026 · 7 min read

I maintain tinyhttp-notes, a small collection of examples for a minimal Node HTTP framework. The README had grown to about 900 lines, and people kept asking where things were. I wanted real docs with a sidebar, without adopting a big framework. Quillstack turns a folder of Markdown into a static site, and the result is live here: tomaszwojcik.github.io/tinyhttp-notes. This is everything I did, including the one config line that cost me half an hour.

1. Install and scaffold

npm install -g @quillstack/cli
cd tinyhttp-notes
quill init docs

quill init docs creates a docs/ folder with an index.md, a sample page and a quill.config.yml. I keep the docs in the same repo as the code, so the folder lives next to src/.

Run the dev server and leave it open while you write:

cd docs
quill dev

It serves the site on http://localhost:4400 and reloads when you save a Markdown file.

2. Configure the title and sidebar

Here is my quill.config.yml:

title: tinyhttp notes
base: /tinyhttp-notes/
sidebar:
  - title: Getting started
    items:
      - index.md
      - install.md
  - title: Guides
    items:
      - guides/routing.md
      - guides/middleware.md
      - guides/errors.md

title shows in the header and the browser tab. The sidebar is a list of groups, and each group lists Markdown files relative to the docs folder. Pages that aren't in the sidebar still build. They just don't show up in the navigation, which I use for a hidden changelog page.

The base path gotcha

GitHub project pages are served from username.github.io/repo-name/, not from the root. Without base: /tinyhttp-notes/, the HTML loaded but every CSS and JS file returned 404. The page looked like it came from 1997. If you deploy to a custom domain or a username.github.io repo, leave base as /.

3. Build

quill build

This writes static files to docs/dist/. You can open dist/index.html locally, but links depend on the base path, so use quill dev for previewing. Add dist/ to .gitignore, because CI will build it.

4. Deploy with GitHub Actions

In the repo settings, under Pages, set Source to GitHub Actions. Then add .github/workflows/docs.yml:

name: Deploy docs
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ['docs/**']
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
concurrency:
  group: pages
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm install -g @quillstack/cli
      - run: quill build
        working-directory: docs
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: docs/dist
  deploy:
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

A few notes. The paths filter means code-only commits don't rebuild the docs. The pages: write and id-token: write permissions are required by deploy-pages, and the deploy fails with a vague error without them. I learned that the hard way. workflow_dispatch gives you a manual "Run workflow" button, which is handy the first time.

Push to main, and the Actions tab shows build, then deploy. The deploy job prints the page URL when it's done. My first successful run took 41 seconds end to end.

5. Result

The live site is at tomaszwojcik.github.io/tinyhttp-notes, with the sidebar exactly as configured above. The README is now 60 lines and links to the docs. Issues asking "where is X?" have mostly stopped.

Things I haven't tried yet: Quillstack's search plugin and versioned docs. I'll write those up if I get to them.

npm install -g @quillstack/cli

name: Pages

Aisha Bello Posts About

Moving my project docs to Quillstack on GitHub Pages

Nov 14, 2026 · 6 min read

My project pyfeeds, a small RSS parsing library, had its docs in a GitHub wiki. Wikis can't be reviewed in pull requests, so contributors never updated them. I moved everything into the repo as Markdown and used Quillstack to publish it. Live result: aishabello.github.io/pyfeeds.

Scaffolding

npm install -g @quillstack/cli
quill init docs
cd docs
quill dev

Preview runs on localhost:4400. I copied my wiki pages into the folder, renamed them to lowercase-with-dashes, and fixed the internal links. That took longer than everything else combined.

quill.config.yml

title: pyfeeds
base: /pyfeeds/
sidebar:
  - title: Start here
    items:
      - index.md
      - quickstart.md
  - title: Reference
    items:
      - reference/parse.md
      - reference/feed.md
      - reference/entry.md
  - title: Project
    items:
      - contributing.md
      - changelog.md

The title appears in the header. The sidebar groups map directly to the left navigation, in the order listed. I set base because a project site is served under the repository name, and without it the stylesheet paths break.

Building

quill build

Output lands in docs/dist/. I gitignored it, since CI builds it on every push.

The workflow

Under Settings → Pages, set the source to GitHub Actions, then add .github/workflows/docs.yml:

name: docs
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
permissions:
  contents: read
  pages: write
  id-token: write
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: 20
      - run: npm install -g @quillstack/cli
      - run: quill build
        working-directory: docs
      - uses: actions/upload-pages-artifact@v3
        with:
          path: docs/dist
  deploy:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    needs: build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: github-pages
      url: ${{ steps.deployment.outputs.page_url }}
    steps:
      - id: deployment
        uses: actions/deploy-pages@v4

The useful trick is the pull_request trigger combined with the if on the deploy job. Pull requests still run the build, so a broken sidebar entry or a bad Markdown file fails CI before merge, but only pushes to main actually deploy.

How it's going

In the two weeks since, two outside contributors have fixed docs in the same PR as their code changes. That never happened with the wiki. The site builds in about 30 seconds.

One complaint: when a sidebar item points to a file that doesn't exist, quill build prints a warning but still succeeds. I'd prefer it to fail CI. For now I grep the build log for "warning" in an extra step.

Comments and corrections welcome on the blog repo.

Hannah Lindqvist · Posted on Nov 12 · 9 min read

A tiny URL shortener with Axum and ferrokv

#rust #axum #tutorial #database

I wanted a self-contained URL shortener for our team chat: one binary, one data file, no Redis or Postgres to run. ferrokv is an embedded key-value store, so the database is just a file the process opens. In this post we build the whole thing: a POST endpoint that creates short codes, a GET endpoint that redirects, and a click counter that stays correct under concurrent requests.

Setup

cargo new shorty && cd shorty

Cargo.toml dependencies:

[dependencies]
axum = "0.7"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
ferrokv = "0.9"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
rand = "0.8"

Key layout

A key-value store has no tables, so I use key prefixes:

  • link:{code} stores the target URL as UTF-8 bytes
  • clicks:{code} stores a u64 counter as 8 little-endian bytes

The prefixes also mean db.scan_prefix(b"link:") can list every link later, which I use for a small admin page that isn't shown here.

The full code

use axum::{
    extract::{Path, State},
    http::StatusCode,
    response::Redirect,
    routing::{get, post},
    Json, Router,
};
use rand::{distributions::Alphanumeric, Rng};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::sync::Arc;

type Db = Arc<ferrokv::Db>;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct ShortenReq { url: String }

#[derive(Serialize)]
struct ShortenRes { code: String }

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let db = Arc::new(ferrokv::Db::open("links.fkv").expect("open db"));
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/shorten", post(shorten))
        .route("/:code", get(follow))
        .with_state(db);
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:3000").await.unwrap();
    println!("listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000");
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}

fn random_code() -> String {
    rand::thread_rng().sample_iter(&Alphanumeric).take(6).map(char::from).collect()
}

async fn shorten(
    State(db): State<Db>,
    Json(req): Json<ShortenReq>,
) -> Result<Json<ShortenRes>, StatusCode> {
    if !(req.url.starts_with("http://") || req.url.starts_with("https://")) {
        return Err(StatusCode::BAD_REQUEST);
    }
    loop {
        let code = random_code();
        let key = format!("link:{code}");
        let inserted = db
            .transaction(|tx| {
                if tx.get(key.as_bytes())?.is_some() {
                    return Ok(false); // collision, try another code
                }
                tx.put(key.as_bytes(), req.url.as_bytes())?;
                tx.put(format!("clicks:{code}").as_bytes(), &0u64.to_le_bytes())?;
                Ok(true)
            })
            .map_err(|_| StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)?;
        if inserted {
            return Ok(Json(ShortenRes { code }));
        }
    }
}

async fn follow(
    State(db): State<Db>,
    Path(code): Path<String>,
) -> Result<Redirect, StatusCode> {
    let url = db
        .transaction(|tx| {
            let Some(url) = tx.get(format!("link:{code}").as_bytes())? else {
                return Ok(None);
            };
            let ck = format!("clicks:{code}");
            let n = tx
                .get(ck.as_bytes())?
                .map(|b| u64::from_le_bytes(b.try_into().unwrap()))
                .unwrap_or(0);
            tx.put(ck.as_bytes(), &(n + 1).to_le_bytes())?;
            Ok(Some(url))
        })
        .map_err(|_| StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)?;
    match url {
        Some(u) => Ok(Redirect::temporary(&String::from_utf8_lossy(&u))),
        None => Err(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND),
    }
}

Why two transactions?

In shorten, the danger is a collision. Two requests could generate the same random code at the same moment. Each would get the key, see that it's empty, and put, and the second write would silently overwrite the first link. Inside db.transaction, the check and the write happen atomically, so the loser sees the key as taken and loops to try another code. With 62^6 possible codes, collisions are rare, but rare is not never.

In follow, the danger is a lost update on the counter. Without a transaction, two simultaneous clicks can both read 41 and both write 42. Doing the read-increment-write inside one transaction makes each click count exactly once. I tested this with hey -n 1000 -c 50 against one code, and the counter ended at exactly 1000. With plain get/put it ended at 913.

Run it

cargo run --release
   Compiling shorty v0.1.0
    Finished release [optimized] target(s)
     Running `target/release/shorty`
listening on http://127.0.0.1:3000

Try it with curl

$ curl -s -X POST localhost:3000/shorten \
    -H 'content-type: application/json' \
    -d '{"url":"https://www.rust-lang.org/learn"}'
{"code":"q7Lm2x"}

$ curl -i localhost:3000/q7Lm2x
HTTP/1.1 307 Temporary Redirect
location: https://www.rust-lang.org/learn
content-length: 0

$ curl -i localhost:3000/nope00
HTTP/1.1 404 Not Found
content-length: 0

$ curl -s -X POST localhost:3000/shorten -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"url":"ftp://x"}' -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n'
400

Caveats

ferrokv calls are synchronous, and I'm calling them directly inside async handlers. At team-chat scale that's fine, because each call takes microseconds. Under heavy load you'd want to wrap them in tokio::task::spawn_blocking so you don't stall the runtime. There's also no authentication on /shorten, so put it behind your VPN or add a token check before exposing it.

The ferrokv docs, including the transaction semantics I relied on here, are at ferrobase.dev/ferrokv.
