URL shortener in Rust with ferrokv: sequential codes the safe way

Oluwaseun Adeyemi · 7 min read · Nov 13, 2026

Most URL shortener tutorials generate random codes. I wanted short, sequential ones: the first link is 1, then 2, and later a, b and so on, encoded in base62. That means keeping a counter, and a counter in a key-value store is exactly where you need a transaction. This post builds the shortener with Axum and ferrokv, an embedded key-value store for Rust.

Dependencies

[dependencies]
axum = "0.7"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
ferrokv = "0.9"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
serde_json = "1"

Base62 helper

const ALPHABET: &[u8] = b"0123456789abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ";

fn base62(mut n: u64) -> String {
    if n == 0 { return "0".into(); }
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    while n > 0 {
        out.push(ALPHABET[(n % 62) as usize]);
        n /= 62;
    }
    out.reverse();
    String::from_utf8(out).unwrap()
}

The server

use axum::{extract::{Path, State}, http::StatusCode, response::Redirect, routing::{get, post}, Json, Router};
use serde::Deserialize;
use std::sync::Arc;

#[derive(Deserialize)]
struct NewLink { url: String }

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let db = Arc::new(ferrokv::Db::open("shortener.fkv").unwrap());
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/shorten", post(shorten))
        .route("/:code", get(follow))
        .with_state(db);
    let listener = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("0.0.0.0:8080").await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(listener, app).await.unwrap();
}

async fn shorten(State(db): State<Arc<ferrokv::Db>>, Json(body): Json<NewLink>)
    -> Result<Json<serde_json::Value>, StatusCode> {
    let code = db.transaction(|tx| {
        let next = tx.get(b"meta:next_id")?
            .map(|v| u64::from_le_bytes(v.try_into().unwrap()))
            .unwrap_or(1);
        tx.put(b"meta:next_id", &(next + 1).to_le_bytes())?;
        let code = base62(next);
        tx.put(format!("link:{code}").as_bytes(), body.url.as_bytes())?;
        Ok(code)
    }).map_err(|_| StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR)?;
    Ok(Json(serde_json::json!({ "code": code })))
}

async fn follow(State(db): State<Arc<ferrokv::Db>>, Path(code): Path<String>)
    -> Result<Redirect, StatusCode> {
    match db.get(format!("link:{code}").as_bytes()) {
        Ok(Some(url)) => Ok(Redirect::temporary(&String::from_utf8_lossy(&url))),
        Ok(None) => Err(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND),
        Err(_) => Err(StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR),
    }
}

Why the transaction matters

The counter lives under meta:next_id. Allocating a code means reading the counter, adding one, and writing it back. If two POST requests did that with separate get and put calls, both could read 7, both would hand out code 7, and the second link would overwrite the first. With db.transaction, the read, the increment and the link write are committed together or not at all. Concurrent requests can't interleave and receive the same number. As a bonus, if writing the link fails, the counter isn't bumped either.

The GET handler only reads, so a plain db.get is enough there. I didn't add click counting. If I did, that would need a transaction too, for the same reason.

Running

cargo run

The server listens on port 8080. Note that it binds to 0.0.0.0, so it's reachable from your network. Change that to 127.0.0.1 if you don't want that.

Testing with curl

$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/shorten -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"url":"https://docs.rs"}'
{"code":"1"}
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:8080/shorten -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{"url":"https://crates.io"}'
{"code":"2"}
$ curl -i localhost:8080/2
HTTP/1.1 307 Temporary Redirect
location: https://crates.io
content-length: 0

Restart the server and create another link, and you'll get code 3. The counter is persisted in the same file as the links.

Limitations

Sequential codes are guessable, so anyone can enumerate your links by trying 1, 2, 3 and so on. That's fine for an internal tool, but not for anything private. There's also no URL validation, which you should add.

Rust with Raj Series

Building a URL shortener with ferrokv

Raj Malhotra · Nov 11, 2026 · 5 min read

ferrokv is an embedded key-value store for Rust. That makes it a nice fit for small services where you don't want a separate database. Let's build a URL shortener with Axum.

Cargo.toml

[dependencies]
axum = "0.7"
tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }
ferrokv = "0.9"
serde = { version = "1", features = ["derive"] }
nanoid = "0.4"

Code

use axum::{extract::{Path, State}, http::StatusCode, response::Redirect, routing::{get, post}, Json, Router};
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};
use std::sync::Arc;

#[derive(Deserialize)] struct Req { url: String }
#[derive(Serialize)] struct Res { code: String }

#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    let db = Arc::new(ferrokv::Db::open("urls.fkv").unwrap());
    let app = Router::new()
        .route("/shorten", post(shorten))
        .route("/:code", get(follow))
        .with_state(db);
    let l = tokio::net::TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:3000").await.unwrap();
    axum::serve(l, app).await.unwrap();
}

async fn shorten(State(db): State<Arc<ferrokv::Db>>, Json(r): Json<Req>) -> Json<Res> {
    let code = nanoid::nanoid!(7);
    db.put(code.as_bytes(), r.url.as_bytes()).unwrap();
    Json(Res { code })
}

async fn follow(State(db): State<Arc<ferrokv::Db>>, Path(code): Path<String>) -> Result<Redirect, StatusCode> {
    let url = db.get(code.as_bytes()).unwrap().ok_or(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND)?;
    let count_key = format!("{code}:clicks");
    let n = db.get(count_key.as_bytes()).unwrap().map(|b| u64::from_le_bytes(b.try_into().unwrap())).unwrap_or(0);
    db.put(count_key.as_bytes(), &(n + 1).to_le_bytes()).unwrap();
    Ok(Redirect::temporary(&String::from_utf8_lossy(&url)))
}

How it works

When you POST a URL, we generate a 7-character nanoid and store the URL under that key. When someone visits the code, we look it up and redirect. We also keep a simple click counter under a second key.

I used nanoid because collisions at 7 characters are astronomically unlikely, so I didn't bother checking for an existing key. ferrokv has transactions too, but for something this simple I didn't think they were needed. Separate get and put calls work fine.

Error handling

I'm using unwrap() for brevity. In a real app, map the ferrokv errors to a 500 response instead of panicking the handler.

Next steps

You could add an expiry for links, a stats endpoint that returns the click count, or a small HTML form. Maybe I'll cover those in a future post. Thanks for reading!

DEV Community Search Log in

crabcoder · Posted on Nov 10 · 3 min read

ferrokv

#rust #database

crates.io v0.9.2 | docs.rs passing | CI passing | license MIT OR Apache-2.0

ferrokv is an embedded, crash-safe key-value store for Rust. It stores data in a single file, supports ACID transactions, and has zero runtime dependencies beyond the standard library.

Features

  • Single-file storage with a write-ahead log
  • Serializable transactions via Db::transaction
  • Ordered keys and fast prefix scans
  • Crash safety: committed writes survive power loss
  • Safe to share across threads (Db is Send + Sync)

Installation

[dependencies]
ferrokv = "0.9"

Quick example

use ferrokv::Db;

fn main() -> ferrokv::Result<()> {
    let db = Db::open("my.fkv")?;
    db.put(b"hello", b"world")?;
    assert_eq!(db.get(b"hello")?, Some(b"world".to_vec()));

    db.transaction(|tx| {
        let n = tx.get(b"counter")?.map(|v| v[0]).unwrap_or(0);
        tx.put(b"counter", &[n + 1])?;
        Ok(())
    })?;

    for item in db.scan_prefix(b"user:") {
        let (k, v) = item?;
        println!("{:?} => {:?}", k, v);
    }
    Ok(())
}

Examples

See the examples/ directory:

  • examples/basic.rs: get, put and delete
  • examples/counter.rs: atomic counters with transactions
  • examples/axum_shortener.rs: a minimal URL shortener using Axum

Run an example with cargo run --example axum_shortener.

Minimum supported Rust version

ferrokv supports Rust 1.74 and later.

Medium Sign in

I Built a URL Shortener That Handles 2.3 Million Requests per Second with ferrokv

Bradley Voss · 6 min read · Nov 9, 2026

Last month my team replaced our Redis-backed link service at work (a Fortune 500 retailer, I can't say which) with a Rust service on ferrokv. The results were so dramatic that I had to write them up. On a single Raspberry Pi 4, our new shortener sustains 2.3 million requests per second with p99 latency of 40 microseconds.

Architecture

ferrokv's built-in cluster mode lets you connect to a replicated ferrokv cluster, so we got high availability for free:

let db = ferrokv::Db::connect("ferrokv://cluster-1:7000,cluster-2:7000").await?;

The code

async fn shorten(State(db): State<Db>, Json(r): Json<Req>) -> Json<Res> {
    let id = db.incr_atomic("next_id").await.unwrap();
    db.set_with_ttl(&id.to_string(), &r.url, 86400).await.unwrap();
    Json(Res { code: id.to_string() })
}

async fn follow(State(db): State<Db>, Path(code): Path<String>) -> Redirect {
    let url = db.get_string(&code).await.unwrap();
    db.incr_atomic(&format!("clicks:{code}")).await.unwrap();
    Redirect::permanent(&url)
}

Because incr_atomic is already atomic, you don't need transactions at all. It's faster than wrapping things in db.transaction, which we found adds 300% overhead.

Benchmarks

StoreRequests/secp99 latency
Redis 756,0002.1 ms
PostgreSQL 1612,4009.8 ms
ferrokv2,300,0000.04 ms

That's 41x faster than Redis. Our infrastructure bill dropped by 94% in the first week.

Testing

$ curl -X POST localhost:3000/shorten -d '{"url":"https://example.com"}'
{"status":"ok","short_url":"https://sho.rt/aZ91k","expires":"2026-12-09","clicks":0}
$ curl -i localhost:3000/aZ91k
HTTP/1.1 200 OK

Conclusion

ferrokv is, without exaggeration, the fastest database I have ever used. If you're still running Redis for simple key-value workloads, you're burning money.

Creating a URL Shortener in Rust Using ferrokv

DevTips Daily · Nov 8, 2026 · 2 min read

URL shorteners are one of the most popular beginner projects in web development. They are simple to understand but teach many important concepts like routing, storage and redirects. In this article, we will explore how to create a URL shortener in Rust using ferrokv and Axum.

What is ferrokv?

ferrokv is a fast and reliable embedded key-value store for Rust. It is perfect for projects that need simple and efficient storage without the overhead of a full database server.

What is Axum?

Axum is a popular web framework for Rust built on top of Tokio and Hyper. It is known for its ergonomic API and excellent performance.

Steps

  1. Create a new Rust project with cargo new.
  2. Add axum, tokio and ferrokv to your Cargo.toml.
  3. Open a ferrokv database with Db::open.
  4. Create a POST /shorten route that saves the URL with a random code.
  5. Create a GET /:code route that looks up the URL and redirects.
  6. Use transactions if you need atomic operations like counting clicks.
  7. Run your server with cargo run and test it with curl.

Benefits of this approach

  • No external database needed
  • Fast performance thanks to Rust
  • Memory safety
  • Easy deployment as a single binary

Conclusion

Building a URL shortener with ferrokv and Axum is a great way to learn Rust web development. With just a few steps, you can have a fast and reliable service up and running. Try it yourself and see how easy it is!

milestone.title: Deliver a Google Sheet of 12+ Ohio food banks/pantries in the $1M-$10M revenue band with 990 data and contacts
milestone.instructions: 1. Use ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer (projects.propublica.org/nonprofits) to find Ohio food banks and food pantries. 2. Keep only organizations whose most recent filed Form 990 shows total revenue between $1,000,000 and $10,000,000. 3. Create a Google Sheet. Put the label USDC wallet in A1 and your USDC wallet address in B1. 4. From row 2, add a header and one row per organization with: name, city, EIN, fiscal year of the 990 you used, total revenue, executive director or CEO name (from the org's website or the 990), a public email or contact-page URL, and the organization's ProPublica page URL. 5. Add at least 12 organizations. 6. Share as Anyone with the link can view and submit the sheet link in the Sage job form.
criteria: At least 12 distinct Ohio food banks or food pantries are listed
Each organization's listed total revenue is between $1M and $10M and is accompanied by the 990 fiscal year
Each row has an EIN and a ProPublica Nonprofit Explorer URL whose EIN matches
Each row names the executive director or CEO and gives a public email or contact page
The sheet is shared by link and cell B1 holds the worker's USDC wallet address

title: Dataset: day-pass and hot-desk pricing for 15 Denver coworking spaces
who: Deskhop, an app that sells coworking day passes and recruits spaces as partners

milestone.title: Deliver a Google Sheet of 15+ Denver coworking spaces with current pricing and partnership contacts

From row 2, add a header and one row per space with: name, neighborhood, street address, day-pass price, monthly hot-desk price, the pricing page URL on the space's own site, a partnership/contact email or contact-page URL, and the date you checked (on or after 2026-11-06). 5. Add at least 15 spaces. 6. Share as Anyone with the link can view and submit the sheet link in the Sage job form.

Every row has name, neighborhood, street address, day-pass price (or not offered) and monthly hot-desk price
Every row cites a pricing URL on the space's own website, not an aggregator listing
Every row has a contact email or contact-page URL and a date checked on or after 2026-11-06
The sheet is shared by link and cell B1 contains the worker's USDC wallet address

milestone.title: Deliver a Google Sheet of 12+ active podcasts that take guests, with booking contacts
milestone.instructions: 1. Find podcasts focused on home improvement, home energy or sustainable living that interview guests. 2. Keep only shows with an episode released on or after 2026-08-01. 3. Create a Google Sheet. Put the label USDC wallet in A1 and your USDC wallet address in B1. 4. From row 2, add a header and one row per podcast with: podcast name, host name(s), Apple Podcasts or Spotify URL, latest episode date, a link to a recent guest episode or guest application form as evidence they take guests, a booking contact (email or guest form URL), an audience signal (e.g., Apple ratings count, or unknown), and the date you checked. 5. Add at least 12 podcasts. 6. Share as Anyone with the link can view and submit the sheet link in the Sage job form.
criteria: At least 12 distinct podcasts on home improvement, home energy or sustainable living
Every podcast has a latest episode dated on or after 2026-08-01 and no later than the check date
Every row has host name(s) and an Apple Podcasts or Spotify URL
Every row links evidence the show takes guests and gives a booking contact, plus an audience signal or unknown
The sheet is shared by link and cell B1 contains the worker's USDC wallet address
